docs.title: Beebo
docs.text:
A MeshCore node that tunes its own radio, changes role without a reflash, and reports to your phone.

Beebo adds four things to stock MeshCore: a repeater that tests its own settings against real traffic and keeps what works; one firmware image that is a companion or a repeater at your command; a feed in your app where the node reports its health and progress; and a monitor ring that records the packets it handles for analysis. It is a drop-in replacement for stock MeshCore v1.18.0 on the Heltec WiFi LoRa 32 V4 (headless): you flash it with the Web Flasher and keep the app you already have.

Get started in ten minutes See every feature

docs.title: What beebo adds
docs.text:
• A status feed in your channel list

    Two channels, beebo-status and beebo-cli, appear in your app. The node reports its boot, health, warnings and tuning progress in one, and answers commands in the other. The app's own CLI screen runs the same commands, with the words of the beebo command line. Switch role, fix the transmit power, check the node's health or start a trial without a computer.

    The phone feed

  • One firmware for both roles and all three transports

    Stock MeshCore ships a separate image for each role and for each companion transport. Beebo is one image that runs as a companion or a repeater, switched with settings board.node.role, and offers BLE, WiFi and USB together. Each role keeps its own keys, name and settings, so switching back restores them. A node that will never switch can run a single-role build, which frees 29 KB of RAM on a repeater.

    Roles

  • A repeater that tunes itself

    A trial runs your repeater's current setting against one alternative in alternating blocks on live traffic, scores both by what the node actually delivered, and keeps the better one. The default profile tests the front-end LNA, channel-activity detection, the retransmit delay and the route retry; the exhaustive profile tests twelve settings. Trials start with one command from the app. An older adaptive tuner, which proposes changes to the timing settings and can apply them live, is still available as an experimental feature, observe-only until you opt each setting in.

    Setting trials

  • Forwards that know if they were heard, and retry if not

    After a repeater forwards a flood, it listens for a neighbor to repeat it, and counts the forward as confirmed or not. A forward nobody echoed can be resent at a more robust LoRa coding rate (4/5 up to 4/8), up to three times. The same confirmed delivery is what the trials score, and beebo analyze retries reports how many retries were heard, the rescue rate and the extra airtime. Retry is off by default: turn it on only once you have verified a gain in service rates: every retry costs airtime, and it can load the mesh unnecessarily if repeaters do not deduplicate correctly.

    How a repeater routes

  • Stable connections, driven by state machines

    BLE and WiFi share one radio, so beebo models their link state explicitly, and runs a separate session state machine so that exactly one transport owns the app conversation. Both follow the connection and pairing handshakes of the protocols instead of working around them: a first BLE pairing waits for encryption so the app does not time out while you type the PIN, and a session waits for its last reply to leave the device before it closes. The failures that are left recover on their own: a reconnecting phone replaces its own stale TCP session, and a client that disappears is dropped within about 25 seconds.

    Connections

  • Full power: 27.3 dBm at the antenna, measured

    On the V4.3's KCT8103L amplifier the stock default radio.txpower of 10 delivers 22.3 dBm at the antenna connector. Beebo ships 18: 27.3 dBm, where the amplifier saturates, measured on the bench with a spectrum analyzer. RSSI and the noise floor are referred to the antenna connector, so readings from the LNA-on and LNA-off paths agree to within about 1 dB on the bench. Local transmit limits still apply: check them before you raise the power.

    Board analysis and RF experiments

  • Updates over the link you already have

    Over-the-air updates run over whichever transport you are connected on, stream straight to flash, take about 30 seconds over WiFi, and roll back automatically if the new image does not boot. A deployed repeater can have its WiFi switched on through the mesh for servicing and switched off again afterwards for low power operation.

    Firmware updates

  • A flight recorder on every node

    An always-on monitor ring records every packet's RSSI, SNR, noise floor and what the node did with it, plus its own tuning and setting changes. A health check turns the data into a verdict on delivery, battery and tuning. The beebo command line pulls, decodes, plots and analyzes it: why a forward was or was not echoed, the routes to each repeater, a console map of the nodes you hear, and a statistical comparison of LNA on and off on your own mesh traffic. A live debug stream shows the node's log and monitor records as they happen.

    Commands

  • RF engineering you can reproduce

    The V4.3's KCT8103L front end has no public datasheet, so beebo works the radio out from first principles and then measures it. The board analysis covers both signal chains: amplifier saturation, thermal noise floor, sensitivity, system noise figure, in-band saturation, out-of-band interference against the LNA, and the regulatory limits on radiated power. The RF experiments check it on the bench: the transmit power curve and compression point, and the system noise floor with and without an antenna and a bandpass filter. beebo measure repeats the noise-floor, bandwidth and transmit-power measurements on your own board, with a test carrier for your analyzer.

    Board analysis · RF experiments

  • A tool chest for fleets

    Named configurations pull a node's whole settings tree into a file, diff it against another node, and push back only what differs in a single flash write. Guided setup walks a new node through its name, role, region preset, admin password and WiFi. Recovery bundles save a node's keys and names. One alias per node picks its transport, beebo -i keeps a connection open, beebo run runs scripts, and a Python API, async or blocking, gives your own code the same operations. beebo admin runs status, telemetry and commands on a distant node over the mesh. Every setting is in one dotted-path tree, with help, valid ranges and choices on each, and the node's own console in the app answers the same names.

    Commands · Settings

  • Battery trend and millisecond time, built in

    The V4.3 has no charge-detect pin, so beebo infers the battery state (charging, discharging, charged, plugged) from how the voltage moves, and the ADC can be calibrated against a voltmeter. Every connection syncs the clock to the millisecond with a round-trip-corrected probe, and the clock survives a full power cycle.

    Battery and clock

  • ESP-IDF 5 and built-in debugging

    Built on ESP-IDF 5.5 and Arduino-ESP32 3.3 through pioarduino, not the IDF 4.4 platform stock uses. The move brings the upstream fix for the native USB transmit hang, which was its reason, 106 kB of free internal heap with WiFi up (82 kB before), and a trimmed BLE stack that leaves about 59 KB of internal RAM free after it starts (about 20 KB with the stock IDF libraries). A continuous live debug stream and JTAG debugging are built in.

    Feature reference

  • Tested on real hardware

    Features are built test-first: native firmware unit tests, thousands of command-line tests, and hardware-in-the-loop tests on real boards for everything that crosses the protocol, so a feature is not done until it works on a node and not only against a mock. Every image is versioned from a single source.

    Platform and quality

  • A drop-in that follows upstream

    Beebo speaks the standard MeshCore companion protocol, so existing apps work unchanged. A board that already runs v1.18.0 keeps its settings and starts in the role it had. Upstream releases are merged file by file, and upstream fixes are reviewed against beebo's own code.

    How beebo follows upstream

docs.text:
1. Quick Start: flash, connect, read the feed, switch a role, run a trial. About ten minutes, phone only.
  2. Using beebo: roles, the phone feed, connections, troubleshooting.
  3. Tuning: setting trials and the performance tuning guide behind them.
  4. Command line: the beebo command line for scripting, fleets and analysis, and updating a node.

For MeshCore itself (protocol, apps, packet formats) see the MeshCore documentation. For a mistake, a missing piece, a bug or an idea, see Support and Feature Requests.

docs.title: The Adaptive Tuner
docs.text: The adaptive tuner is the older, experimental optimizer. For deciding single settings use setting trials.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
$ beebo settings repeater.routing.tuning.adaptive.enabled on      # start observe-only logging
$ beebo monitor capture tuning on                # make sure tuning records are captured
$ beebo monitor decode -k adaptive --limit 20      # see recent proposals
$ beebo monitor pull                           # pull a full capture for offline analysis
$ beebo monitor decode --save                  # convert the pulled capture for `analyze`
$ beebo analyze tuning indicators --window 5  # per-window diagnostics (delivery proxy, TX success, ...)
$ beebo settings repeater.routing.tuning.adaptive.applied 1        # promote rx_delay_base (bit 0) to live actuation

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: AdaptiveController (src/helpers/AdaptiveController.h) runs one small multi-choice bandit (UCB1) per parameter, round-robin — every measurement window it advances exactly one parameter's bandit by one tick, trying a neighboring value (-step/stay/+step) and recording the objective score observed just before the change. A full cycle through all 6 parameters (rx_delay_base, tx_delay_factor, direct_tx_delay_factor, agc_reset_interval, interference_threshold, airtime_factor) takes six windows.

docs.title: Decision windows
docs.text: The optimizer judges each change by the measurement window that follows it. A window closes once the node has heard at least one packet and has run at least tuning.adaptive.window.min_s seconds (default 300); if it heard nothing at all by tuning.adaptive.window.max_s (default 3600) it counts as insufficient data and nothing is changed. A window with real reception but few or no actual forwards still closes and counts — for a repeater, failing to convert reception into forwards is itself the service quality being measured, not noise to discard. Busy nodes therefore close windows in minutes and quiet ones take longer. A change is rolled back if the next window's confirm ratio falls well below the one before it or the packet pool ran close to full; each window is logged as a MON_EVAL record (beebo monitor decode -k eval). These settings are RAM-only and reset on reboot.

docs.title: Observe-only by default
docs.text: Every decision is logged as a MON_ADAPTIVE MonRing record (beebo monitor decode -k adaptive) regardless of whether anything was actually changed — old_value, proposed_value, the reward that preceded the decision, and whether it was applied. This is deliberate: the reward signal and bandit behavior can (and should) be validated against real traffic before trusting the optimizer to change anything live. Turn it on with beebo settings repeater.routing.tuning.adaptive.enabled on.

docs.title: Live actuation, per parameter
docs.text: A separate bitmask (repeater.routing.tuning.adaptive.applied) promotes individual parameters from observe-only to actually writing the value — through the exact same setter path a human changing that setting by hand would use, so a live-applied change can't drift from manual behavior. Every other parameter stays observe-only regardless. Every current parameter, including interference_threshold, can be live-actuated this way — interference_threshold's getter is not hardcoded to 0 as it is upstream (a stale leftover from before hardware CAD superseded it, which silently discards any value written to it): beebo reads the stored value.

docs.title: Automatic rollback
docs.text: After a live change, the parameter's next visit compares the freshly-observed confirm ratio against the one recorded just before that change. A drop of more than 15 percentage points reverts to the most recently confirmed-good value (not the very first value the parameter ever had) instead of trying a new step — a live-tuned parameter can regress, but it won't be left in a state that measurably hurt delivery.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text: Analysis works on the data the node records. beebo rxlog --compare compares the LNA on and off live over the companion link. beebo analyze reads a pulled monitor dataset offline and never connects to a device. For the health verdict of the live node see Health Check. Every command and option is listed in the CLI Reference.

docs.title: In-Field LNA Comparison
docs.text:
The RX signal chain analysis in Board Analysis and the bench measurements in RF Experiments estimate the KCT8103L LNA's tradeoff (<role>.fem.rxgain) from datasheet parameters and lab equipment — a spectrum analyzer, a 50-ohm stub, a bandpass filter. That answers the question for one bench, once. It doesn't answer it for a specific deployment site, where the real question is whether the local RF environment is quiet enough for the LNA's ~6 dB of sensitivity over bypass to be worth its ~17 dB of reduced out-of-band tolerance — and that can only really be judged with the antenna connected, in place, listening to real traffic.

beebo rxlog --compare does exactly that, entirely over the companion link, with the chassis closed and no bench equipment at all:

$ gatto rxlog --compare

It listens to the node's live RX feed and automatically toggles the live role's fem.rxgain on/off every --interval packets (default 30) while packets keep arriving from ordinary mesh traffic — no synthetic test source is generated or required. Toggling by packet count rather than by a timer keeps the on/off sample sizes balanced regardless of how much traffic the node is actually seeing at that moment. Every captured packet is tagged with whichever LNA state was active when it arrived, and the run keeps cycling until at least 4 toggle cycles have completed and both groups' mean SNR has converged to --precision (95% CI half-width, default ±0.5 dB) — so a busy node with a lot of traffic finishes fast, and a quiet one just keeps sampling until the numbers are trustworthy. --duration forces a fixed window instead, and Ctrl-C stops it early at any point. Either way, the node's original LNA state is always restored automatically on exit.

At the end it reports, both on the console and (unless --no-csv) to a CSV + markdown sidecar under ~/.beebo/nodes/<node>/data/:

  • a per-metric on/off comparison table (SNR/RSSI/noise floor — mean, σ, min, max, median for each LNA state),
  • a Welch's t-test on SNR/RSSI between the two groups, with an explicit p < 0.05 significance verdict, so a difference can be told apart from ordinary traffic/propagation drift rather than eyeballed off two numbers,
  • a packets-per-minute reception rate for each LNA state, with a plain-language verdict — a lower LNA-on rate is flagged as the front-end saturating and dropping packets, a higher one as the LNA genuinely helping.
A 4-minute run on a repeater (68 packets, the LNA toggled every 20 packets): the on and off groups differ in RSSI and noise but not significantly in SNR, and the LNA-on state heard fewer packets a minute. A run this short is only an illustration; the default stops when the SNR means converge. Neighbor names are replaced by numbers

Because interleaving many short on/off windows over the same live session cancels out drift far better than one long bench sweep with the LNA on followed by one with it off, this in-field comparison is arguably a more representative answer for a given site than the bench numbers in RF Experiments — it is measuring the real deployment's actual RF environment and actual traffic pattern, not a lab bench's.

A saved CSV can be re-analyzed later without a device connection:

$ beebo rxlog --analyze ~/.beebo/nodes/gatto/data/rxlog_tx18_lna_compare_20260722-091500.csv

docs.title: Retrospective Analysis (beebo analyze)
docs.text:
beebo analyze reads locally pulled data only, never a device. --dir names the root (default ~/.beebo/nodes, the layout monitor decode --save writes to). Run through a node alias (for example gatto analyze list) it only sees that node's own data; the bare beebo sees every node. A data set can be named right after analyze, before the report, so a command reads as English: gatto analyze trials rate (a monitor pull --to trials file, a day file such as monring_2026-09-28, or a saved set's tag), or given as a FILE after the report (a path relative to --dir; a bare name such as trials or trials.bin that is not a file there is looked up by name, so gatto analyze rate trials works too). Subcommands:

Command Reports analyze list The pulled monitor sets (per-profile CSV/JSON and the raw monring_<date>.bin days and --to named files) with basic stats analyze link-quality Per-neighbor SNR/RSSI summary and a mean ± std chart per metric; --hash/--name for one neighbor: statistics and distribution charts, --trend adds hourly charts. Optional SVG chart with --chart analyze neighbors Neighbor activity: node and packet counts and a packets-per-neighbor chart; --hourly adds packets by hour of day analyze noise Noise-floor statistics, distribution histogram and hourly trend analyze packets Search and filter individual rx/tx packets analyze rate RX/TX packets per minute: statistics and a time-series chart analyze latency Checks the time limits the node judges packets with against the captured traffic. A packet is duplicated when we already heard it; one we route is echoed when a neighbor relays it and we hear that relay within the echo window of our transmission. A Limits table gives the echo window (the firmware logs it with each verdict, 4500 ms + 6 x airtime), seen_window (a settings event in the capture, else the newest saved config of the alias, else the firmware default, or --seen-window SECONDS as a what-if) and --max-latency (default 100 s, a duplicate later than this after the first reception is a reused hash). Packet Statistics shows received (individual, duplicated, excluded as hash reuse) and routed packets: a 0-hop echo (the neighbor's own relay, heard straight from it), an n-hop echo (relayed on by more repeaters first) and a duplicate by another route, all in the echo window; any duplicate heard after the window within seen_window (outside window); and not heard, a neighbor stays silent when it already has the packet. The echoes are told from other routes by the RX record's path flags (monitor format 4, exact; an older capture falls back to the hop count, an upper bound). A duplicated section and an echoes section each give the delay table (n, p50, p90, p99, max in ms), a histogram with the limits as x ticks (the echo histogram stacks the 0-hop echoes under the n-hop ones), and a check table with a check mark or a cross: seen_window covers 99.9% of the duplicates and the dedup table holds a hash for it; the echo window covers 99% of the echoes, the echo ring holds a packet for it and never overflowed, with the recommended value and the fit of base + factor x airtime. A raw monring .bin carries the echo events; any other set gives the duplicated packets only. --detail adds the echo window table, the hop tables, the duplicate report and the slowest pairs; --json prints it as JSON. analyze timing and analyze dup-latency still work, one half each analyze routing Why a packet we route is, or is not, echoed by a neighbor, from the RX and TX records and the echo verdicts of a raw monring .bin. A table counts the routed packets by scenario: a 0-hop echo, an n-hop echo, another route (a neighbor sent its own copy), an echo after the window, and silence (a neighbor had already relayed it before our send, or no duplicate was heard at all: neighbors may hold it from repeaters we do not hear). A second table tests whether a duplicate heard before our send keeps the neighbors silent. One typical packet of each scenario is drawn as a sequence of events with the neighbor, the hop count and the time from the first reception. The last-hop neighbors are ranked (heard, first, duplicates, SNR, duplicates delivered ahead of our sends, 0-hop echoes of ours; --top N, 0 for all) with the hops of the first receptions. The RX record names the last hop only, so the topology is the direct neighbors; an older capture without the path flags judges echoes by hop count. --seen-window, --max-latency, --hours, --json analyze paths The routes to repeaters and the links between them, from the RX path records of a raw monring .bin captured with monitor capture path on (an RX record then holds the last three hops of its path, one byte each, instead of the last hop's identity). For each repeater seen in a path, the chains of hops from us to it, with the packets that took each, their share and the SNR of the last hop; and the repeater links ranked (the second heard the first). With 2- and 3-byte hashes two repeaters can share a byte. --top N (0 for all), --hours, --json analyze mesh A console map of the nodes we hear and how their packets connect them, from a raw monring .bin and the neighbors.json positions (beebo neighbors pull): ours, and the ones the neighbors advertise. A schematic that fills the console, not to scale: the nodes keep their true west-to-east and north-to-south order (a node west of another is drawn west of it, one north of another north of it) and are spread by rank, not by distance; each carries its number and name. Each last-hop neighbor is joined to us by a link and, on a capture with rx path mode (monitor capture path on), the busiest links between the other repeaters of the paths are added, drawn as ○ node. A link is colored by its packets on a log scale, blue for the least to red for the most, with the scale under the map. A table lists the numbers: name, heard / first / duplicates, median SNR, echoes of ours, links, distance and compass direction; nodes with no position stay in the table only. --top N (neighbors, default 8), --links N (repeater links, default 6, 0 for none), --width COLS, --height ROWS, --hours, --json analyze retries Route retry outcome: forwards retried after an echo timeout, retries heard (echoed), unanswered or pending, the rescue rate and the extra airtime; analyze packets shows each retry in its Try column (retry number and coding rate) analyze tuning indicators The tuning trial indicators per window (Score, Delivered and per minute, TX Dispatched, Received, RX Invalid, RX Errors, Nbr Heard, Nbr Marginal, Pool Busy, CAD Busy, Noise dBm; the counts are per minute, as the table caption says; --window MINUTES sets the window, default 5, minimum 1): statistics and one chart each. Names after the command pick the charts (indicators received delivered; an indicator selects the chart it is drawn in, so dispatched shows Routed; case and spaces ignored, a unique part of the name is enough); tuning indicator NAME analyzes one indicator's dips in depth. Score is the trial objective computed for the window, with the objective weights the capture recorded. The event-based rows need a raw .bin set; RX Errors, Pool Busy and CAD Busy come from the route_stats event that firmware logs every minute. --score NAME=WEIGHT,... re-scores the windows with other score weights. analyze tuning indicator INDICATOR Looks into one indicator of the table above (name by label or row key, case and spaces ignored). Dips, or bursts where high is bad (RX Invalid, RX Errors, Nbr Marginal, Pool Busy, CAD Busy, Noise dBm): a run of windows more than K robust deviations (MAD) from the median, --sensitivity K (default 3), listed with start, duration, depth. Every window is shown; each dip is tagged load when Received in it is under half its median (over double for burst indicators: more traffic explains it) or degraded when Received was normal, in a chart legend, a Cause column and a summary line with the correlation to Received. Suspects and nearby changes cover the degraded dips only. A median under 5 events per window warns to use a larger --window. Service level (share of time in that state, longest run, mean of the worst 5%, gaps without data), level shifts, repeat period, spacing between dips (when at least 5 and evenly spaced), and time-of-day. Suspects, ranked and not proven: other indicators inside versus outside the dips with their best lagged correlation (an indicator's own components are left out), the load (Received) at which it starts to worsen, and setting changes, trial starts and fault events near the dips (raw .bin set). indicators NAME is accepted as a shorthand analyze tuning trial One setting trial (a combined trial lists its participants), or a sequence (Trial Reference), with a chart of each pair's gain and the decision interval at every look analyze tuning phi How noisy the paired trial differences are, pooled over every finished trial (Trial Reference) analyze tuning effect The indicators split by setting assignment over the whole capture, with grouped bars per assignment

docs.title: Example: the mesh map
docs.text:
analyze mesh draws the nodes a repeater hears as a console map, from a day of its own capture. The nodes keep their west-to-east and north-to-south order, each link is colored by the packets it carried, and the table under the map gives the counts: packets heard, first copies and duplicates, median SNR, echoes of our sends, and the distance and direction when the node has a position. Node names are replaced by numbers here.

beebo analyze mesh on a day of a repeater's capture: eight neighbors, the busiest (Nbr-1) heard 9,372 times

The reports share one shape. After Analyzing <file> comes a Data <start> to <end> line (with the set's full span when --hours narrows it), then statistics (mean, median, P95, peak and when it happened, plus span, idle share and the longest gap for windowed reports), then charts. Charts plot every window: nothing is reduced to fit the terminal, so a chart always shows the same windows the statistics are computed on, and --window zooms. Idle stretches of an hour or more show as a gap in a time chart, not as zero traffic. --table adds the per-row table that a chart replaces (rate, noise, tuning indicators, link-quality in detail mode, neighbors --hourly), and --json prints raw rows where a report has it. Time axes are labeled on round clock times, with the date only on the first tick and where the day changes; y axes use round steps (multiples of 1, 2, 2.5 or 5 times a power of ten) on equally spaced rows. --style (before the report name, like --dir) picks the chart style: line markers braille (default), fhd, hd, sd, dot, unjoined points sample (+) or star (*), or vertical bar; bars average consecutive windows when there are more windows than terminal columns. Charts need plotext; without it the report falls back to its tables.

beebo monitor is a separate, always-on background capture (see Diagnostics and Protocol Additions) — it isn't itself an A/B tool, but if fem.rxgain happens to be toggled manually while it's running, beebo monitor decode --save splits the downloaded ring into one directory per distinct radio profile it saw (including the lna state), and beebo analyze's report commands accept --lna on/--lna off filters to retroactively split any of its reports by LNA state:

$ beebo analyze link-quality --lna on
$ beebo analyze link-quality --lna off

This is a manual, eyeball comparison — run the same report twice and compare the printed tables — not the automated statistical verdict rxlog --compare gives; it's most useful for mining LNA on/off data out of a long background capture that was already running for other reasons, rather than as the primary tool for the LNA decision itself.

docs.title: Python API Reference
docs.text: The public methods and properties of beebo.api and beebo.trials, generated from the classes themselves. For an introduction and examples see Python API. SyncNode has the same operations as Node, blocking instead of async.

docs.title: beebo.api.Node
docs.text:
A single device connection, resolved explicitly -- never from sys.argv[0]/the currently-invoked CLI alias.

  • await advert(self, flood: bool = False) -> None: Send a direct (default) or flood advert. Raises BeeboDeviceError on a device-level ERROR reply.
  • await battery(self) -> dict: Battery voltage/state/presence as plain data -- see node.py's _fetch_battery_data for the returned keys. Raises BeeboDeviceError on a device-level failure.
  • await channel_get(self, channel) -> dict: One channel by slot index or name -- see channels.py.
  • await channel_remove(self, channel) -> int: Empty a channel's slot (channels.json keeps the entry); returns the slot index.
  • await channel_send(self, channel, text: str, *, max_hops: int | None = None) -> int: Send a flood group message; max_hops (1-21, None or 0 = no cap) limits how many repeaters forward it. Returns the slot index.
  • await channel_set(self, idx: int, name: str, secret: str | None = None, *, random: bool = False) -> dict: Write slot idx and record it in <root>/mesh/channels.json. secret is 32 hex digits; random generates one; a '#name' channel derives its own (give neither). Returns {"idx", "name", "secret"}. Raises BeeboError on a bad or conflicting secret.
  • await channels_list(self) -> list: The node's configured channels as [{"idx", "name", "secret" (hex)}] -- see channels.py's list_channels. Companion role only.
  • await channels_pull(self) -> list: Record the node's channels into channels.json; returns the names.
  • await channels_push(self) -> dict: Write channels.json to the node; returns {name: slot index}.
  • await connect(self, *, node: str | None = None, ble: str | None = None, tcp: str | None = None, usb: str | None = None, raw: bool | None = None) -> 'Node': Open the connection, optionally choosing the target here.
  • await disconnect(self) -> None: Explicitly close the connection -- the disconnect() counterpart to connect(). A no-op if not connected (mirrors release_cmd's tolerance of "nothing to release").
  • await download_messages(self, *, limit: int = 0) -> list: Drain every pending message off the node -- see messages.py's drain_messages for the returned row shape. limit (0 = whole backlog) stops early after that many messages.
  • await get(self, path: str) -> str: Value of the setting at a dotted path, e.g. await node.get("repeater.fem.rxgain") -> "on". Raises BeeboError for an unknown path or a group.
  • lookup_contact(self, token: str | None) -> tuple: (contact, matches) for token against the local contacts.json cache -- see contacts.py's lookup_contact. Synchronous: reads only the local cache file, no device round trip.
  • mc (property): The underlying meshcore.MeshCore (companion) or beebo.common_link.CommonLink (repeater/raw text) connection -- pass this to any command module's _foo(mc, ...) helper.
  • await monitor_clear(self) -> None: Clear the monitoring ring. Raises BeeboDeviceError on failure.
  • await monitor_pull(self, incremental: bool = True, clear: bool = False, to: str | None = None) -> list: Pull the monitoring ring into this node's local dataset (what monitor pull does) and return every monring_<date>.bin file there, oldest first -- hand them to Trial.from_files(). incremental=False re-fetches everything; clear=True empties the ring afterwards. to=NAME appends to NAME.bin instead (monitor pull --to) and returns just that file.
  • await monitor_stats(self) -> dict | None: Raw MonRing ring header -- occupancy, capture state, start/end/ per-kind record counts -- see monitor.py's _get_header/ _get_header_repeater for the returned dict's keys (they differ slightly between companion/multi_role and repeater). Returns None if the ring itself isn't available (older firmware).
  • await monitor_status(self) -> dict | None: Health/service counters as plain data -- see monitor.py's get_monitor_status_data for the returned dict's shape. Returns None if the ring itself isn't available.
  • name (property): The live device's board.node.name, from the connect handshake.
  • await reboot(self) -> None: Reboot the device and sync its clock. No reply either way (the device restarts immediately) -- returns once the command is sent, not once the device is back up.
  • await refresh_contacts(self) -> dict: Re-query the node's contact list and merge into the local contacts.json cache; returns the merged cache dict -- see contacts.py's refresh_cache. Already plain data-in/data-out, no Rich/console output, so no error-path conversion was needed here.
  • await region_define_tree(self, segments: str) -> str | None: Bulk-define a region subtree in one round trip -- see region.py's define_region_tree for the segment syntax.
  • await region_put(self, name: str, parent: str = '') -> None: Define a region, or re-parent it if it already exists.
  • await region_remove(self, name: str) -> None: Remove a region -- must have no child regions.
  • await region_save(self) -> None: Explicitly persist the region tree to flash.
  • await region_set_flood(self, name: str, allow: bool) -> None: Allow (allow=True) or deny (allow=False) flood traffic tagged with this region.
  • await region_tree(self) -> tuple: (raw export text, default_scope) for the repeater's named- region registry -- see region.py's get_region_tree_data.
  • role (property): 'companion' or 'repeater', resolved the same way connect.py's own identity check does -- None if the connection is a CommonLink (a CommonLink only ever reaches the live repeater role, but it doesn't carry adv_type to derive that from generically) or the adv_type is unrecognized.
  • await send_message(self, target: str, text: str, *, flood: bool = False, direct: bool = False, force: bool = False) -> dict: Send a text message to a contact and wait for delivery confirmation -- see messages.py's send_message for the full flood/direct/force semantics and the returned dict's shape. Raises BeeboDeviceError on any failure.
  • await set(self, path: str, value) -> str: Set the setting at a dotted path (value is str()-converted, as typed on the CLI) and return the value read back. An invalid value raises BeeboError.
  • await status(self) -> dict: Node/radio/resources status as plain data -- the same fields beebo status renders, without building a Rich table. Returns {"node": {...}, "radio": {...}, "resources": {...}}; each section's keys are documented on its own _fetch_*_data helper in node.py (they differ slightly between companion/multi_role and repeater, since the two protocols expose different raw fields). Raises BeeboDeviceError if the device's role can't be read.
  • await sustain_start(self, channel, rate: int) -> int: Have the (companion) node inject on a channel to sustain rate RX packets a minute by itself; returns the slot -- see sustain.py.
  • await sustain_status(self) -> dict: {channel (None = off), rate, sent} of the node's injector.
  • await sustain_stop(self) -> None: Stop the node's traffic injector.
  • await traffic_inject(self, channel, rate: float, *, size: int = 32, duration: float | None = None, count: int | None = None, max_hops: int | None = None, on_send=None) -> int: Send rate flood group messages per minute on a channel until count sent, duration seconds elapsed, or the task is cancelled; returns the number sent -- see traffic.py's inject. on_send(n, idx, text) is called after each send.
  • transport (property): Which transport this connection uses: 'tcp', 'usb', or 'ble'.
  • transport_selected (property): Whether a target has been resolved yet -- False for a bare Node() whose transport comes later, on connect().

docs.title: beebo.trials.Trial
docs.text:
One trial run: its blocks, paired statistics and the node's result.

  • alternative (property): Value compared against it (side B), None when unknown.
  • blocks (property)
  • change (property): Mean paired score difference B - A, in ln units (e^x - 1 is the relative gain).
  • confidence (property): Two-sided t confidence (percent) that change is not zero.
  • finished (property): The node closed the trial (its MON_TRIAL end record exists).
  • from_files(files, score: str | None = None) -> List[Trial]: Every trial in these monring_<date>.bin files, oldest first. score ("received=10") re-scores the blocks with those weights, as analyze tuning trial --score does.
  • latest(files, score: str | None = None) -> Trial | None: The newest trial in these files, None when there is none.
  • original (property): Value before the trial (side A), None when the start record is missing.
  • outcome (property): The node's result: keep_a, adopt_b, inconclusive, aborted_*; None while running.
  • pairs (property): Matched A/B pairs behind the statistics.
  • parts (property): A combined trial's participants as (setting, A value, B value); [] for a single switch.
  • report(self, blocks: bool = False) -> str: The analyze tuning trial report as text; blocks=True adds every block.
  • se (property): Standard error of change.
  • setting (property): The setting the trial switches, e.g. 'fem.rxgain'.
  • started (property): Start time, epoch seconds.
  • verdict (property): The offline replay's decision from the recorded blocks.

docs.title: Battery State and Calibration
docs.text:
The board has no charge-detect pin, so beebo infers the battery state from how the voltage moves, and the ADC can be calibrated against a voltmeter.

Voltage alone can't tell "charging" from "fully charged and plugged in" — both sit above the same rest-voltage-adjacent threshold. The Heltec V4.3 has no charge-detect GPIO (unlike some other supported boards), so beebo derives a charge trend purely from how the battery-sense voltage moves over time, shared identically between companion_radio and simple_repeater firmware (src/helpers/BattTrend.h).

Every resample tick (battery.sample_period seconds, default 300s/5min, 0 = default), the current reading is compared to the previous one:

State (BATT_STATE_*) Meaning init No confirmed trend yet — boot, or fewer than BATT_STABLE_CONFIRM_CYCLES (2) consecutive in-band samples since the last edge. Also what a real battery reports once settled with no charge edge since boot. charging Voltage rose more than the hysteresis band (25mV) since the last sample. discharging Voltage fell more than the hysteresis band since the last sample. charged 2 consecutive in-band samples, and a charge edge has fired at some point since boot — a real battery that has topped out. plugged battery.present is explicitly set to no — external power only, no cell attached.

There's no absolute-voltage "is this plugged in?" threshold: once adc.multiplier is properly calibrated, a real LiPo's own max voltage (~4.2V) is what an uncalibrated-board threshold would have used, so a full battery and "no battery, running on the charger IC's no-load rail" become indistinguishable by voltage alone. plugged is instead driven directly by the persisted battery.present setting, and every other state assumes a battery is actually attached.

Two consecutive in-band samples are required before calling a reading init/charged rather than trusting the first one — a sample taken right after a charge/discharge edge can still be settling (IR drop between the cell and the board's sense point relaxing), so one flat-looking reading isn't enough on its own; while current is actually flowing that's caught by the delta check instead, so only the settle-time case needs the debounce.

seen_activity (and therefore charged vs init) latches for the life of the boot and is only reset by a reboot — once a real edge has fired, the node won't drop back to reporting init just because it goes quiet again.

beebo battery state and the node console's battery state print the state; init shows as UNKNOWN. battery state <state> forces it for testing (RAM-only, refused while battery.present is no). On the wire it is CMD_GET_BATT_STATE (companion binary protocol) and the battery.state plain-text command (repeater/room-server/sensor CLI).

The sample period is a persisted preference, beebo settings board.battery.sample_period [seconds] (battery.sample_period on the plain-text CLI, backed by NodePrefs.batt_sample_period_secs in src/helpers/CommonCLI.h). A separate board.battery.sample_window (batt_sample_window_secs) controls how long before the period elapses the firmware starts trying for an idle-gated sample. How long the radio must have been quiet before a sample is taken at all is IDLE_MARGIN_DEFAULT_MS (BattTrend.h, 100ms) — a compiled constant, not a settings-tree leaf. The plain-text commands are also reachable remotely over the mesh admin channel — the MeshCore Phone/Desktop app's admin cmd <target> "<cmd>" and beebo admin both forward raw text straight into the same CommonCLI/handleCommand parser, so get battery.sample_period, set battery.sample_period <secs>, battery.state, etc. work identically whether sent over a direct link or relayed through the mesh (see Admin Transport Control).

beebo status node's Battery row renders the trend state rather than a bare voltage-derived percentage:

State Rendered as charging ⚡ N% — voltage-curve percent, capped at 99% (never claims full while current is still flowing). charged 🔋 100% — the only state allowed to show 100% outright. plugged 🔌 — no percent shown; battery.present says there's no cell to read a percent from. discharging 🔋/🪫 N% — voltage-curve percent, low-battery icon under 20%. init Plain voltage-curve percent, or ⚡ alone if the voltage is already above the plugged threshold before a trend has been established.

docs.title: Calibrating the ADC
docs.text:
Since the ADC reading is only ever as good as adc_multiplier's calibration, a plugged/no-battery reading is also a convenient calibration reference: with no LiPo attached, \(V_{BAT}\) is just the charger IC's (CN3165) no-load CV setpoint (~4.20V, its standard single-cell regulation voltage — see the board schematic), not a real cell voltage. Comparing that known target against the raw reading gives a direct multiplier correction: new_multiplier = old_multiplier × (4.20 / measured_volts), set via beebo settings board.adc.multiplier <value>.

beebo battery calibrate does this for you: it reads the reported voltage and the current multiplier, asks for a voltmeter reading between V_{BAT} and GND (defaulting to 4.2 V), and solves for the new multiplier. Give the reading as an argument, battery calibrate 4.18, and it is applied at once. The node console takes the same command, so a phone can calibrate with a meter at hand. See Commands.

The 4.2 V default is the charger's regulation voltage, which a fully charged battery sits at. To calibrate against it without a meter, charge the battery until the charger stops, and set board.battery.present to yes first, so the node treats the reading as a real cell. With a meter, enter its reading instead.

docs.title: ADC resolution
docs.text: The battery ADC sample resolution is itself configurable, beebo settings board.adc.resolution <10|12>, defaulting to 12 bits. At 10-bit resolution and the calibrated multiplier above, each ADC LSB is ≈ 17 mV at the battery (3.3V / 1024 × multiplier), which is coarse enough to show up as a visible jump between two readings taken seconds apart even while the underlying voltage is essentially flat. 12-bit resolution (the default) quarters the step size to ≈ 4 mV/step. The ESP32-S3 ADC is natively 12-bit; 10-bit mode just discards the bottom 2 bits in software, so switching resolution doesn't change the amount of analog noise on VBAT — only how visibly it shows up in the reading. At 10-bit, small fluctuations get absorbed inside a single coarse 17 mV step and the reading looks artificially stable; at 12-bit, the same fluctuations move the reading across several 4 mV steps and it looks noisier, even though nothing about the underlying signal changed. Neither mode filters or averages beyond the existing 8-sample readout, so this is purely a resolution/visibility tradeoff, not a change in accuracy or conversion speed.

docs.text:
Remote node administration authorization and commands.

beebo admin <target> login [password] # mesh admin login (prompts if omitted) beebo admin <target> logout beebo admin <target> forget # drop the cached password beebo admin <target> cmd <command...> # run an admin CLI command remotely beebo admin <target> cli <command...> # run a companion CLI command remotely (needs cli-allow on the target's side) beebo admin <target> cli-allow [on|off] # show or set whether <target> may run CLI commands on this node beebo admin <target> status beebo admin <target> neighbors beebo admin <target> telemetry beebo admin <target> owner # anonymous, no login needed beebo admin <target> regions # anonymous, no login needed beebo admin <target> clock # anonymous, no login needed beebo admin <target> acl beebo admin <target> mma <start> <end> # sensor (type 4) nodes only beebo admin <target> transport [<usb|ble|tcp> [on|off]] # get all, get one, or set one beebo admin self cmd <command...> # run on THIS node directly, no contact/login/mesh relay needed

Offline analysis of downloaded data.

Options

docs.title: beebo analyze latency
docs.text:
Size the windows that declare a packet duplicated and delivered.

Checks the time limits the node judges packets with against the captured traffic. A packet is duplicated when we already heard it; one we route is echoed when a neighbor relays it and we hear that relay within the echo window of our transmission. The report shows the limits in use, what falls inside and outside them, the delay distributions, and the window each needs. --seen-window and --max-latency try other limits.

Of the valid rx packets received, some are duplicated (a packet we already heard) and some are routed to neighbors; a routed packet is delivered when its echo, a duplicated packet a neighbor causes by relaying it, comes back. Each declaration waits a window for it: seen_window for duplicated (from the first reception), the echo window for delivered (from our transmission), and each window holds its candidates in a queue: the dedup table (160 first receptions) and the echo ring (16 routed packets). The window must cover the late arrivals and the queue must not fill before it ends, or duplicated and delivered packets are missed. The report gives the delay distributions (percentiles and a histogram each), the window each needs, and whether its queue holds that long.

The echoes come from the echo events of a raw monring .bin; any other set gives the duplicated packets only. A duplicate is an echo when the RX record flags that the hop before the last in the path is our own hash (monitor format 4, exact), else by the hop count (the first reception's + 2, an upper bound: a route of the same length through other repeaters reads the same). --detail adds the full echo window table, the hop tables, the duplicate report and its slowest pairs. analyze timing and analyze dup-latency still print one half each.

Arguments

  • FILE (optional): A combined monitor_<tag>.csv/json set written by monitor decode --save, or a raw monring_<date>.bin file straight from monitor pull (decoded on the fly, no --save needed first). A relative FILE is resolved against --dir, not the current directory; a bare name with no directory (whip, whip.bin) that is not a file there is looked up as a dataset NAME. Defaults to the most recently pulled raw set, falling back to the most recently saved combined set if no raw data has been pulled, under <dir>/data/ (--dir, default ~/.beebo). A dataset can also be named directly by writing its NAME right after analyze, before the report, e.g. analyze trials rate instead of analyze rate trials.bin -- see analyze list's File column for NAMEs available. NAME and FILE are mutually exclusive.

Options

  • --hours H or H1-H2: Restrict samples to this local hour-of-day range (0-23), e.g. '22-6' for overnight (wraps past midnight). Records with no timestamp are dropped. Off (all hours) by default.
  • --limit, -l N: Show at most N packets. 0 = no limit. Default: 20.
  • --max-latency SECONDS: Discard matched pairs whose Δt exceeds SECONDS as a pkt_hash collision (the same hash reused by an unrelated later packet), not a real duplicate -- a genuine dedup-table hit arrives within the dedup window, tens of seconds at most. 0 disables this filter. Default: 100.0.
  • --seen-window SECONDS: What-if: judge the echoes against this seen_window instead of the one the node ran with (a settings event in the capture, else the firmware default).
  • --json: Print the statistics as JSON.
  • --detail: Also print the echo window table, the hop tables, the duplicate report and the slowest duplicate pairs.

docs.title: beebo analyze link-quality
docs.text:
Per-neighbor SNR/RSSI summary from a downloaded monitor set, with a mean +- std chart per metric. With --hash/--name: statistics and distribution charts for one neighbor (--trend adds the hourly charts, --table the text tables).

Arguments

  • FILE (optional): A combined monitor_<tag>.csv/json set written by monitor decode --save, or a raw monring_<date>.bin file straight from monitor pull (decoded on the fly, no --save needed first). A relative FILE is resolved against --dir, not the current directory; a bare name with no directory (whip, whip.bin) that is not a file there is looked up as a dataset NAME. Defaults to the most recently pulled raw set, falling back to the most recently saved combined set if no raw data has been pulled, under <dir>/data/ (--dir, default ~/.beebo). A dataset can also be named directly by writing its NAME right after analyze, before the report, e.g. analyze trials rate instead of analyze rate trials.bin -- see analyze list's File column for NAMEs available. NAME and FILE are mutually exclusive.

Options

  • --resolve, -R, --no-resolve: Resolve each neighbor hash to a contact name using the contacts.json cache. On by default.
  • --min-packets, -m N: Only include neighbors with at least N RX packets. Default: 1.
  • --by-name, -N, --by-hash: Aggregate by resolved contact name instead of raw neighbor hash, merging different hash-prefix lengths seen for the same node. Needs --resolve (on by default); hashes that don't resolve still group by hash. Off by default.
  • --sort-by, -s n|snr-mean|snr-std|snr-min|snr-max|rssi-mean|rssi-std|rssi-min|rssi-max: Sort the summary table by this column, descending. n = packet count (default).
  • --chart, -c, --no-chart: Also write an SVG bar chart (SNR/RSSI mean ± std per neighbor) alongside the source file, one per radio-config permutation. Off by default.
  • --hash HEX: Show detailed stats (SNR/RSSI distribution + trend) for one neighbor matched by hash or hash-prefix, instead of the summary table. Mutually exclusive with --name.
  • --name NAME: Show detailed stats for one neighbor whose resolved contact name starts with NAME (case-insensitive), instead of the summary table. Mutually exclusive with --hash.
  • --hours H or H1-H2: Restrict samples to this local hour-of-day range (0-23), e.g. '22-6' for overnight (wraps past midnight). Records with no timestamp are dropped. Off (all hours) by default.
  • --snr, --no-snr: Include SNR in the summary table / detail view. On by default.
  • --rssi, --no-rssi: Include RSSI in the summary table / detail view. Off by default.
  • --trend, --no-trend: Include the hourly SNR/RSSI trend table. Only applies to the single-neighbor detail view (--hash/--name). Off by default.
  • --bin-size DB: Histogram bin width in dB/dBm, for the single-neighbor detail view (--hash/--name). Default: 1.
  • --align-bins, --no-align-bins: Shift the histogram bin grid so the first bin is centered on the nearest integer dB/dBm value, instead of on the raw data minimum. Only applies to the single-neighbor detail view (--hash/--name). On by default.
  • --lna on|off: Only include samples captured with the FEM LNA on/off. Records with no known radio config are dropped when set. Unfiltered (both) by default.
  • --rxgain on|off: Only include samples captured with SX1262 RX boost (rxgain) on/off. Records with no known radio config are dropped when set. Unfiltered (both) by default.
  • --min-snr DB: Only include samples with SNR >= DB. Records with no known SNR are dropped when set. Unfiltered by default.
  • --max-snr DB: Only include samples with SNR <= DB. Records with no known SNR are dropped when set. Unfiltered by default.
  • --table, --no-table: Also print the per-row table (one row per window or hour; long on multi-day sets). Off by default.

docs.title: beebo analyze list
docs.text:
List downloaded monitor sets under <dir>/<node>/data/<profile>/ with basic stats, plus the binary sets themselves (monring_<date>.bin day files and any monitor pull --to NAME named <NAME>.bin) under <dir>/<node>/data/. --profile only filters the combined sets (binary sets aren't split per profile). Scoped to the invoking node alias when run through a real node symlink (e.g. gatto-mr analyze list); a bare beebo analyze list lists every node's data.

Options

  • --device NAME: Only sets under a device directory whose name starts with NAME (case-insensitive). Unfiltered by default.
  • --profile NAME: Only sets under a radio-profile directory whose name starts with NAME (case-insensitive). Unfiltered by default.
  • --start WHEN: Only sets modified at/after WHEN -- 'HH:MM' (today) or 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM'. Unfiltered by default.
  • --end WHEN: Only sets modified at/before WHEN -- 'HH:MM' (today) or 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM'. Unfiltered by default.
  • --min-size KB: Only sets at least KB kilobytes. Unfiltered by default.
  • --max-size KB: Only sets at most KB kilobytes. Unfiltered by default.

docs.title: beebo analyze mesh
docs.text:
A console map of the nodes we hear and how their packets connect them.

Needs a raw monring .bin and the neighbors.json cache (beebo neighbors pull) for positions: ours and those the neighbors advertise. A schematic that fills the console, not to scale: the nodes keep their west-to-east and north-to-south order and are spread by rank. Each direct neighbor is a link and, on a capture with rx path mode on, the busiest links between the other repeaters of the paths are added; a link is colored by its packets, blue for the least to red for the most. A table lists the numbered nodes with their counts, distance and compass direction.

Arguments

  • FILE (optional): A combined monitor_<tag>.csv/json set written by monitor decode --save, or a raw monring_<date>.bin file straight from monitor pull (decoded on the fly, no --save needed first). A relative FILE is resolved against --dir, not the current directory; a bare name with no directory (whip, whip.bin) that is not a file there is looked up as a dataset NAME. Defaults to the most recently pulled raw set, falling back to the most recently saved combined set if no raw data has been pulled, under <dir>/data/ (--dir, default ~/.beebo). A dataset can also be named directly by writing its NAME right after analyze, before the report, e.g. analyze trials rate instead of analyze rate trials.bin -- see analyze list's File column for NAMEs available. NAME and FILE are mutually exclusive.

Options

  • --hours H or H1-H2: Restrict samples to this local hour-of-day range (0-23), e.g. '22-6' for overnight (wraps past midnight). Records with no timestamp are dropped. Off (all hours) by default.
  • --max-latency SECONDS: Discard matched pairs whose Δt exceeds SECONDS as a pkt_hash collision (the same hash reused by an unrelated later packet), not a real duplicate -- a genuine dedup-table hit arrives within the dedup window, tens of seconds at most. 0 disables this filter. Default: 100.0.
  • --seen-window SECONDS: What-if: judge the echoes against this seen_window instead of the one the node ran with (a settings event in the capture, else the firmware default).
  • --resolve, -R, --no-resolve: Resolve each neighbor hash to a contact name using the contacts.json cache. On by default.
  • --top N: Neighbors drawn, busiest first. Default: 8.
  • --links N: Links between repeaters drawn, busiest first; 0 draws none. Default: 6.
  • --width COLS: Map width in columns (default: the console width).
  • --height ROWS: Map height in rows (default: the console height less the text).
  • --json: Print the nodes and links as JSON.

A relative FILE is resolved against --dir, not the current directory; a bare name with no directory (whip, whip.bin) that is not a file there is looked up as a dataset NAME. docs.title: beebo analyze packets
docs.text:
Search/filter individual rx/tx packets from a downloaded monitor set.

Arguments

  • FILE (optional): A combined monitor_<tag>.csv/json set written by monitor decode --save, or a raw monring_<date>.bin file straight from monitor pull (decoded on the fly, no --save needed first). A relative FILE is resolved against --dir, not the current directory; a bare name with no directory (whip, whip.bin) that is not a file there is looked up as a dataset NAME. Defaults to the most recently pulled raw set, falling back to the most recently saved combined set if no raw data has been pulled, under <dir>/data/ (--dir, default ~/.beebo). A dataset can also be named directly by writing its NAME right after analyze, before the report, e.g. analyze trials rate instead of analyze rate trials.bin -- see analyze list's File column for NAMEs available. NAME and FILE are mutually exclusive.

Options

  • --resolve, -R, --no-resolve: Resolve each neighbor hash to a contact name using the contacts.json cache. On by default.
  • --resolve-by RULES: The criteria used to resolve a colliding hash prefix to one hash/name: a comma list of rules, tried in order, drawn from active, heard, distance. A rule that doesn't apply to a candidate (e.g. no known location, for distance) is skipped rather than counted as a tie. Default: active,heard,distance.
  • --name NAME: Only packets whose resolved node name starts with NAME (case-insensitive). Needs --resolve (on by default). Mutually exclusive with --hash.
  • --hash HEX: Only packets whose neighbor/destination hash matches or is a prefix/extension of HEX. Mutually exclusive with --name.
  • --kind rx|tx: Only rx or tx packets. Omit for both.
  • --type TYPE: Only packets whose payload type starts with TYPE (case-insensitive), e.g. advert, text, ack, path, trace. Pass with no value to list the available types.
  • --route ROUTE: Only packets whose route type starts with ROUTE (case-insensitive), e.g. direct, flood. Pass with no value to list the available route types.
  • --outcome TEXT: Only packets whose outcome contains TEXT (case-insensitive) -- an rx verdict/routing label (accepted, forwarded, dup, wrong_hop, ...), or for tx: the send result (ok, timeout) plus, once resolved, 'ack:<verdict>' (DIRECT) or 'echo:<verdict>' (FLOOD), verdict one of success/timeout/overflow.
  • --invalid-only: Only rx packets whose header/path did not parse. Off by default.
  • --where EXPR: Filter expression over a record's raw fields -- same COLUMN<op>VALUE mini-language as monitor decode's --where (==, !=, >=, <=, >, < or a bare = for ==; ~ is a case-insensitive substring match; and/or, parens): --where "(snr>=5 and kind=rx) or (kind=tx and status=ok)" --where node~f5 . Fields: ack, ack_nbr, ack_nbr_hash, ack_nbr_name, airtime_ms, hops, invalid, kind, node, node_hash, node_name, pkt_hash, pos, route, routing, rssi, snr, status, type. Repeatable (ANDed). Default: [].
  • --hide COLS: Comma-separated column names to omit from the table (data is still fetched/filtered/sorted as usual). Choose from: pos, time, kind, node, type, route, hops, status, routing, ack, ack_nbr, snr, rssi, airtime, hash. Example: --hide airtime,status
  • --short-names, --full-names: Truncate a resolved name (Node/AckNbr) to its first 5 characters so the table stays narrow. Raw hashes are unaffected -- they're already short. On by default.
  • --group-by COLS: Comma-separated field(s) to group the matched packets by, printing one row per distinct combination with its packet count instead of the usual per-packet table. Groups are sorted by count (descending, or ascending with --asc) and --limit caps the number of groups shown, not packets -- --sort-by/--hide don't apply. Fields: ack, ack_nbr, ack_nbr_hash, ack_nbr_name, airtime_ms, hops, invalid, kind, node, node_hash, node_name, pkt_hash, pos, route, routing, rssi, snr, status, type. Example: --group-by kind,type
  • --hops N: Only rx packets received with exactly N path hashes on the wire -- 0 means heard directly, before any relay appended its own hash (same check the direct-neighbor table uses for an ADVERT). tx packets never match, since they have no hop count of their own. Records from before MonRing ABI version 2 have no known hop count and never match any N. Unfiltered by default.
  • --sort-by, -s time|kind|node|type|route|hops|status|routing|ack|ack_nbr|snr|rssi|airtime|hash: Sort by this column: time (capture order, default), kind, node (name if resolved else hash), type, route, hops, status, routing, ack, ack_nbr (the confirming neighbor on a successful tx echo), snr, rssi, airtime, hash. A record missing the sorted field (e.g. hops on a tx packet) sorts as the lowest value.
  • --asc, --desc: Sort ascending instead of descending. Off (descending) by default, so --sort-by time shows the most recent packets first.
  • --limit, -l N: Show at most N packets. 0 = no limit. Default: 100.
  • --hours H or H1-H2: Restrict samples to this local hour-of-day range (0-23), e.g. '22-6' for overnight (wraps past midnight). Records with no timestamp are dropped. Off (all hours) by default.

docs.title: beebo analyze paths
docs.text:
The routes to repeaters and the links between them.

Needs a raw monring .bin captured with rx path mode on (monitor capture path on). For each repeater seen in a path, lists the chains of hops from us to it with the share of its packets that took each, and ranks the links between repeaters.

Arguments

A relative FILE is resolved against --dir, not the current directory; a bare name with no directory (whip, whip.bin) that is not a file there is looked up as a dataset NAME. A dataset can also be named directly by writing its NAME right after analyze, before the report, e.g. analyze trials rate instead of analyze rate trials.bin -- see analyze list's File column for NAMEs available. NAME and FILE are mutually exclusive.

docs.title: beebo analyze rate
docs.text:
Per-window RX/TX packets-per-minute: summary statistics and a time-series chart from a downloaded monitor set.

Every value here is derived from MonRing's existing MON_RX/MON_TX record timestamps, no firmware change needed. Idle stretches of an hour or more (device off / no capture) show as a gap in the chart, not as zero traffic.

Arguments

  • FILE (optional): A combined monitor_<tag>.csv/json set written by monitor decode --save, or a raw monring_<date>.bin file straight from monitor pull (decoded on the fly, no --save needed first). A relative FILE is resolved against --dir, not the current directory; a bare name with no directory (whip, whip.bin) that is not a file there is looked up as a dataset NAME. docs.title: beebo analyze retries
docs.text:

docs.title: beebo analyze routing
docs.text:
Why a packet we route is, or is not, echoed by a neighbor.

Needs a raw monring .bin (its echo verdicts and RX path flags). Each packet we sent on lands in one scenario: a 0-hop echo (a neighbor relayed ours), an n-hop echo (relayed on by more repeaters), another route (a neighbor had it already), an echo after the window, or silence, told apart by whether a duplicate was heard before our send (a neighbor already relayed it). The report draws one typical packet of each as a sequence of events, tests whether neighbors stay silent once another has relayed the packet, and ranks the last-hop neighbors and the hops of the first receptions. The RX record names the last hop only: the topology is the direct neighbors, further repeaters appear as hop counts.

Arguments

  • FILE (optional): A combined monitor_<tag>.csv/json set written by monitor decode --save, or a raw monring_<date>.bin file straight from monitor pull (decoded on the fly, no --save needed first). A relative FILE is resolved against --dir, not the current directory; a bare name with no directory (whip, whip.bin) that is not a file there is looked up as a dataset NAME. A dataset can also be named directly by writing its NAME right after analyze, before the report, e.g. analyze trials rate instead of analyze rate trials.bin -- see analyze list's File column for NAMEs available.   • --seen-window SECONDS: What-if: judge the echoes against this seen_window instead of the one the node ran with (a settings event in the capture, else the firmware default).
  • --resolve, -R, --no-resolve: Resolve each neighbor hash to a contact name using the contacts.json cache. On by default.

docs.title: beebo analyze tuning
docs.text:
Dynamic-tuning optimizer analysis: per-window indicators, the setting trial, and per-setting effect.

Commands: effect, indicator, indicators, phi, trial

docs.title: beebo analyze tuning effect
docs.text:
How setting assignments affect the delivery indicators.

The capture is split into intervals of constant assignment. Each assignment gets its pooled indicators (eval confirm ratio and goodput, rx/tx rates, delivery, wrong-hop, SNR, noise), then a delta against the longest-running assignment computed hour by hour over the hours both ran, so time-of-day load differences cancel. z is the delta over its standard error across those hours.

Arguments

  • [FILE] (optional): One raw monring_<date>.bin day file. A relative FILE is resolved against --dir. Defaults to the most recently pulled one.

Options

  • --from NAME: Read the file monitor pull --to NAME writes instead of the day files.
  • --param, -p KEY: Setting key(s) that define an assignment (repeatable), e.g. lna, rxgain, tx_power, a setting name. Default: every key that changes value in the capture.
  • --min-hours MIN_HOURS: Hide assignments that ran less than this. Default: 0.25.
  • --json: Print JSON instead of tables.

docs.title: beebo analyze tuning indicator
docs.text:
Look into one indicator's peculiarities: dips (or bursts, for an indicator where high is bad) with their depth and spacing, the share of time in a bad state, level shifts, a repeat period, the time-of-day profile, and what moves with the dips: other indicators (co-movement and lead/lag), the load at which it degrades, and setting changes, trial starts and fault events near them. It ranks suspects, it does not prove a cause.

Arguments

  • INDICATOR: An analyze tuning indicators row, e.g. Score, 'Received', 'Noise dBm' (case and spaces ignored).
  • FILE (optional): A combined monitor_<tag>.csv/json set written by monitor decode --save, or a raw monring_<date>.bin file straight from monitor pull (decoded on the fly, no --save needed first). A relative FILE is resolved against --dir, not the current directory; a bare name with no directory (whip, whip.bin) that is not a file there is looked up as a dataset NAME. Defaults to the most recently pulled raw set, falling back to the most recently saved combined set if no raw data has been pulled, under <dir>/data/ (--dir, default ~/.beebo). A dataset can also be named directly by writing its NAME right after analyze, before the report, e.g. analyze trials rate instead of analyze rate trials.bin -- see analyze list's File column for NAMEs available. NAME and FILE are mutually exclusive.

Options

  • --window, -w MINUTES: Window size in minutes (not seconds) for aggregation. Default 5.
  • --hours H or H1-H2: Restrict samples to this local hour-of-day range (0-23), e.g. '22-6' for overnight (wraps past midnight). Records with no timestamp are dropped. Off (all hours) by default.
  • --sensitivity, -k K: A dip is a run of windows K robust deviations (MAD) below the median; lower finds more. Default: 3.0.
  • --limit LIMIT: Longest dips or bursts listed (deepest first). Default: 10.
  • --json: Print one JSON object per window instead of a table -- for piping into further analysis (e.g. correlating candidate parameter values against these indicators offline). Off by default.
  • --score NAME=WEIGHT,...: Re-score the blocks or windows offline with these weights (tenths, -50 to 50) instead of the ones the node used: routed, delivered, received; one not named is 0. E.g. --score received=10 judges on what was heard alone. The node's own verdict is unchanged.

docs.title: beebo analyze tuning indicators
docs.text:
The tuning trial indicators per window (Routed, Delivered, Received, TX Dispatched, RX Invalid, RX Errors, Nbr Heard, Nbr Marginal, Pool Busy, CAD Busy, Noise dBm; counts per minute), rebuilt from the raw records of a downloaded set: summary statistics and one chart per indicator (--table adds the per-window table). The event-based rows (RX Invalid, RX Errors, Pool Busy, CAD Busy) need a raw .bin set; the last three come from route_stats events, which newer firmware logs every minute. Followed by indicator names (indicators received delivered) it shows only their charts; indicator NAME analyzes one in depth.

Arguments

  • [FILE] [INDICATOR]... (optional): Show only the charts of these indicators or chart keys (the key before the colon in a chart title; case, spaces and punctuation ignored, a unique part of the name is enough: 'dispatched' draws the Routed chart). Default: every chart. FILE is as for the other reports.

Options

  • --window, -w MINUTES: Window size in minutes (not seconds) for aggregation. Default 5.
  • --hours H or H1-H2: Restrict samples to this local hour-of-day range (0-23), e.g. '22-6' for overnight (wraps past midnight). Records with no timestamp are dropped. Off (all hours) by default.
  • --json: Print one JSON object per window instead of a table -- for piping into further analysis (e.g. correlating candidate parameter values against these indicators offline). Off by default.
  • --table, --no-table: Also print the per-row table (one row per window or hour; long on multi-day sets). Off by default.
  • --score NAME=WEIGHT,...: Re-score the blocks or windows offline with these weights (tenths, -50 to 50) instead of the ones the node used: routed, delivered, received; one not named is 0. E.g. --score received=10 judges on what was heard alone. The node's own verdict is unchanged.

docs.title: beebo analyze tuning phi
docs.text:
Noise of the trials' paired score differences: phi and the block spread.

A block's variance is v + c: v the counting noise, 1 / N for N the counts per block of the score weights (the confirmed deliveries for the default weights), c the block spread, the part that longer blocks do not average away, shown as the relative standard deviation sqrt(c) in percent. phi = var(d) / (2 v), d the ln score difference B - A of a pair, is 1 for pure counting noise. Prints each trial, the pool per switch and block length, and the overall pool with 95% intervals: phi, and the spread with the block size N = 1 / c beyond which longer blocks add little. The reference spread is the value the planned trial planner starts from.

Arguments

  • [FILE] (optional): One raw monring_<date>.bin day file. A relative FILE is resolved against --dir. Defaults to the most recently pulled one.

Options

  • --from NAME: Read the file monitor pull --to NAME writes instead of the day files.
  • --json: Print JSON instead of tables.
  • --all: Read every raw set under --dir, not just one.
  • --score NAME=WEIGHT,...: Re-score the blocks or windows offline with these weights (tenths, -50 to 50) instead of the ones the node used: routed, delivered, received; one not named is 0. E.g. --score received=10 judges on what was heard alone. The node's own verdict is unchanged.

docs.title: beebo analyze tuning trial
docs.text:
Paired A/B result of the latest on-device trial (--all: every trial in the file).

Re-derives the trial's decision from its MON_EVAL blocks with the device's own sequential rule (confidence interval on the paired score difference, confirm ratio within 2 pp, aborts on a guardrail trip) and compares it with the device's MON_TRIAL end record. Blocks are paired (2k, 2k+1). --blocks additionally prints every block in chronological order, to spot drift or an anomaly the paired summary averages away.

Arguments

  • [FILE] (optional): One raw monring_<date>.bin day file. A relative FILE is resolved against --dir. Defaults to the most recently pulled one.

Options

  • --from NAME: Read the file monitor pull --to NAME writes instead of the day files.
  • --json: Print JSON instead of tables.
  • --legend, --no-legend: Print the Definitions table (indicators, columns, verdicts) before the trial(s). Off by default; turn on when you need a reminder of what the columns mean.
  • --blocks: Also print every block in chronological order, one row per block with every indicator -- off by default since a long trial can run to dozens of blocks.
  • --all: Report every trial in the file, not just the latest.
  • --diagnostics: Also chart the diagnostic indicators (TX Dispatched, RX Invalid, ...); by default only the score and its indicators (Routed, Delivered, Received) are charted. The table lists all.
  • --score NAME=WEIGHT,...: Re-score the blocks or windows offline with these weights (tenths, -50 to 50) instead of the ones the node used: routed, delivered, received; one not named is 0. E.g. --score received=10 judges on what was heard alone. The node's own verdict is unchanged.

docs.title: beebo battery
docs.text:
Battery monitoring and management.

Commands: calibrate, state

docs.title: beebo battery calibrate
docs.text:
Measure Vbat with a voltmeter and calibrate board.adc.multiplier.

Reads the node's currently-reported battery voltage, asks for a real voltmeter reading at the Vbat JST pigtail (defaulting to the V4.3 regulator's 4.2V charge setpoint, which has measured accurate), and sets board.adc.multiplier so the node's reported voltage matches. With VOLTS the reading is given up front and applied without asking.

Arguments

  • [VOLTS] (optional): The voltmeter reading at the Vbat pigtail. Given, it is applied without prompting (the node console takes the same argument); omit it to be asked.

Options

  • --target VOLTS: Expected Vbat voltage, used as the default voltmeter reading (default 4.2V, the V4.3 regulator's charge setpoint).
  • --yes, -y: Accept --target as the measured reading and apply the new multiplier without prompting -- for non-interactive/cron use.

docs.title: beebo battery state
docs.text:
Voltage, the raw BATT_STATE_* classifier state from BattTrend.h, and the symbol status node would render -- separate from status node so the classifier state is visible even when it disagrees with the voltage. Give VALUE to force the state instead of just reading it.

Arguments

  • VALUE (optional): Omit to show the current state. Give one of: charging, discharging, charged, plugged, unknown (INIT) to force the BattTrend.h classifier into that state -- useful for testing the status node/battery state symbol without waiting for a real charge/discharge edge. RAM-only, not persisted; the firmware re-seeds the trend anchor to the current voltage so the forced state isn't immediately undone by the next sample.

docs.title: beebo channels
docs.text:
Manage a companion's group channels and the shared channels.json.

list channels on the node. get CHANNEL one channel's slot, name and secret. set IDX NAME write a slot: '#name' derives a public secret, else --secret HEX or --random; recorded in <root>/mesh/channels.json. remove CHANNEL empty a slot (channels.json keeps the entry). send CHANNEL TEXT send a flood group message (--max-hops N limits how many repeaters forward it). push write channels.json to the node. pull record the node's channels into channels.json.

CHANNEL is a slot index or a name.

Commands: get, list, pull, push, remove, send, set

docs.title: beebo channels get
docs.text:
Show one channel.

Arguments

  • CHANNEL: Slot index or channel name.

docs.title: beebo channels list
docs.text: List the node's channels.

docs.title: beebo channels pull
docs.text: Record the node's channels into channels.json.

docs.title: beebo channels push
docs.text: Write channels.json to the node.

docs.title: beebo channels remove
docs.text:
Empty a slot.

Arguments

  • CHANNEL: Slot index or channel name.

docs.title: beebo channels send
docs.text:
Send a flood group message.

Arguments

  • CHANNEL: Slot index or channel name.
  • TEXT

Options

  • --max-hops MAX_HOPS: Limit the flood to this many repeater hops (1-21; 0 = no limit): the packet is sent with a pre-filled path, so any repeater stops forwarding it.

docs.title: beebo channels set
docs.text:
Write slot IDX and record it in channels.json.

Arguments

  • IDX
  • NAME

Options

  • --secret SECRET: 16-byte secret, 32 hex digits.
  • --random: Generate a random secret.

docs.title: beebo check
docs.text:
Health/optimization check-up: a verdict (OK / WARN / FAIL / PENDING) per indicator -- QoS, SoH, TX power, RX/FEM gain, RX capacity, active faults, battery, and tuning-optimizer state -- each with what's "in range" and what to do if it isn't, the way a blood-test report reads rather than a raw numbers dump. Just the verdict table -- for the underlying detail, beebo monitor/beebo monitor decode/beebo analyze tuning already cover it. Settings-derived checks (TX power, RX/FEM gain, BLE PIN, admin password, dedup window, completeness/sanity) are shared with beebo config check -- see config.py's run_settings_checks().

Reads the ring the same way monitor pull does (briefly pausing capture on the firmware side, resumed automatically when it completes) plus the current radio/repeater.routing.tuning.*/monitor settings. Nothing is written to disk or changed on the device. multi_role only (MonRing has no CommonLink/legacy simple_repeater equivalent) -- unlike most of repeater_settings.py's dual-mode leaves, this isn't ported to the repeater's plain-text CLI, so it's rejected the same way any other non-ported command is (see connect.run's raw_ok default).

docs.title: beebo clock
docs.text:
Show the device's time and drift from host, or set it explicitly.

Arguments

  • TIME (optional): epoch seconds to set the device clock to; omit to read/sync against this host.

Options

  • --boot: If the device is found ahead, reboot it immediately to apply the correction instead of waiting for a future reboot.

docs.title: beebo config
docs.text:
Save, list, diff, and apply named device configurations.

Commands: backup, check, create, delete, diff, identity, list, onboard, pull, push, recover, show, switch

docs.title: beebo config backup
docs.text:
Capture a full-device recovery bundle for disaster recovery.

Both roles' private keys and complete settings, gated behind ONE password -- board.node.password, a dedicated backup/recovery credential present on every build. Prompts to set it now if it's never been set (it exists solely for this command, no reason to require a separate prior step); otherwise the device verifies you already know it before unlocking repeater.guest.password/ node.wifi.password/repeater.admin.password too. That same password then encrypts the whole bundle.
