repeater. covers repeater-only CommonCLI prefs with no companion_radio opcode equivalent, nested to mirror CommonCLI's own dotted keys (repeater.node.repeat, repeater.node.name, repeater.node.allow.read.only, repeater.node.advert.interval, repeater.node.advert.flood_interval, repeater.guest.password, repeater.node.owner.info). advert.interval and advert.flood_interval are presence/broadcast policy (how often this node announces itself, at local vs flood scope), not forwarding/routing behavior, so both stay under repeater.node.advert. rather than repeater.routing.. Everything that actually shapes forwarding/routing behavior lives under repeater.routing. instead: timing/collision-avoidance/ duty-cycle knobs and the tuning optimizer's own switches (rxdelay, airtime, dutycycle, txdelay, direct.txdelay, agc.reset.interval, interference.threshold, tuning.adaptive., tuning.score., tuning.trial.*), plus flood-routing behavior (loop.detect, flood.max/max_advert/max_unscoped) — see the "Dynamic Repeater Tuning" doc page.

board.adc.multiplier works for both companion (dedicated binary opcode) and repeater (CommonCLI adc.multiplier) nodes, so it lives outside repeater.*.

beebo settings show the whole tree beebo settings companion.radio show the companion radio subtree beebo settings companion.radio.lora.freq show the freq leaf beebo settings companion.radio.lora.freq 868 set freq to 868 MHz beebo settings companion.radio.lora.preset "USA/Canada" apply a named preset quadruplet beebo settings console.transport tcp change the CLI's default transport beebo settings companion.node.transport.tcp off disable the node's TCP transport beebo settings --reboot companion.node.transport.ble on enable ble and reboot immediately beebo settings companion.monitor.rx off stop capturing rx records beebo settings commit flush in-RAM prefs to flash beebo settings restore discard in-RAM prefs, reload flash

Arguments

  • PATH (optional): Dotted setting path, e.g. companion.radio.lora.freq, or 'commit'/'restore'. Omit to show the whole tree.
  • VALUE (optional): New value for a leaf. Omit to read.

Options

  • --reboot: Reboot immediately to apply the change, instead of the leaf's default (live-apply or wait-for-next-reboot). Only valid when setting a leaf that supports it, e.g. 'beebo settings --reboot node.transport.ble on'.
  • --about, -a: Show this leaf's or category's help text instead of its live value -- purely local, no device connection needed. E.g. 'beebo settings -a board.battery'.

docs.title: beebo status
docs.text:
Runtime node, radio, resource status.

Options

  • --timing: Print per-command round-trip latency to diagnose which query dominates.

Commands: node, radio, resources

docs.title: beebo status node
docs.text:
Identity (name, role, model, version, build, transport), uptime, battery, MCU temp.

Options

  • --timing: Print per-command round-trip latency to diagnose which query dominates.

docs.title: beebo status radio
docs.text:
Noise floor, last RSSI/SNR, TX/RX airtime.

Options

  • --timing: Print per-command round-trip latency to diagnose which query dominates.

docs.title: beebo status resources
docs.text:
Heap/PSRAM/flash usage, MCU temp, contacts, pending messages, MonRing state.

Options

  • --timing: Print per-command round-trip latency to diagnose which query dominates.

docs.title: beebo trace
docs.text:
Trace the path to a target, printing each hop's SNR.

Arguments

  • TARGET: Contact name, public-key hex prefix, or raw path (hex[:flags] or comma list).

docs.title: beebo traffic
docs.text:
Inject flood group traffic on a channel.

Commands: send, sustain

docs.title: beebo traffic send
docs.text:
Send flood group messages on CHANNEL at a constant rate (Ctrl-C stops).

Keeps a tuned node's counted events (confirmed deliveries for the default score) above tuning.trial.min_pkt_rate while the mesh is quiet. Needs a companion connection with the channel set (see channels).

Arguments

  • CHANNEL: Slot index or channel name.

Options

  • --rate, -r RATE: Packets per minute.
  • --size SIZE: Text length, 6-100. Default: 32.
  • --duration, -d DURATION: Stop after this many seconds.
  • --count, -n COUNT: Stop after this many packets.
  • --max-hops MAX_HOPS: Limit the flood to this many repeater hops (1-21; 0 = no limit): the packet is sent with a pre-filled path, so any repeater stops forwarding it.

docs.title: beebo traffic sustain
docs.text:
Have a companion node sustain an RX rate on CHANNEL by itself.

The node sends flood group text at random times, only while the packets it hears per minute are below --rate. RAM-only: a reboot stops it. With no arguments, shows the current state.

Arguments

  • CHANNEL (optional): Slot index or channel name.

Options

  • --rate, -r RATE: Target RX packets per minute, 1-255.
  • --off: Stop the injector.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
beebo is a single Typer application. Along with the global transport options (-u/--usb, -b/--ble, -t/--tcp) described in Install and Connect, there is a set of subcommands (status, settings, admin, ota, trace, discover, contacts, messages, neighbors, rxlog, monitor, check, clock, config, analyze, ...) that act on whichever node is connected. The same global flags are reused by every subcommand, so once a transport is chosen it stays consistent across the whole session.

Every command and option is listed in the CLI Reference, which is generated from the command line itself. Some commands have a page of their own:

Command Documented in settings Settings monitor Monitoring check Health Check analyze, rxlog --compare Analysis ota, admin ... transport Update and Service a Node battery Battery State and Calibration measure RF Experiments

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Running beebo --help on its own lists the global transport options and every top-level command:

$ beebo --help

 Usage: beebo [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

 CLI for Heltec ESP32-S3 V4.3 MeshCore Beebo Nodes.

╭─ Options ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ --ble          -b   ADDRESS  Connect via BLE to ADDRESS ('scan' to discover).│
│ --tcp          -t   HOST     Connect via TCP to HOST[:port].                 │
│ --usb          -u   PORT     Connect via USB serial PORT.                    │
│ --raw          -r            Force the plain-text CommonCLI protocol instead │
│                              of the companion binary protocol.               │
│ --log-level    -l   LEVEL    Logging level: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR,     │
│                              CRITICAL.  [default: WARNING]                   │
│ --profile / --no-profile     Enable CLI level command profiling.             │
│ --interactive  -i            Open a 'beebo() -> ' prompt; `connect` and      │
│                              `release` manage the device session explicitly. │
│ --version      -v            Show version and exit.                          │
│ --help         -h            Show this message and exit.                     │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
╭─ Commands ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ admin      Remote node administration authorization and commands.            │
│ advert     Send a direct or flood advert.                                    │
│ analyze    Offline analysis of downloaded data.                              │
│ battery    Battery monitoring and management.                                │
│ channels   Manage a companion's group channels and the shared channels.json. │
│ check      Health status and service quality dashboard.                      │
│ clock      Show the device's time and drift from host, or set it explicitly. │
│ config     Save, list, diff, and apply named device configurations.          │
│ connect    Connect the -i session's device (only inside -i).                 │
│ contacts   Show or refresh the local contact cache.                          │
│ discover   Probe the mesh for nodes and show responders type and SNR.        │
│ measure    RF bench measurements: noise floor, BW sweep, TX-power curves.    │
│ messages   Download pending messages, or send a new one.                     │
│ monitor    Health and service monitoring management and dashboard.           │
│ neighbors  List and manage the node's direct neighbors.                      │
│ ota        Upload a firmware image to the node over the air.                 │

╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

docs.title: Host CLI and node console
docs.text:
The beebo command line runs on a computer. The node also answers a text console, in the beebo-cli channel and the CLI screen of a MeshCore app and on USB, so a phone alone can check and tune a node. The console uses the words of the command line, so the same name does the same thing in both places. This table lists every command and where it runs.

A reply on the app's CLI screen is cut at 160 characters; the beebo-cli channel splits a longer one into up to four parts. The console answers in plain text: no tables, charts or files, which stay on the host.

Command Host CLI Node console Node form and limits settings yes yes settings <path> [value], settings, settings <branch>. The paths with a plain value: trial, routing, radio, FEM, battery, node and board settings. The composite settings (radio.lora.*, coordinates, regions), secrets, console.* and the --reboot option are host only; monitor.* is the monitor capture command on the node status, status node, status radio, status resources yes yes one line each; bare status is the three lines check yes partly QoS and SoH verdicts with the CLI's bands and wording; the battery, tuning and settings checks are host only config check yes no monitor yes yes capture state and ring fill monitor status, ... health, ... service, ... rates yes yes the host prints the Health Status, Service Status and Service Rates tables; the node prints name=value lines of the counters that are not zero monitor start, monitor stop, monitor clear yes yes monitor capture [leaf on\|off] yes yes leaves enabled, rx, tx, radio, env, batt, tuning, event (also setting, command, route, debug, the same bit) and path monitor events yes no monitor tuning trial, ... start [switch...\|all], ... stop yes yes repeater role. start enables the named switches and turns the trial on, as on the host. The other trial subcommands are the settings routing.tuning.trial.* paths monitor tuning trial * yes no the other trial subcommands (profile, enable, values, score, block_size_s, ...) are the settings routing.tuning.trial.* paths monitor tuning, monitor tuning adaptive yes no the adaptive settings are settings paths monitor pull, monitor decode, monitor list, monitor debug, monitor watch, monitor plot * yes no records, charts and streams analyze * yes no works on downloaded files battery state [state] yes yes reads, or forces the charge classifier to charging, discharging, charged, plugged or unknown (a test aid, RAM-only, refused while battery.present is no) battery calibrate yes yes battery calibrate <volts> applies the voltmeter reading at once, on the node and on the host. On the host, without a reading it asks for one clock yes yes the node prints its own time; drift against the host, setting a time and --boot need the host reboot yes yes advert flood, advert direct yes yes flood reaches the whole mesh, direct (zero-hop) only the nodes in radio range. The node's bare advert floods, the stock meaning; on the host a bare advert is direct. Use the explicit forms neighbors yes yes repeater role: the node lists its live table, as neighbors peek does on the host neighbors peek, neighbors forget, neighbors discover yes yes repeater role: peek lists the live table, forget <hex> prunes one entry (the host also takes names and comma lists), discover [-t type]... sends the request and the answers appear in neighbors peek (the host also has --resolve, --timeout, --passive) neighbors ping, probe, poke, resolve, promote, pull, update, remove yes no the probes wait for replies, the rest keep files on the host region tree, region allow, region deny, region put, region remove, region save, region def yes yes repeater role, the node's own region command profile, profile clear yes no ota yes no the upload is the host's job; start ota on the node opens the receiver admin *, discover, trace yes no active mesh requests channels *, contacts *, messages *, traffic * yes no the app handles channels, contacts and messages config * yes no files and prompts on the host measure *, rxlog, run * yes no bench tools and scripts connect, release yes no the host session ver no yes firmware version and build date

The older text commands (get, set, ver, reboot, clock, region, ...) keep working on the node. Phone Feed shows the console in use.

docs.title: Interactive mode and completion
docs.text:
Add -i/--interactive to connect once and open a beebo(<name>) -> prompt instead of running a single command: every line typed there is dispatched over that same connection (history and tab completion via prompt_toolkit), until Ctrl-D or exit/quit disconnects. beebo run (curated scripts shipped in the package, plus anything dropped in scripts_dir, default ~/.beebo/scripts — see beebo run --list) is built the same way every other command is, so a script run from inside -i reuses the live connection automatically; the same script also runs standalone (e.g. cron'd on a Raspberry Pi) without going through beebo at all.

Beebo supports shell autocompletion out of the box (standard Typer --install-completion, for bash/zsh/fish) — run it once and tab-completion covers every command and option:

$ beebo --install-completion
bash completion installed in /home/<user>/.bash_completions/beebo.sh
Completion will take effect once you restart the terminal

That installed script only wires up completion for the literal beebo command, though -- symlinking a device alias (ln -s $(which beebo) gatto picks up its own ~/.beebo/nodes/gatto/profile.toml) doesn't get tab completion for free, since Click derives the completion trigger from sys.argv[0]'s basename (_GATTO_COMPLETE for a gatto symlink, not _BEEBO_COMPLETE). Run --install-completion again through each alias you use and Typer generates that alias's own correctly-named file the same way:

$ gatto --install-completion
bash completion installed in /home/<user>/.bash_completions/gatto.sh

docs.title: Node status and control
docs.text:
Each command has its own --help. For example, status:

$ beebo status --help

 Usage: beebo status [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

 Runtime node, radio, resource status.

╭─ Options ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ --timing            Print per-command round-trip latency to diagnose which   │
│                     query dominates.                                         │
│ --help    -h        Show this message and exit.                              │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
╭─ Commands ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ node       Identity (name, role, model, version, build, transport), uptime,  │
│            battery, MCU temp.                                                │
│ radio      Noise floor, last RSSI/SNR, TX/RX airtime.                        │
│ resources  Heap/PSRAM/flash usage, MCU temp, contacts, pending messages,     │
│            MonRing state.                                                    │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

beebo status node (or radio, resources) prints just one section. Packet counters and the drop/fault totals are under beebo monitor status (health, service or rates prints one table).

  • reboot — reboot the node and synchronize its clock. No options.
  • advert flood, advert direct — send a self advert to the whole mesh, or zero-hop to the nodes in radio range. A bare advert sends a direct one.
  • clock — show Device/Source from the connection's own auto-sync (see Auto Time Sync) with no extra round trip; clock TIME sets the device clock to an explicit epoch instead; --boot forces an immediate corrective reboot if the device is found ahead (the RTC cannot go backwards).
  • ota <firmware.bin> — upload a firmware image over the air (see Update and Service a Node for the full procedure, chunking, and progress display). --priority/--no-priority controls whether the node skips radio dispatch during the transfer (every transport; on by default).

docs.title: Battery
docs.text:
How the state is derived, and how to calibrate the ADC, is on Battery State and Calibration.

battery state reports the raw BATT_STATE_* classifier value from BattTrend.h alongside the rendered symbol, separately from status node, since the two can disagree while a trend is settling:

$ beebo battery --help

 Usage: beebo battery [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

 Battery monitoring and management.

╭─ Commands ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ state      Voltage, the raw BATT_STATE_* classifier state from BattTrend.h,  │
│            and the symbol `status node` would render. Give VALUE to force   │
│            the state instead of just reading it.                            │
│ calibrate  Measure Vbat with a voltmeter and calibrate board.adc.multiplier. │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

battery calibrate reads the node's currently-reported voltage and board.adc.multiplier, asks for a real voltmeter reading at the Vbat JST pigtail (defaulting to 4.2V, the V4.3 regulator's charge setpoint, which a fully charged battery sits at — accepting the default recalibrates against the reported-vs-expected gap with no meter in hand, so charge the battery fully and set board.battery.present to yes first), and solves for the new multiplier linearly. Given the reading as an argument (battery calibrate 4.18) it applies it at once, as the node console does; --yes/-y skips the prompts for scripted/cron use. It's also the first beebo run use-case script (beebo run calibrate-vbat, same command either way) and doubles as a standalone script — see beebo run --list.

docs.title: Identity and saved configurations
docs.text:
Identity management lives under beebo config, alongside the rest of the node-identity and profile management (beebo config --help lists all of these).

  • config identity — show the device's current identity (public key), or replace it with import FILE, or save it with export [FILE]/save. Without FILE, export (and its save shorthand) writes to BEEBO_ROOT/nodes/<node>/identity.json, the node's own directory in the config fs layout ($BEEBO_ROOT is ~/.beebo by default). generate [FILE] creates a brand new Ed25519 keypair purely locally (no device connection) and saves it the same way — pair it with a separate import FILE to apply it to a device. Replacing the identity invalidates every contact's cached shared secret on the device and changes the hash the node is known by on the mesh — existing peers see it as a new, unrecognized node until they re-hear its advert. The table below lists the subcommands.
Command Example What it does config identity beebo config identity Print the connected device's current public key and name. config identity export [FILE] [--role ROLE] beebo config identity export --role repeater Save the device's keypair to FILE (default BEEBO_ROOT/nodes/<node>/identity.json). config identity save [--role ROLE] beebo config identity save Shorthand for export with no FILE. config identity import FILE [--role ROLE] [--yes] beebo config identity import backup.json Replace the device's identity with a saved keypair. config identity generate [FILE] [--role ROLE] beebo config identity generate --role companion Generate a brand-new keypair locally (no device connection) and save it. config create ROLE NAME [--copy EXISTING] beebo config create repeater gatto Generate a fresh named identity purely locally, under nodes/NAME/. config switch NAME [--yes] beebo -t gatto config switch gatto Apply a saved named identity to the connected board (import keypair + set name + role-switch-if-needed + reboot, atomic). config list [KIND] beebo config list nodes List saved configs, templates, backups and/or nodes (named identities). config delete KIND NAME [--role ROLE] [--yes] beebo config delete node old-name Delete one saved config, template, backup or node. config show NAME [PATH] beebo config show gatto repeater.radio Print a saved configuration's values (offline), optionally narrowed to a settings path. config pull [NAME] [PATHS...] [--role ROLE] [--factory] beebo config pull Snapshot the live device's settings into a named file (default <node>-<role>); --factory also writes verified firmware defaults as a validation template. config diff [NAME] [PATHS...] [--role ROLE] beebo config diff Compare a saved configuration against the live device. config push [NAME] [PATHS...] [--role ROLE] [--confirm] beebo config push Apply a saved configuration to the live device (--confirm asks per changed setting). config onboard [SAVE_AS] [--against TEMPLATE] [--default] beebo config onboard Guided first-time setup, prompting through each templated setting. config check [--role ROLE] [--against TEMPLATE] [--fix] beebo config check Validate live settings against a template's [ranges]/[defaults] (default factory), optionally auto-fixing. config backup [NAME] [--note TEXT] beebo config backup Password-gated snapshot of every secret (WiFi/repeater/guest passwords) plus settings, to devices/<board>/recovery/. config recover NAME beebo config recover 2026-08-20T10-00-00 Restore a device from a prior config backup snapshot.

--role companion|repeater|all on pull, diff, push and check targets that role's persisted settings without switching board.node.role. PATHS are dotted settings-path prefixes (for example board repeater.routing) restricting what is captured, compared or applied; when given, NAME must be given first.

docs.title: Guided setup and saved configurations
docs.text:
Once connected over USB or BLE (WiFi needs its credentials first, from the app or the command line, see Install and Connect), the fastest way to configure a fresh device is beebo config onboard — a guided, question-driven wizard that walks through node name, role (companion/repeater), a LoRa region preset, the repeater admin password (forced if it's still the firmware's public default), and WiFi/TCP provisioning, defaulting every question to the device's current value so it's also safe to re-run later as a review:

$ beebo -u /dev/ttyACM0 config onboard
beebo onboard -- guided setup. Press Enter to keep the current value;
safe to re-run on an already-configured device.

Node name [beebo]: gatto
Node role [companion/repeater] (companion): repeater
Set a LoRa region preset? (current: (custom)) [y/n]: n
The repeater admin password is still the firmware's built-in default --
that default is public and known, so this isn't optional.
New repeater.admin.password: ********
Confirm new repeater.admin.password: ********
Set a guest password too? [y/n]: n
Enable WiFi (TCP transport)? [y/n]: y
WiFi SSID [myssid]: myssid
Set/change the WiFi password? [y/n]: y
New companion.node.wifi.password: ********
Confirm new companion.node.wifi.password: ********

Setup complete.
Save this as a named configuration? [y/n]: y
Configuration name: home-repeater
Saved as 'home-repeater': 41 setting(s) captured, 2 secret(s) skipped.

That last save step is the other half of beebo config: a saved name captures the whole (role-filtered) settings tree and can later be compared or re-applied to any device —

$ beebo -t gatto config diff home-repeater      # what's changed since?
$ beebo -t gatto config push home-repeater      # push it back
$ beebo -t gatto config check                   # sanity/completeness check-up
$ beebo config list                              # every saved configuration

NAME is optional on pull/diff/push -- it defaults to <node_name>-<role>, built from whatever device you're connected to.

config push only writes settings that actually differ, batched into a single flash write where the firmware supports it, and offers to reboot at the end only if something it changed actually needs one. config check is the settings-only half of beebo check — unset owner info, a LoRa setup matching no known preset, a still-default admin password, that sort of thing — worth running before handing a repeater off. beebo check adds the live health verdicts (delivery, battery, tuning).

The wizard drives the same one-setting-at-a-time beebo settings commands shown in Settings — use those directly for scripting, or for anything the wizard doesn't ask about (beebo settings --help covers the full tree).

docs.title: Regions
docs.text:
Command Example What it does region tree gatto region tree Show the region hierarchy (green = flood-allowed, red = flood-denied, ★ = home). region put NAME [PARENT] gatto region put pnw Define a region, or re-parent an existing one. region remove NAME gatto region remove pnw Remove a region (must have no children). region allow NAME gatto region allow pnw Allow flood traffic tagged with this region to be relayed. region deny NAME gatto region deny pnw Deny (stop relaying) flood traffic tagged with this region. region def SEGMENTS gatto region def "west pnw|pdx wa|kls or wv,sle" Bulk-define a region subtree in one round trip. region save gatto region save Explicitly persist the region tree (every other subcommand already auto-persists).

beebo settings repeater.node.region.home (home region) and repeater.node.region.default (default region) are reached through Settings, not region — region itself only manages the RegionMap tree/flood-policy structure.

docs.title: Mesh discovery and routing
docs.text:
• discover [filter] — probe the mesh for nodes and show each responder's type and link SNR. filter narrows by node type (all, an int mask, or a comma list of cli/rep/room/sens); --timeout sets how long to wait for stragglers, --full requests full 32-byte public keys instead of prefixes.

$ beebo discover rep,room --timeout 8
- trace <target> — trace the path to a target (contact name, public-key hex prefix, or a raw path) and print each hop's SNR. - neighbors — the node's own RAM-only table of everything heard via a zero-hop advert (CMD_GET_NEIGHBORS), independent of the saved contact list — useful because auto-add is usually off on a busy mesh, so a real immediate neighbor often isn't a saved contact yet. Subcommands: discover (send a direct advert, wait, then list what was heard), pull (re-query the table, merge it into neighbors.json and list the merged view), peek (the live RAM table only, without the cache), resolve <id> (request a neighbor's name/owner string), probe <id> (zero-hop reachability check of one neighbor), promote <id> (save a neighbor as a node contact), remove <id> (delete a previously promoted contact), forget <id> (prune an entry from the neighbor table itself, RAM-only, mirrors the text CLI's neighbor.remove), plus ping and poke (see below). beebo contacts refresh also merges these neighbors into the resolver cache and promotes fresh ones automatically. - contacts — list (offline, from the local contacts.json cache) or refresh (contacts refresh, re-queries the node and merges) the contact list, with heavy filtering (--name, --hash, --type, --neighbors, --active/--inactive, --located, --near KM, --collisions) and sort/group options for large meshes. contacts active <target> (or --off) flags a cached node reachable/unreachable by hand; contacts remove <name|hash>... deletes contacts from the node (--all removes every one, --yes skips the prompt), including ones that are not direct neighbors; contacts free-1b lists unused 1-byte hash prefixes, handy when hand-picking a distinguishable node name. Backs the neighbor-name resolution used by rxlog, discover, trace, and others.

docs.title: beebo neighbors update — complete partial neighbors from a node directory
docs.text:
A neighbor heard only through a control or relayed packet is saved in neighbors.json with just a 1-3 byte key prefix, no name and no location. beebo neighbors update completes those entries from a mesh node directory, the directory.json downloaded from cascadiamesh.org and placed in $BEEBO_ROOT/mesh/. It is offline and never connects to a device.

An entry is completed only when its prefix matches exactly one node in the whole directory (a 1-byte prefix shared by several nodes never qualifies) and that node is within --max-km (default 100) of this node's own location. That location is recorded in neighbors.json (the self block) by beebo neighbors pull, which reads it from the node: the repeater's repeater.coords, or the companion's advertised location. A companion node also has it in contacts.json. Run neighbors pull once if update says the location is unknown, or give it explicitly with --origin LAT,LON. The name, type and location fill the blanks, and the key becomes the full 32-byte one. The proposals are shown in a table first, and nothing is written until you answer y:

$ gatto neighbors update
$ gatto neighbors update --max-km 30 --dry-run
$ gatto neighbors update --yes

--dry-run only prints the proposals and --yes applies them without asking. The table caption counts the entries that were skipped and why (ambiguous prefix, too far, not in the directory, no location in the directory).

docs.title: beebo neighbors poke and beebo neighbors ping — single-peer, on-demand checks
docs.text:
rxlog --compare needs organic RX traffic to accumulate its samples, which can be slow against a quiet or distant neighbor. beebo neighbors poke and beebo neighbors ping get a data point on demand instead, useful for a quick manual before/after check against one specific direct neighbor around a manual beebo settings companion.fem.rxgain on|off toggle — both target a known direct (zero-hop) neighbor, resolved by name or public-key prefix against neighbors.json (run beebo neighbors pull first to populate/update it):

  • beebo neighbors poke <target> --pokes N sends a direct-route round trip and asks the neighbor to report its own atomically-measured RSSI/SNR/noise-floor for the poke it just received, alongside our own reading of its reply — unlike a trace/ping round trip, which only ever reports SNR back to us, a poke tells us how well the other side is hearing us, and gives us a fresh RX reading of our own in the same exchange:
$ gatto neighbors poke beebo --pokes 5
  • beebo neighbors ping <target> --converge runs repeated direct-trace round trips until the SNR mean statistically converges, tagging its output filename with the LNA state in force at the time (..._lna_on_.../..._lna_off_...) — run once per LNA state against the same peer and compare the two converged means directly.

docs.title: Channels and messages
docs.text:
• channels (companion only) — list, get, set IDX NAME, remove, send CHANNEL TEXT [--max-hops N], push, pull manage the node's group-channel slots. A #name channel derives its public secret; any other name needs --secret HEX or --random. Every set records the channel in <root>/mesh/channels.json (mode 0600, keyed by name), which push writes to a node and pull fills from one, so nodes share a private channel. --max-hops N (1-21; 0 = no limit) limits how many repeaters forward the message, whatever their own settings, by sending it with a pre-filled path.
  • traffic send CHANNEL --rate N — injects fixed-size flood group messages at a constant rate per minute (--size, --duration or --count, --max-hops), so a quiet mesh still gives a tuned node the RX rate tuning.trial.min_pkt_rate requires.
  • messages download / messages send — download drains the full pending message backlog (CMD_SYNC_NEXT_MESSAGE looped until empty) across every channel and direct contact, saving to CSV or JSON (--format); send <target> <text> sends a direct message and reports whether it was ACK'd or timed out. Every message is tagged with the radio's rxgain/fem.rxgain at receive time and carries rxlog-comparable SNR/RSSI/path fields, so a backlog drain doubles as another source of LNA on/off data.
  • traffic sustain [CHANNEL --rate N | --off] — companion only: the node itself sends flood group messages on a private channel, at random (Poisson-spaced) times and at most one every 2 s, only while the packets it hears per minute are below N, so a tuned repeater nearby keeps its tuning.trial.min_pkt_rate without a held connection. RAM-only: a reboot or role switch stops it. No arguments shows the state.

docs.title: Monitoring and diagnostics
docs.text:
• monitor — controls for the always-on background capture ring. With no subcommand it shows the ring's fill, capture state, window and packet totals, and an RX-conditions histogram. Its subcommands are below; Monitoring has the full record-kind and event-type reference.

  • monitor status [health|service|rates]: the lifetime drop and fault counters plus the live RX, TX, CLI and idle time split. Bare, it prints three tables; a section name prints one.

  • monitor start, monitor stop: resume or pause the capture (the same as monitor.enabled on|off). monitor clear empties the ring.
  • monitor capture [leaf] [on|off]: read or set which record kinds are captured: enabled, rx, tx, radio, env, batt, tuning, event and path.
  • monitor events [name] [on|off]: a finer, RAM-only filter per event type.
  • monitor pull: fetch the ring's raw records into a local per-node dataset, incremental by default. --full refetches everything, --clear empties the ring afterwards, and --to NAME appends everything to one file NAME.bin with its own resume cursor (read it back with --from NAME on decode and analyze tuning trial or effect). monitor list shows per-file and per-kind counts of what has been pulled.
  • monitor decode: view and filter that dataset as a console table, or --save it as CSV or JSON split per radio-config profile under ~/.beebo/nodes/<node>/data/<radio_profile>/. See Analysis and In-Field LNA Comparison for how this feeds beebo analyze.
  • monitor tuning trial and monitor tuning adaptive: the tuning session at a glance, below. All take --json, and the views write nothing to disk.

monitor tuning trial prints a state line (off, running a switch, waiting for RX traffic, idle), then per switch in run order its stored value, value list and status (running n/blocks plus the side of the running block, A or B in the A B B A order; next, waiting, queued, pending, decided, off). It also lists every trial the live ring holds, oldest first: A, B, the pairs used of those planned, N (the counts per block that set its noise: confirmed deliveries for the default score), the Change (mean ± SE per pair), Bounds (the decision interval at the pairs so far; adopt B when its lower end is above 0), Conf (the confidence that interval amounts to, to compare with confidence_pct), the Verdict (use A or use B) and the duration. Its subcommands:

  • start [SWITCH...|all] starts the sequence, and is refused while it is already on. stop turns it off and aborts a running trial.
  • enable|disable SWITCH...|all changes only the named switches' enable bits.
  • values SWITCH [A,B,...] shows or sets a switch's value list (A, then up to three challengers, in the setting's own units); values default [SWITCH|all] resets lists.
  • score [routed|delivered|received] [WEIGHT] shows or sets the score weights in tenths.
  • profile (main or exhaustive, see the setting trial), gain (min_gain_pct), confidence (confidence_pct), min_pkt_rate, block_count and block_size_s (0 = planned from the node's traffic, see Automatic schedule), and combined (on or off: one combined trial of the selected switches instead of one per switch) show or set the matching setting.
  • Every set and reset is refused while the trial is on: stop it first. monitor tuning adaptive shows the adaptive tuner's settings and the latest proposal per parameter.
  • monitor debug / monitor watch — stream the firmware's live debug and monitor-ring events (transport connect/disconnect/lock, faults, ...); debug replays the ring's current backlog first, watch shows only events from now on (see Diagnostics and Protocol Additions).
  • monitor plot rssi — live chart of each received packet's RSSI per last-hop neighbor (every neighbor heard, or the --top N most heard, or -n HEX to pick) plus the noise floor, with a table of last RSSI, average over the window, best since the start, packets in the window and packets per minute for each neighbor, and a line with the total rate of all packets, updated per packet, and a level line at the best RSSI since the start; for placing an antenna. --span sets the rolling window the average and the rate cover (shorter reacts faster to antenna moves; the rate is over the time seen until the window is full); --grid adds a dim dotted grid and minor ticks where there is room.
  • monitor plot tuning indicators [INDICATOR]... — live charts of the tuning indicators, the charts of analyze tuning indicators (Score, Routed, Delivered, Received, Neighbors, Busy, RSSI, SNR), drawn and updated like monitor plot rssi: a dot at each measured point, the last --span seconds (default 60), --grid for a dotted grid, and a readout under the charts (now, average, min, max, point count, age and unit per line). Each chart title says what it measures and over how long, for example Received: packets/min, trailing 15s: the rate is the packets heard in the last 15 s scaled to a minute, so it moves in steps of 4 per packet and falls back when traffic stops. It starts empty and fills as records arrive, like plot rssi; once the first record has arrived the chart stays, and a node that hears nothing reads 0 a minute; Errors, Pool and CAD come from the route_stats event the firmware logs once a minute and only when a value changed, so Errors holds the last interval's rate (0 until the first) and Pool and CAD show - until one arrives; until a window has been watched, a rate is what was heard so far, scaled to a minute. --replay fills it from the ring first: the whole ring plays oldest first, minutes on a full one, with the chart following it forward in time until it reaches the present, so it only helps a long --span. Each line is a moving average: the indicator over the trailing --window seconds (default 15; rates are per minute over it), with the definitions of analyze, evaluated on a regular time grid and at each event, with a dot at each event. It follows every event and steps back down as events leave the window, to 0 once none come. Names pick the charts as in analyze (monitor plot tuning indicators received delivered; case and spaces ignored, a unique part of the name is enough, all for every chart; default Score), and --score NAME=WEIGHT,... re-scores. Charts that do not fit the terminal are left out with a note. Ctrl-D or Ctrl-C quits.
  • monitor plot tuning trial — live view of the setting trial, re-reading the monitor ring every 30 s (--every): the running block, its side (A or B) and time left, the A B B A strip, the paired statistics so far and a chart of A and B per pair. Follows the running trial, else the latest; --switch NAME pins one, names after trial pick the charts: Score or indicators of analyze tuning indicators (monitor plot trial received delivered; case and spaces ignored, a unique part of the name is enough, all for every chart). Ctrl-D or Ctrl-C quits. --score NAME=WEIGHT,... re-scores the trial with other score weights, as in analyze tuning trial.
  • profile — the command-latency profiling ring: merges the firmware's own per-command timing with the host-side round-trip log recorded when the global --profile flag is set, sorted/limited/filtered with --sort, --reverse, --limit; --raw prints the firmware's raw per-event timeline instead of the aggregated table. profile clear resets both rings.
  • check — a one-shot health check-up: a per-indicator verdict (OK/INFO/PENDING/WARN/FAIL) covering QoS, RoS, SoH, the settings checks (TX power, RX/FEM gain, PIN, password, dedup window, ...), battery, and the dynamic-tuning optimizer's state (see Performance Tuning). Reads the monitor ring's live counters and latest resident snapshot the same way monitor pull does — nothing new is captured, this just turns what's already being collected into a verdict per indicator instead of cross-referencing several commands by hand. See Health Report for what each indicator means and where its data comes from. multi_role only (no legacy simple_repeater/-r equivalent).
  • run — curated and user-provided use-case scripts (beebo run --list): calibrate-vbat, api-demo, api-sync-demo. They reuse the live connection under -i; the same logic is available to your own scripts through the Python API.

docs.title: Remote mesh admin
docs.text:
• admin <target> <action> — remote mesh-admin auth and repeater/room-server queries: login/logout/forget (credential lifecycle), cmd <text...> (run any admin CLI command remotely), cli <text...> (run a companion CLI command on a contact that allows it), cli-allow [on|off] (show or set whether that contact may run CLI commands on this node), status/neighbors/telemetry/acl (authenticated queries), owner/regions/clock (anonymous, no login needed), mma <start> <end> (sensor/type-4 nodes only), and transport [usb|ble|tcp [on|off]] (see Admin Transport Control).

beebo admin <target> <action> [args...] authenticates against and queries another node over the mesh (not the locally-connected one) — target is a contact name or public-key hex prefix.

Action Example What it does login [PASSWORD] beebo admin gatto login Log in (prompts for the password if omitted; caches it on success). logout beebo admin gatto logout Log out of an active admin session. forget beebo admin gatto forget Forget the locally cached password. cmd COMMAND... beebo admin gatto cmd "get radio" Run any admin text-CLI command remotely (see the text commands below) — requires an active login. status beebo admin gatto status Authenticated status query. neighbors beebo admin gatto neighbors Authenticated neighbor-table query. telemetry beebo admin gatto telemetry Authenticated telemetry query. acl beebo admin gatto acl Authenticated ACL (client login table) query. owner beebo admin gatto owner Anonymous owner-info query, no login needed. regions beebo admin gatto regions Anonymous region-list query, no login needed. clock beebo admin gatto clock Anonymous clock query, no login needed. mma START END beebo admin sensor1 mma 0 100 Min/max/avg sensor telemetry query (sensor/type-4 nodes only). transport [usb\|ble\|tcp [on\|off]] beebo admin gatto transport tcp off Show or set which transports the target accepts admin logins on (see Admin Transport Control).

cmd self <command> runs <command> locally on the connected companion node instead of relaying it to <target> over the mesh. It is the way to run a command on the connected node from an app whose CLI screen is not available.

docs.title: Status and telemetry rendering
docs.text: beebo admin <target> status and ... telemetry render the raw core-stats/permission payloads as Rich tables with units instead of dumping hex or bare numbers — uptime is formatted human-readable, error-flag bitfields are decoded into named, colored fault labels, and the ACL permission byte is decoded into a colored admin/guest role label alongside the raw value (beebo/src/beebo/admin.py, beebo/src/beebo/node.py). Battery voltage is additionally paired with a charge-trend-aware state-of-charge estimate — see Battery State and Calibration.

docs.title: admin ... cmd text commands
docs.text:
The stock text commands, kept for third-party apps and old scripts: what a MeshCore app or -r/--raw sends to a node, and what beebo admin <target> cmd ... can send once logged in. The beebo command line and the node console use one set of names, shown in the last column; use those.

$ beebo admin gatto login
$ beebo admin gatto cmd "get radio"
> 910.525,62.5,7,5
$ beebo admin gatto cmd "set tx 18"
ok
Stock command What it does Same as reboot Reboot the device. reboot clkreboot Reset RTC to a fixed date and reboot. poweroff | shutdown Power off the device. advert Send a flood advert. advert flood advert.zerohop Send a zero-hop (local only) advert. advert direct clock Show RTC time as HH:MM - D/M/Y UTC. clock clock sync Set RTC from this command's send time (cannot go backwards). clock.epoch Show RTC time as bare epoch seconds (beebo-only). time <epoch> Set RTC to <epoch> seconds (cannot go backwards). start ota Begin an OTA firmware update. ota (host) ver Show firmware version and build date. ver (node only) board Show board/manufacturer name. neighbors Show the neighbor table. neighbors peek neighbor.remove <pubkey-hex> Remove a neighbor by pubkey hex. neighbors forget tempradio <freq> <bw> <sf> <cr> <mins> Apply temporary radio params for <mins> minutes. password <new> Change the admin password. settings repeater.admin.password (host only, it prompts) clear stats Reset packet/radio stats counters. get <key> Read a config setting (see Settings for the same values by dotted path). settings <path> get transports Read usb/ble/tcp enable bits in one reply (beebo-only). settings node.transport.usb\|ble\|tcp set <key> <value> Write a config setting. settings <path> <value> region [<region>] Show or set the LoRa region. region tree sensor list [<start>] List custom sensor settings. sensor get <key> Read a custom sensor setting. sensor set <key> <value> Write a custom sensor setting. powersaving [on\|off] Show or set power-saving mode. log start | log stop Enable/disable file logging. log erase Erase the log file. log Dump the log file (unauthenticated targets only). stats-core | stats-radio | stats-packets Show stats counters (unauthenticated targets only). status node, status radio, monitor status service gps [on\|off\|sync\|setloc\|advert [none\|share\|prefs]] GPS control (boards with GPS only). gps diag Show GPS diagnostics, if available. power Show battery and power-source status. battery state (voltage and charge state) erase Erase the node's file system. USB serial text CLI only. discover.neighbors Probe for neighbors. USB serial text CLI only. neighbors discover monring.header Show the monitor ring's counters (beebo-only). monitor status monring.clear Clear the monitor ring (beebo-only). monitor clear

docs.title: get and set keys
docs.text:
get <key> and set <key> <value> take these keys. A key without a meaning below has the meaning of the same-named leaf in the Settings Reference; beebo settings is the preferred form, and these stay for scripts written for stock MeshCore.

Key Read Write Meaning adc.multiplier yes yes advert.interval yes yes Local (zero-hop) advert interval in minutes, 0 = off, up to 240. af yes yes agc.reset.interval yes yes allow.read.only yes yes on or off: allow read-only (guest) logins. ble yes yes bootloader.ver yes Bootloader version. bridge.baud yes yes Bridge build only. bridge.channel yes yes Bridge build only. bridge.delay yes yes Bridge build only. bridge.enabled yes yes Bridge build only. bridge.secret yes yes Bridge build only. bridge.source yes yes Bridge build only. bridge.type yes Bridge build only. cad yes yes direct.txdelay yes yes dutycycle yes yes extra.sf yes yes Up to three extra spreading factors the radio also listens on (side detectors), for example set extra.sf 8 9. flood.advert.interval yes yes Flood advert interval in hours, 0 = off, 3 to 168. flood.max yes yes flood.max.advert yes yes flood.max.unscoped yes yes freq yes yes guest.password yes yes identity.generate yes Generate a new identity (write only). int.thresh yes yes lat yes yes lon yes yes loop.detect yes yes multi.acks yes yes name yes yes node yes set node <name> <privkey_hex>: set the name and private key together (write only). node.role yes yes companion or repeater; a change reboots the node. owner.info yes yes Owner text; a vertical bar stands for a newline. path.hash.mode yes yes pin yes yes prv.key yes yes Private key. Reading it works from the USB serial text CLI only. public.key yes The public key. pwrmgt.bootmv yes pwrmgt.bootreason yes pwrmgt.source yes pwrmgt.support yes radio yes yes radio.rxgain yes yes repeat yes yes role yes The live role. rxdelay yes yes transmit yes yes tx yes yes txdelay yes yes tz.offset yes yes usb yes yes wifi.enabled yes yes wifi.rssi yes WiFi signal strength. wifi.status yes WiFi connection status. tuning.* yes yes The tuning settings, for example tuning.trial.enabled. See Settings.

This table is beebo admin's own built-in ADMIN_CLI_HELP reference (beebo admin --help prints it in full); it's kept here so it shows up alongside the rest of the command surface without needing --help.

docs.title: RF bench measurement
docs.text:
measure groups the lab-equipment-based procedures detailed in RF Experiments — as opposed to rxlog --compare's no-equipment, in-field alternative:

  • measure cw --power <dBm> [--secs N] — key a manual continuous-wave carrier at one TX power level, for spot-checking with a spectrum analyzer. --secs is the carrier duration (default 30); 0 keeps it on until Ctrl-C, with no firmware auto-stop, so the PA stays keyed if the connection is lost.
  • measure txpower [--carrier advert|cw] [--optimize/--no-optimize] — the automated TX power sweep described in TX Radiated Power.
  • measure noise {internal|combined|in_band} — the noise-floor characterization procedures in System Noise Floor (50-ohm stub / antenna / bandpass filter), across every rxgain/fem.rxgain permutation. Values are raw SX1262 input unless --antenna-ref keeps the node's FEM RSSI offsets; combined/in_band also print the LNA gain against the latest internal run.
  • measure rssi-by-bw — sweep LoRa bandwidth with transmit turned off by the test. A 50-ohm stub measures the receiver's internal noise; the real antenna measures the in-band environment noise. It shows how the noise floor scales with bandwidth (verifying the thermal-noise relationship in Thermal Noise).

docs.title: Connections
docs.text: A beebo node offers three ways in: BLE, WiFi (TCP) and USB. This page explains how the firmware decides which one is talking to the node, what it does when clients come and go, and what you can rely on. None of it needs configuration. It is here so that the behavior you see in the app, such as a second client being refused, makes sense.

docs.title: What is on by default
docs.text:
Transport Default Notes BLE on Pairing PIN 123456 (node.ble.pin). USB on Companion session over the cable, beside BLE or WiFi. WiFi (TCP) off Needs an SSID and password first, which the MeshCore app or the beebo command line can set. The node listens on TCP port 5000.

BLE and WiFi share the board's single 2.4 GHz radio and are mutually exclusive: turning one on turns the other off. USB is independent of both. At least one transport is always available at boot, so a node can never be left unreachable. If a change would switch off the last transport, USB is turned on instead. The WiFi credentials are entered from the app or the command line over USB or BLE.

docs.title: One conversation at a time
docs.text:
The app protocol is a single conversation, so the node gives it to exactly one transport. All enabled transports listen while the node is idle. The first one that delivers a real command frame becomes the session owner, and the others are held back until it disconnects.

  • A second client is turned away, not queued. A phone that connects over BLE while a laptop is on USB does not get a half-working link: the node drops the stray connection. A brand new connection is given a short grace period (300 ms, 3 s for BLE) to send its first frame, so a client that is merely slow is not mistaken for a stray.
  • USB does not starve wireless. A USB session can be pre-empted if BLE or WiFi wants the lock.
  • Closing releases the lock. When the owner disconnects, the lock is released and every transport listens again. Only the transport that was used is cycled; the others stay up.

docs.title: Two state machines
docs.text:
The firmware models the problem with two small state machines instead of scattered flags, which is why the behavior above is predictable.

Link state answers "is this transport's radio on?". BLE and WiFi are one state variable, so a state that means "BLE and WiFi both up" does not exist.

State Meaning OFF Neither BLE nor WiFi is up. BLE_UP_WAIT, BLE_UP, BLE_OFF_WAIT BLE is starting, up, or waiting to be torn down. TCP_UP_WAIT, TCP_UP, TCP_BACKOFF, TCP_OFF_WAIT WiFi is joining, up (an IP and an open listener), waiting before it retries after a lost connection, or waiting to be torn down.

USB has its own small state (OFF, UP, OFF_WAIT) because it needs no radio.

A wait state is what keeps a switch from cutting its own reply. If you turn WiFi off from a session that is running on WiFi, the link stays fully up until that session ends, and only then is it taken down. The same goes for turning BLE on while WiFi is in use. Requests from another transport apply at once. One function brings each radio up and one takes it down, so the sequence is the same every time, and a lost WiFi connection is retried from one place only, after a backoff.

Session state answers "who owns the conversation?".

State Meaning DISABLED No transport is serviced. IDLE Every enabled transport is polled for a first frame. ACTIVE One transport owns the session. Every other one is still polled, and evicted if it reports itself connected. CLOSING The owner asked to disconnect. The node waits for its last bytes to leave.

docs.title: Reconnecting and dead clients
docs.text:
Phones drop off the network without saying goodbye. For WiFi:

  • A reconnecting phone replaces its own stale session. A new connection from the same IP address as the current client takes over at once.
  • A different IP is refused and never pre-empts the session.
  • A client that disappears is dropped in about 25 seconds. TCP keepalive probes it after 10 seconds of silence, three times, 5 seconds apart. Until then, a reconnect from the same address still works.

docs.title: Closing cleanly
docs.text: When an app asks to disconnect, the node first sends its answer, then waits for it to drain before it drops the link (up to 250 ms). BLE waits for two connection events, because a notification only leaves the radio at one. Without that wait, about a quarter of BLE sessions ended with a GATT "Unlikely Error" on the phone's final write.

docs.title: BLE pairing
docs.text:
BLE uses a static passkey with display-only I/O, so there is no screen: the app asks for the PIN, you type 123456 (or your own node.ble.pin), and the node bonds with secure connections.

On a first pairing you take several seconds to type the PIN, and the app starts its own 5-second command timeout as soon as it subscribes. Beebo makes the subscription wait until the link is encrypted, so the app does not time out and report "Failed to fetch device info". A bonded reconnect never asks for the PIN and connects in about half a second.

If the app cannot connect after you flash beebo over firmware you paired with before, remove the node from the phone's Bluetooth list and pair again: bonds made by an older BLE stack do not carry over.

docs.title: USB
docs.text: USB needs no pairing, but it has its own pitfall: when the host stops reading, the USB driver can discard queued bytes after 100 ms and still report the writes as done. Beebo only writes a frame that fits in the transmit buffer, so large downloads (contacts, neighbors, the monitor ring) cannot be silently truncated. A USB session is considered gone after 30 seconds without a byte.

docs.title: Looking inside
docs.text: The node keeps a ring of connect, disconnect and lock events. Stream it with beebo monitor debug, or read the detail in the firmware internals. From a phone, the troubleshooting table maps what you see to a cause.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
Everything beebo adds to stock MeshCore v1.18.0 on the Heltec V4, grouped by what you want to do. Each row says what the feature does and where to read more. For a quick tour see the home page; to try it, start with the Quick Start.

Features marked phone work from the MeshCore app alone. The rest need the beebo command line, which is optional.

docs.title: Phone and app control
docs.text: Feature What it does Read more Node console phone The v1.18 app's CLI screen sends commands to the node you are connected to. Beebo answers them in either role, with the words of the beebo command line: settings <path> reads and settings <path> <value> writes (settings board.node.role, settings radio.txpower), and status, check, monitor, battery, advert, neighbors and region work as on the computer. The stock get, set and ver commands keep working. Phone feed Status feed phone The channel beebo-status carries the node's own reports: boot (version, role, reset reason), an hourly monitor line (packets, health score), trial progress, and warnings such as a transmit power under 16 dBm. Phone feed Command channel phone The channel beebo-cli runs any command typed into it and posts the reply, split into up to four numbered parts if it is long. Both channels are private and never transmitted over the air. Phone feed Role switch phone settings board.node.role repeater or companion from the CLI screen: one reboot, no reflash. Roles Trials from the app phone settings routing.tuning.trial.enabled on or monitor tuning trial start starts the trial sequence and sets up the monitor for it. Progress arrives as feed lines. Setting trials App sync with a repeater phone A repeater answers the app's sync commands (contacts, messages, channels) with valid, mostly empty replies, so the app can stay connected to it. Phone feed Remote CLI on companions A contact that has the remote-CLI permission can run commands on a companion over the mesh. Commands self admin command admin <contact> cmd self <command> runs a command on the companion you are connected to, for apps without a CLI screen. Commands RSSI with every message A synced message carries its received RSSI beside the SNR, in bytes older apps ignore. Firmware internals Extended statistics Heap, PSRAM and flash use, packet and duplicate counts, and a command-latency ring through the companion stats commands. Firmware internals

docs.title: Roles, identity and builds
docs.text: Feature What it does Read more One image, either role The same firmware runs as companion or repeater, chosen by a setting. Roles Separate identities Companion and repeater each have their own Ed25519 keypair, node name, contacts, access list and settings, all kept on the node while the other role is live. Firmware internals Identity tools Export, save, import and generate identities, and swap a whole identity, name and role in one call (beebo config identity …, beebo config switch). Commands First boot from stock A board that runs stock v1.18.0 keeps its settings: beebo reads the stock preferences once, works out whether the board was a companion or a repeater, and starts in that role. Firmware internals Static role builds --companion or --repeater images compile the other role out. The repeater build does not link the contact, channel and connection tables at all: 138 KB of static RAM against 168 KB for the multi-role image. Firmware internals Node names and aliases board.node.name is the node's name; the device id is the board's MAC address; a local alias maps either to a transport. Commands

docs.title: Connections
docs.text: Feature What it does Read more Three transports in one image BLE, WiFi (TCP) and USB, each switched by a setting. Default: BLE and USB on, WiFi off. Connections Link state machine BLE and WiFi share one radio and are one state variable, so "both up" cannot happen. Switches defer until a live session ends, so a switch never cuts its own reply. Connections Session state machine One transport owns the app conversation. Stray connections are evicted after a short grace period, and USB cannot starve wireless. Connections Stale-session takeover A reconnecting phone replaces its own stale TCP session at once. A different address is refused. A client that vanishes is dropped in about 25 s. Connections Clean close A session waits for its last reply to drain before it releases, which ended a class of BLE "Unlikely Error" disconnects. Connections BLE pairing A first pairing waits for link encryption so the app does not time out while you type the PIN. Connections USB write pacing Frames are written only when they fit the transmit buffer, so bulk downloads are not silently truncated. Connections Remote transport control Switch a deployed repeater's WiFi on or off through the mesh (beebo admin <node> transport), to service it and return it to its low-power state. Update and service

docs.title: Radio and RF
docs.text: Feature What it does Read more Default transmit power 18 Measured at the antenna connector: 22.3 dBm at the stock setting of 10, 27.3 dBm at 17 and above, where the KCT8103L saturates. Beebo ships 18. Check your local limits. RF experiments Antenna-referenced RSSI Per-path offsets (board.fem.rssi_offset.lna and .bypass) refer packet RSSI and the noise floor to the antenna connector, so the LNA-on and LNA-off paths agree to about 1 dB on the bench. RF experiments LNA control The KCT8103L low-noise amplifier is a setting (fem.rxgain), off by default as in stock. It buys about 6 dB of sensitivity over the stock bypass setting (4.3 dB better than the bare SX1262) and costs about 17 dB of tolerance to out-of-band interference (the intermodulation threshold falls from −3 dBm to −20 dBm). Board analysis In-field LNA comparison beebo rxlog --compare toggles the LNA against your real mesh traffic and compares the two with a statistical test, with the chassis closed and no bench equipment. Analysis RX boosted gain The SX1262 boosted-gain mode is a per-role setting, on by default. Firmware internals Per-role radio settings Receive delay, airtime budget, boosted RX gain, CAD, FEM gains, timezone and WiFi are separate for each role. The transmit delays, interference threshold and AGC interval belong to the repeater. Firmware internals CW test carrier A continuous carrier with a safety auto-stop, for bench transmit-power measurement. Commands Bench measurement beebo measure runs noise-floor, bandwidth-sweep and transmit-power-curve measurements, with plotting scripts. RF experiments Board analysis A written analysis of the V4.3 transmit and receive chains: power amplifier, sensitivity, saturation, regulatory limits. Board analysis Hardware detection The power amplifier type (KCT8103L or GC1109) is detected and logged at boot. Firmware internals

docs.title: Routing and self-tuning
docs.text: Feature What it does Read more Setting trials A repeater compares two values of one setting in alternating A/B/B/A blocks on live traffic, scores each, and keeps the better. Twelve settings can be trialed; the main profile runs four. Setting trials Automatic schedule Block length and count follow the traffic the node counts, so the confidence you ask for is reachable. A trial ends early when the evidence settles. Trial reference Dead-side check A setting that deafens the radio is caught during the trial instead of winning by default. Trial reference Objective function Trials and the tuner score what the node actually delivered: forwards confirmed by an echo or ACK. The weights are settings. Scoring Adaptive tuner A bandit scores the forwarding-timing knobs and proposes changes. It starts observe-only, each knob is opted in separately, and a change that measurably hurts delivery is rolled back. Adaptive tuner Route retry A repeater that hears no echo of a forward resends it, each retry at its own LoRa coding rate. How a repeater routes Echo window from the send The echo timeout starts when the packet is sent, so it measures the neighbor's turnaround and not queue time. How a repeater routes Hop-capped group sends --max-hops N sends a group message that only N repeaters can forward. Commands Traffic injection beebo traffic send sends at a constant rate from the host, and beebo traffic sustain makes the firmware keep a node counting the traffic its trials need. Commands Region management The repeater region map, with the stock region commands available from the CLI. Commands

docs.title: Observability and health
docs.text: Feature What it does Read more Monitor ring A continuous ring of 65,536 records in PSRAM: every packet's RSSI, SNR, noise and disposition, radio and environment changes, tuning and trial records, setting changes and commands. Monitoring Pull, decode, plot beebo monitor pull builds an incremental local dataset, decode filters it, plot draws live charts. A timer or cron job can keep it current. Monitoring Analysis beebo analyze reads the dataset offline: packets, retries, timing, mesh paths, and trial results with noise and confidence. Analysis Health check beebo check gives a verdict on delivery, battery and tuning, plus a settings check-up. Health Check Service scores A confirm ratio (QoS) and a health score (SoH) computed on the node and shown in the hourly feed line. Scoring Time accounting Where the loop's time goes (RX, TX, the host link, housekeeping, idle), loop headroom, and routing latency split into busy and waiting. Time accounting Neighbors and paths neighbors, discover, trace, and single-peer poke and ping. Commands Battery state Charging, discharging, charged or plugged, inferred from how the voltage moves over time. The ADC multiplier can be calibrated against a voltmeter. Battery Clock An RTT-corrected, millisecond-precision sync on every connect, and a clock that survives a power cycle. Firmware internals Live debug stream A continuous stream of the node's debug log over USB, and of its monitor records over USB or the session's own transport, with replay on enable. Commands Transport debug ring Connect, disconnect and lock events across BLE, WiFi and USB, streamed by beebo monitor debug. Connections JTAG debugging A debug build, gdb and OpenOCD launchers and VS Code configurations for the board's built-in JTAG. Firmware internals

docs.title: Fleet operation
docs.text: Feature What it does Read more Over-the-air update Over BLE, WiFi or USB, streamed straight to flash. About 30 s over WiFi. The new image is validated on first boot and rolled back if it fails. Update and service Named configurations beebo config pulls a node's whole settings tree into a file, diffs it against a node, pushes it back (writing only what differs, in one flash write), and keeps validation templates. Secrets are never stored. Commands Guided setup beebo config onboard asks for name, role, LoRa preset, a new admin password and WiFi, defaulting each answer to the node's current value. Commands Recovery bundles beebo config backup and recover save and restore a node's keys, names and passwords. Commands Remote administration beebo admin <node> status, telemetry and commands over the mesh, rendered as tables with units and decoded fault flags. Commands Aliases and sessions One symlink per node pre-fills its transport. beebo -i keeps one connection open, and beebo run runs curated or personal scripts. Commands Python API beebo.api offers the same operations to your own scripts, with an async Node and a blocking SyncNode. Python API Settings tree One dotted-path tree covers radio, board, transports, WiFi, monitoring and tuning, with help, ranges and choices on every leaf. Settings

docs.title: Platform and quality
docs.text: Feature What it does Read more ESP-IDF 5.5 platform Arduino-ESP32 3.3 on pioarduino, with IDF libraries rebuilt for beebo's configuration. Stock builds on IDF 4.4 with Arduino-ESP32 2.0.17. Firmware internals USB transmit fix The Arduino-ESP32 fix for the native USB transmit hang came with the move. A five-minute load test passes, but it passed on IDF 4.4 as well, so it does not by itself prove the old hang is gone. Firmware internals Lean BLE stack One connection, no central role, host memory in PSRAM: about 59 KB of internal RAM free after BLE starts, against about 20 KB with the stock IDF libraries. Connections More free heap 106 kB of free internal heap with WiFi up, against 82 kB before the move. The offline message queue lives in PSRAM. Firmware internals Headless board GPS, display and button are compiled out. The node reports as "Heltec V4.3 Headless". Builds exist for the R2 and R8 PSRAM variants. Firmware internals Tests Native firmware unit tests, thousands of command-line tests, and hardware-in-the-loop tests on real boards for every feature that crosses the protocol. Commands Build tooling build.sh and release.sh version every image consistently, with a shared compiler cache. fw/ also builds standalone with plain pio run. Firmware internals

docs.title: Compatibility and upstream
docs.text:
Beebo is built to stay a drop-in replacement:

  • Existing apps work unchanged. Beebo implements the standard companion protocol. Its additions travel in one wrapper command, and anything that has no stock counterpart is invisible to an app that does not know it.
  • Stock commands remain. The rule is that every stock text command keeps a binary or beebo command counterpart, even where beebo has a better way, so scripts written for stock keep working. Beebo-only fields in shared code sit behind their own build flags, so other boards build unchanged.
  • Upstream is tracked. fw/ shares no git history with MeshCore, so each release is merged file by file. The v1.18.0 pass resolved 95% of 375 files mechanically and the rest by hand, and every upstream fix is checked against beebo's own copy of the code: the 1.17.1 pass found a path-length validation fix this way. A stock checkout must still build its own targets. The v1.18.0 additions beebo adopted include the remote companion CLI, the local CLI command, stricter input validation (ciphertext length, region transport code, raw data lengths), and hidden-node discovery.
  • Your settings carry over. A board that runs stock v1.18.0 keeps its settings when you flash beebo on top.

For MeshCore itself see the MeshCore documentation.

docs.title: Install and Connect
docs.text: The Quick Start needs only a phone and covers flashing the firmware (a board that never ran MeshCore needs a stock image first, see Troubleshooting); later updates go over the air, see Update and Service a Node. This page is for the optional beebo command line: installing it, choosing a transport (USB, BLE or WiFi), connecting from the CLI or from a MeshCore app, and node aliases. Interactive mode, completion and the guided setup are under Commands.

docs.title: Install the CLI
docs.text:
The beebo CLI is a Python package for beebo-specific device operations: OTA updates, transport selection, RF measurement and analysis. It needs Python 3.11 or newer (tested up to 3.14) and nothing else: no git and no source checkout.

$ python -m venv beebo-env
$ source beebo-env/bin/activate        # Windows: beebo-env\Scripts\activate
$ pip install beebo-cli
$ beebo --version

The CLI installs from PyPI. To get the CLI that matches a firmware release, pin its version, which the release notes give: pip install "beebo-cli==<version>". Update with pip install --upgrade beebo-cli.

The charts and statistics of beebo analyze and beebo monitor plot need extra libraries, which are not installed by default:

$ pip install "beebo-cli[analysis]"

The CLI holds cryptography below version 49, because later releases ship macOS wheels for Apple silicon only and an Intel Mac would try to compile Rust. The CLI carries its own copy of the MeshCore library, with beebo's additions, so it installs beside the standard meshcore-cli without touching it. beebo --install-completion sets up tab completion (see Commands).

For general mesh usage (messaging, contacts, channels), and some beebo features, install the standard meshcore-cli the same way:

$ pip install meshcore-cli

docs.title: Select Transport
docs.text:
Beebo supports three transports — BLE, TCP (WiFi), USB — each individually enabled by a persistent setting.

BLE and TCP share the board single 2.4 GHz radio and are mutually exclusive at runtime: only one of them is active, and enabling one disables and powers down the other, so there is no BT/WiFi coexistence overhead to worry about. USB is not part of this exclusion — it stays available alongside whichever of BLE/TCP is active, and can run a companion session over the cable without disturbing wireless. Among enabled transports, the first to deliver a frame locks the session; the others stay disabled until it disconnects. Although it is possible to turn off all transports to minimize power consumption, at least one transport is always available at boot time, so the node is never left physically unreachable.

The default out of the box is BLE and USB on, TCP off.

docs.title: Connecting with USB
docs.text:
Plug the board in over USB and pass its serial port with -u/--usb. For instance in Linux (use equivalent port in Windows or MacOS):

Reading a node over USB through its alias, with the serial port given by -u (the device id is masked)

docs.title: Connecting with BLE
docs.text:
USB is enabled by default alongside BLE, so it is the simplest way to get connected on first boot without pairing over the air. BLE itself is also on by default — pass its address with -b/--ble (or scan to discover nearby devices):

$ beebo -b scan status node
Scanning for BLE devices...
  beebo   AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF

$ beebo -b AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF status node
╭─────────────┬─────────────────────────╮
│ Name        │ beebo                   │
│ Role        │ companion               │
│ Model       │ Heltec V4.3 Headless    │
│ Version     │ 1.18.0.beebo.1.0        │
│ Build       │ 04-Jul-2026             │
│ Transport   │ BLE - AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF │
╰─────────────┴─────────────────────────╯

docs.title: Connecting with WiFi
docs.text:
WiFi is off by default and needs an SSID and password before first use. Enter them over a transport that is already working, USB or BLE, in either of two ways.

From the MeshCore app (v1.18.0 or newer), in the CLI screen of the node you are connected to. The password is written but never read back:

set wifi.ssid myssid
OK - reboot to apply
set wifi.pwd mypassword
OK - reboot to apply
settings node.transport.tcp on

Turning WiFi on turns BLE off, because they share the radio, so an app connected over BLE loses the link. Reconnect over WiFi with the node's IP address, or keep USB for the app.

From the beebo command line (BLE works identically, just swap -u /dev/ttyACM0 for -b <address>):

$ beebo -u /dev/ttyACM0 settings companion.node.wifi.ssid myssid
companion.node.wifi.ssid = myssid

$ beebo -u /dev/ttyACM0 settings companion.node.wifi.password
New companion.node.wifi.password:
Confirm companion.node.wifi.password:
companion.node.wifi.password = ********

$ beebo -u /dev/ttyACM0 settings companion.node.transport.tcp on
companion.node.transport.tcp = on

Once provisioned and enabled, connect with -t/--tcp and the device's IP address or name, or through an alias that already holds it:

Reading a repeater over WiFi, through its alias: the host is stored in the alias, so no option is needed (the SSID and device id are masked)

docs.title: Connecting with MeshCore Apps
docs.text:
Beebo FW is backward compatible with the standard MeshCore companion applications, both desktop and smartphone, so no beebo-specific client is required for everyday mesh use — the beebo CLI is only needed to unlock beebo-specific features (OTA, transport selection, RF measurements).

The MeshCore companion apps (Android, iOS, Web) connect over BLE or WiFi.

  • BLE — The board advertises as a MeshCore BLE device. The default pairing PIN is 123456.
  • WiFi — Once provisioned, the board listens on TCP port 5000. Connect using the device IP.

docs.title: Connection options and node aliases
docs.text:
Every command shares one set of transport options — -u/--usb PORT, -b/--ble ADDRESS, -t/--tcp HOST — to pick how it reaches a node; at most one may be given, and omitting all three falls back to console.transport (see Console Configuration).

Rather than typing -t <host> on every invocation, each node gets its own device alias: a plain ln -s $(which beebo) <alias> symlink whose own ~/.beebo/nodes/<alias>/profile.toml pre-fills the transport (per-alias completion needs its own --install-completion step, see Commands). Our example companion and repeater nodes are set up this way as beebo and gatto — beebo status and gatto status below are exactly beebo status and gatto status with the host baked into the alias, connecting over WiFi/TCP by default. For a node with no alias yet, or to override one for a single call, pass -t/-u/-b directly (with a node name/IP for -t, since that assumes it resolves on your local network).

docs.title: Board Analysis
docs.text:
Although the board is ready to use after applying default configurations, a few parameters can be tuned for the node optimal TX/RX operation in different environmental conditions. The main settings under analysis are the radio RX boosted mode, the fem LNA low power mode, and the radio TX power.

The following sections model the board's transceiver from first principles (noise, sensitivity, saturation and regulatory limits) and set the models against the bench measurements in RF Experiments.

docs.title: Board Specs
docs.text:
The HTIT-WB32LAF board that beebo targets is the high-power version in the Heltec WiFi LoRa 32 V4.3 compact IoT development board product line. The board is built around the ESP32-S3R2 SoC with an integrated SX1262 LoRa transceiver and a KCT8103L front-end module (FEM). The FEM provides a power amplifier (PA) for transmission and a switchable low-noise amplifier (LNA) for reception. The board includes WiFi 802.11 b/g/n, Bluetooth 5.0 LE, 2 MB PSRAM, 16 MB flash, a USB-C port with native CDC, and IPEX 1.0 antenna connectors for LoRa and 2.4 GHz. It operates at 3.3V with an optional LiPo battery input and solar charging support. In contrast, the V4.2 revision uses a GC1109 FEM instead of the KCT8103L — the firmware auto-detects which is present at boot.

Table 1: HTIT-WB32LAF Board Specifications

Parameter Value Notes SoC ESP32-S3R2 Dual-core Xtensa LX7, 240 MHz LoRa transceiver SX1262 Sub-GHz, 863–928 MHz Front-end module KCT8103L PA + switchable LNA (V4.3) Max TX power 28 ± 1 dBm Board-level conducted power RX sensitivity -137 dBm / -122 dBm SF12 / SF7, BW 125 kHz WiFi 802.11 b/g/n Up to 150 Mbps Bluetooth BLE 5.0, Bluetooth mesh Memory 384 KB ROM, 512 KB SRAM, 2 MB PSRAM 16 MB external flash Power supply 3.3–4.2 V (battery), 4.7–6 V (USB) Solar panel input supported Deep sleep current 20 µA Battery powered TX current 750 mA 27 dBm, USB powered, 868 MHz RX current 75 mA Board-level, USB powered Antenna connectors 2 × IPEX 1.0 LoRa + 2.4 GHz Interface USB Type-C (native CDC) SH1.25 battery + solar connectors Operating temperature -40 to +85 °C Dimensions 51.7 × 25.4 × 10.7 mm Pin-compatible with WiFi LoRa 32 V3

Max TX power is the maximum conducted power the board delivers at the antenna connector, measured in dBm (decibels relative to 1 mW). At 28 ± 1 dBm the board outputs approximately 500–800 mW. This is a board-level figure that accounts for the entire TX chain — SX1262 transceiver, attenuator, and KCT8103L power amplifier — not the output of any single component. The ± 1 dB tolerance reflects manufacturing variation across boards.
