RX sensitivity is the weakest signal the board can receive at the antenna connector while still demodulating it correctly, also in dBm. A more negative number means better sensitivity. At -137 dBm (SF12, 125 kHz) the receiver can detect signals below a femtowatt. Sensitivity depends on the spreading factor and bandwidth: SF12 trades data rate for ~15 dB more sensitivity than SF7. These are the datasheet values at BW 125 kHz; the component-level analysis in the sections that follow derives the expected sensitivity at BW 62.5 kHz used by the MeshCore US/Canada preset.

docs.title: LoRa Settings
docs.text:
The analysis in this document uses the default LoRa radio settings as they appear in the MeshCore companion app after selecting the US/Canada preset [6] on a stock firmware:

Table 2: MeshCore US/Canada Default Radio Settings

Parameter Value Frequency 910.525 MHz Spreading factor 7 Bandwidth 62.5 kHz Coding rate 5

Frequency is the RF carrier center frequency. The US/Canada preset uses 910.525 MHz within the 902–928 MHz ISM band. Spreading factor (SF) controls the trade-off between range and data rate: higher SF encodes each symbol over more chirps, improving sensitivity at the cost of longer airtime. At SF7 each symbol carries 7 bits. Bandwidth (BW) is the frequency span of the chirp. Narrower bandwidth improves sensitivity (~3 dB per halving) but slows the data rate proportionally. At 62.5 kHz the receiver noise bandwidth is half that of the 125 kHz LoRaWAN default. Coding rate (CR) sets the forward error correction ratio — CR 5 means 4/5, adding 25% redundancy. Higher values (6, 7, 8) add more redundancy for better error recovery at the cost of airtime.

Once a LoRa preset is chosen, the radio can be further configured by the following parameters, where default values are specified in the FW for the V4.3 model.

Table 3: MeshCore Tunable Radio Settings

Parameter Values Default Interface Notes txpower -9dbm to +22dBm 10 App/CLI At SX1262 output rxgain on, off on CLI SX1262 Boosted/Power save fem.rxgain on, off off CLI KCT8103L LNA/Bypass

The defaults above are stock MeshCore's. Beebo ships txpower 18; the other two are unchanged.

docs.title: SX1262 LoRa Transceiver
docs.text:
The SX1262 is a sub-GHz LoRa/FSK transceiver from Semtech, covering 150–960 MHz [1]. It integrates a power amplifier, low-noise amplifier, and LoRa modem.

Table 4: SX1262 Key Parameters

Parameter Value Notes Frequency range 150-960 MHz TX max output power +22 dBm Maximum output power TX power range -9 to +22 dBm Programmable in 31 steps TX power accuracy +/-2 dB TX current 118 mA +22 dBm, 868 MHz RX sensitivity -137 dBm SF12, BW 125 kHz, RX Boosted -124 dBm SF7, BW 125 kHz, RX Boosted RX current 4.6 mA LoRa 125 kHz, DC-DC RX current (Boosted) 5.3 mA LoRa 125 kHz, DC-DC RX max input power 10 dBm Maximum input power RX input power 0 dBm Operating input power IIP3 -5 dBm

TX output power is the power the SX1262's internal PA delivers at its RF output pin, measured in dBm (decibels relative to 1 mW). The SX1262 can be programmed from -9 to +22 dBm in 1 dB steps, with a typical accuracy of +/-2 dB. At the maximum +22 dBm setting the transmitter draws 118 mA.

RX sensitivity is the weakest signal the receiver can demodulate at a given error rate, also in dBm. A more negative number means the receiver can hear weaker signals. Sensitivity depends on the spreading factor (SF) and bandwidth (BW): higher SF uses longer symbol times, allowing the receiver to pull signals further out of the noise at the cost of lower data rate. The SX1262 datasheet [1] specifies sensitivity only at BW 125 kHz. MeshCore US/Canada uses BW 62.5 kHz, which halves the receiver noise bandwidth and improves sensitivity by approximately \(10 \log_{10}(125/62.5) \approx 3\) dB, giving estimated values of -127 dBm at SF7 and -140 dBm at SF12. The SX1262 offers two receive gain settings, selected via the Rx Gain register (0x08AC): a power-saving mode (default, 0x94) drawing 4.6 mA, and a Boosted mode (0x96) at 5.3 mA. Boosted mode increases the internal LNA gain step, which lowers the receiver's effective noise figure and improves sensitivity by about 2 dB at the cost of 0.7 mA additional current. Both stock MeshCore and Beebo enable Boosted mode by default for the Heltec V4. The setting can be changed at runtime with settings radio.rxgain on|off.

IIP3 (third-order input intercept point) characterizes the receiver's linearity — its ability to handle strong nearby signals without generating spurious intermodulation products. A higher IIP3 means the receiver is more resistant to interference from strong off-channel transmitters. At -5 dBm the SX1262's IIP3 is modest, which is relevant when a front-end LNA is placed before it: the LNA amplifies both the desired signal and any interferers, potentially pushing the receiver into non-linear behavior.

docs.title: KCT8103L Front-End Module
docs.text:
The KCT8103L is an 860–930 MHz front-end module from Kangxi Communication Technologies (kxcomtech) [2], integrating a power amplifier (PA), low-noise amplifier (LNA), and a TX/RX switch. The TX/RX mode is selected by the CTX control pin, driven by the ESP32-S3 via GPIO 5.

Table 5: KCT8103L Key Parameters

Parameter Value Notes Frequency range 860-930 MHz ISM sub-GHz PA saturated output (Psat) 28.0 dBm PA gain 33.0 dB TX current 75 mA LNA gain 15 dB LNA noise figure 1.9 dB Bypass insertion loss 2.0 dB LNA bypassed Max TX input power +8 dBm Absolute max [3] Max ANT input power +5 dBm Absolute max [3]

The Heltec V4.3 operates the KCT8103L at 3.3V. The V4.2 board uses a GC1109 FEM instead, which has a fixed (always-on) LNA with no bypass mode — the firmware auto-detects which FEM is present at boot.

Note: the KCT8103L datasheet is not publicly available, so the limits here come from the related KCT8101L [3], which specifies a maximum TX input power of +8 dBm and a maximum antenna input power of +5 dBm. They may be lower for the KCT8103L, which has a higher gain.

PA saturated output (Psat) is the maximum power the PA can deliver before its gain compresses — pushing the input harder yields diminishing (and increasingly distorted) output. At 3.3V the KCT8103L saturates at 28.0 dBm (~630 mW). With 33.0 dB of gain, the PA reaches saturation at an input of about -5 dBm.

PA gain is the ratio of output power to input power through the amplifier, in dB. At 33.0 dB the KCT8103L amplifies the SX1262's signal by a factor of about 2000x in power.

LNA gain is the amplification the low-noise amplifier applies to the received signal before passing it to the SX1262. At ~15 dB the LNA boosts the signal by a factor of about 32x in power, improving the system's ability to detect weak transmissions. However, this gain also amplifies noise and interferers, which is why the LNA noise figure and the SX1262's IIP3 matter.

LNA noise figure is the amount of noise the LNA itself adds to the signal, in dB. A lower noise figure means the LNA preserves more of the signal-to-noise ratio. At 1.9 dB the KCT8103L adds relatively little noise, which is important because the first amplifier in the receive chain dominates the overall system noise figure.

Bypass insertion loss is the signal attenuation when the LNA is switched off and the receive path goes through a passive bypass instead. At 2.0 dB the bypass trades the LNA's 15 dB of gain for a cleaner signal path with no added noise or non-linearity — useful in strong-signal environments where the LNA would drive the SX1262 past its IIP3.

Max TX input power is the maximum RF power that can be applied to the PA input (TX pin) without risking permanent damage to the device. This is an absolute maximum rating, not an operating condition — the PA may already be deep in compression well below this level. The KCT8101L specifies +8 dBm; the SX1262 can output up to +22 dBm, so attenuation between the transceiver and the PA input is essential. The TX path section below details how this constraint is satisfied.

Max ANT input power is the maximum RF power that can be applied to the antenna port while the FEM is in receive mode. In RX mode the signal arriving at the antenna port passes through the internal switch and into the LNA (or bypass path), which has limited power handling. The KCT8101L specifies +5 dBm. In normal mesh operation received signals are far weaker than this, but co-located transmitters or reflected power from a mismatched antenna could approach the limit.

docs.title: RF Signal Chains
docs.text:
The diagram below summarizes the TX and RX signal paths in the Heltec V4.3 board, derived from the V4.3 schematic. Note how the TX path includes a 17 dB π-attenuator between the SX1262 and the FEM PA input, whereas the RX path connects the FEM LNA/bypass output directly to the SX1262.

    SX1262                                 KCT8103L                        ANTENNA  
  ┌─────────┐      ┌──────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐                   ┌─────────┐
  │         │  TX  │   17 dB π    │    │    Power    │    ┌─────────┐    │   \|/   │
  │  LoRa   │----->│  attenuator  │--->│  Amplifier  │--->│         │    │    |    │
  │  Radio  │      └──────────────┘    │             │    │   SMA   │<-->│    |    │
  │         │<-------------------------│  LNA/Bypass │<---│         │    │    |    │
  └─────────┘  RX                      └─────────────┘    └─────────┘    └─────────┘

docs.title: TX Signal Chain
docs.text:
During TX, a signal is transmitted by the SX1262 with transmission power \(P_{tx}\) set by parameter radio.txpower (compile-time default LORA_TX_POWER). The signal passes through the 17 dB pi-attenuator, which reduces it to a level safe for the KCT8103L PA input. The PA amplifies it with a gain \(G_{PA} = 33\) dB up to its saturation power \(P_{sat} = 28\) dBm, and delivers it to the antenna. The resulting power at the antenna is:

\[P_{out} = \min(P_{tx} - A_{pad} + G_{PA},\; P_{sat}) = \min(P_{tx} + 16,\; P_{sat}) \quad \text{[dBm]}\]

where \(A_{pad} = 17\) dB is the attenuator loss.

docs.title: Maximum TX Power
docs.text:
Our objective is to achieve maximum conducted power \(P_{out}\) with minimum distortion. LoRa uses chirp spread spectrum (CSS), a constant-envelope modulation that encodes information in frequency, not amplitude. This is a property shared with FSK, MSK, GMSK, and other angle modulations: because the envelope carries no information, PA linearity is not required. A saturated PA compresses the amplitude but preserves the frequency content that carries the data — the demodulator recovers the chirp frequency trajectory regardless of amplitude distortion. This means the PA can operate at saturation — its most power-efficient point — without degrading the signal.

However, driving the PA well beyond the onset of saturation provides no additional output power (\(P_{out}\) is clamped at \(P_{sat}\)) while increasing harmonic distortion and wideband noise emissions. The optimal radio.txpower is therefore the lowest value that reliably reaches \(P_{sat}\) — maximizing output while minimizing spurious emissions.

To determine the maximum transmission power under these conditions, we can set \(P_{out} = P_{sat}\) and solve for \(P_{tx}\):

\[P_{tx,sat} = P_{sat} - G_{PA} + A_{pad} = 28 - 33 + 17 = 12 \; \text{dBm}\]

At radio.txpower=12 the PA input reaches the saturation drive level of \(P_{in,sat} = P_{sat} - G_{PA} = -5\) dBm. Any setting above 12 drives the PA further into saturation without increasing \(P_{out}\).

This is the analytical estimate based on nominal component specs. In practice, the PA compression characteristic is gradual and the actual \(G_{PA}\) and \(P_{sat}\) may differ from nominal values. The P1dB compression point of the TX chain identifies the actual onset of saturation on real hardware. It is measured using the txpower_curve sweep described in TX Radiated Power.

As a safety check: the speculated absolute maximum PA input power is \(+8\) dBm (from the KCT8101L datasheet, see above), corresponding to \(P_{tx} = 8 + 17 = 25\) dBm — above the SX1262 maximum of 22. No firmware setting can exceed the absolute maximum rating.

To account for losses in the TX chain due to PCB, connectors, SMA pig tail, etc. we add a system loss \(L_{tx}\), which the bench measurement in TX Radiated Power puts at about 4 dB. The output power becomes:

\[P_{out} = \min(P_{tx} - A_{pad} + G_{PA},\; P_{sat}) - L_{tx}\]

The maximum transmission power at SX1262 radio output becomes:

\[P_{tx,sat} = P_{sat} - G_{PA} + A_{pad} + L_{tx} = L_{tx} + 12 \; \text{dBm}\]

that is, to overcome the transmission chain losses the radio power at saturation inception is higher than the ideal case: with the measured \(L_{tx} \approx 4\) dB the output compresses around radio.txpower 16 and reaches 27.3 dBm at 17 and above.

docs.title: Default TX Power Setting
docs.text:
The stock MeshCore default is radio.txpower=10. On V4.3 boards with the KCT8103L, radio.txpower=10 yields \(P_{in} = 10 - 17 = -7\) dBm at the PA input, below the saturation onset of \(-5\) dBm. Measured at the antenna connector it delivers 22.3 dBm, about 5 dB under the 27.3 dBm plateau, so V4.3 users running stock firmware without increasing radio.txpower are not reaching the PA's rated output. Beebo ships radio.txpower 18.

This default setting was likely tuned for the V4.2 board, which uses the GC1109 FEM with a lower \(P_{sat}\). Community measurements on V4.2 hardware confirm ~20 dBm conducted output at this setting [5].

docs.title: EIRP and Regulatory Limits
docs.text:
The effective isotropic radiated power adds the antenna gain \(G_{ant}\) to the conducted power:

\[EIRP = P_{out} + G_{ant} \quad \text{[dBm]}\]

Under FCC Part 15.247 [4], the limits for digitally modulated spread-spectrum systems in the 902–928 MHz band are:

  • Maximum conducted power: 30 dBm (1 W) at the antenna connector
  • Antenna gain baseline: 6 dBi — no power reduction required for antennas at or below this gain
  • Maximum EIRP: 36 dBm (4 W)
  • Above 6 dBi: conducted power must be reduced dB-for-dB by the amount the antenna gain exceeds 6 dBi
\[P_{out} \leq 30 \quad \text{[dBm]}\] \[P_{out} \leq 36 - G_{ant} \quad \text{(if } G_{ant} > 6 \text{ dBi)}\] \[EIRP \leq 36 \quad \text{[dBm]}\]

With \(P_{out} = P_{sat} = 28\) dBm at saturation:

Table 6: EIRP and Regulatory Headroom

\(G_{ant}\) EIRP Conducted headroom EIRP headroom 2.15 dBi 30.15 dBm (1.04 W) 2.0 dB 5.85 dB 5.6 dBi 33.6 dBm (2.29 W) 2.0 dB 2.4 dB

Both antennas are below the 6 dBi baseline, so only the 30 dBm conducted limit applies. At 28 dBm the PA operates 2 dB below the conducted limit and well within the 36 dBm EIRP ceiling with either antenna. The bench measurement reaches 27.3 dBm, slightly more headroom still.

docs.title: RX Signal Chain
docs.text:
During RX, a signal arrives at the antenna and enters the KCT8103L FEM, which routes it through either the low-noise amplifier (LNA) or a passive bypass path, then directly into the SX1262 receiver. The signal chain has two independently controllable gain stages: the KCT8103L LNA (fem.rxgain) and the SX1262 internal RX gain (rxgain), both introduced in Table 3.

The KCT8103L LNA (fem.rxgain on/off) is the first active element in the receive chain. When enabled, it amplifies the incoming signal by \(G_{LNA} \approx 15\) dB with a noise figure \({NF}_{LNA} = 1.9\) dB. When bypassed, the signal passes through a passive path with \(L_{bypass} = 2.0\) dB insertion loss.

The SX1262 RX Boosted gain (rxgain on/off) is the second stage. As described in the SX1262 section above, this setting selects between a power-saving gain mode and a Boosted mode that increases the internal LNA bias, improving sensitivity by about 2 dB at the cost of 0.7 mA.

The combination of these two settings yields four RX configurations, ranging from minimum gain and current (both off) to maximum sensitivity (both on). The trade-off is not just sensitivity vs power — the LNA also amplifies interferers and noise, raising the noise floor and potentially driving the SX1262 past its IIP3 (-5 dBm) in the presence of strong nearby transmitters. The optimal configuration depends on the RF environment: the LNA helps in quiet, long-range scenarios but can hurt in dense or noisy deployments.

docs.title: Thermal Noise
docs.text:
Every conductor at a non-zero temperature generates random voltage fluctuations due to the thermal motion of charge carriers. This is Johnson-Nyquist noise [8], and it sets the absolute lower bound on the noise present at any receiver input. The noise power spectral density depends only on temperature. It is computed as \(N_0 = kT\), where \(k = 1.381 \times 10^{-23}\) J/K is Boltzmann's constant and \(T\) is the absolute temperature. At the standard reference temperature of \(T = 290\) K (17°C):

\[N_0 = -174\ \text{dBm/Hz}\]

This is a universal constant of RF engineering — the thermal noise power spectral density at room temperature. Thermal noise is white: its power is distributed uniformly across frequency, so \(N_0\) is the same at every hertz. The total thermal noise power captured by a receiver is therefore \(N_0\) integrated over its bandwidth \(BW\). Since \(N_0\) is constant, the integral reduces to a multiplication — or in dB, an addition:

\[N_{thermal} = N_0 + 10\log_{10}(BW)\ [\text{dBm}]\]

For the US/Canada preset, \(BW = 62500\) Hz, \(10\log_{10}(62500) = 48\) dB·Hz:

\[N_{thermal} = -174 + 48 = -126\ \text{dBm}\]

docs.title: Noise Floor
docs.text:
The thermal noise computed above represents an ideal (noiseless) receiver. A real receiver chain adds noise of its own, quantified by the system noise figure \({NF}_{sys}\). The noise floor in dBm is then the sum of the two [9]:

\[N_{floor} = N_{thermal} + {NF}_{sys}\]

\({NF}_{sys}\) is determined by the RX chain configuration.

docs.title: Required SNR
docs.text:
A signal is detectable when it rises above the noise floor by at least the minimum signal-to-noise ratio required by the modulation scheme, \({SNR}_{req}\). The LoRa chirp spread spectrum modulation can extract signals well below the noise floor — the required SNR is negative. Higher spreading factors use longer symbols that spread the signal energy over more chips, allowing the receiver to recover signals deeper in the noise — at the cost of lower data rate.

From the SX1262 datasheet sensitivity table [1] (Table 3-8), we can derive the typical LoRa \({SNR}_{req}\) at each spreading factor by rearranging the sensitivity formula. The resulting values follow a linear pattern:

\[{SNR}_{req} = -2.5 \times {SF} + 10 \text{dB}\]

which gives the per-spreading-factor values in Table 7.

Table 7: LoRa Required SNR by Spreading Factor

Spreading factor \({SNR}_{req}\) SF7 -7.5 dB SF8 -10 dB SF9 -12.5 dB SF10 -15 dB SF11 -17.5 dB SF12 -20 dB

Note that \({SNR}_{req}\) is independent of bandwidth. Bandwidth affects sensitivity through \({N}_{thermal}\) instead: halving the bandwidth reduces the thermal noise power by \(10\log_{10}(2) = 3\) dB. The two effects are independent and additive — moving from SF7/125 kHz to SF12/62.5 kHz would gain \(12.5 + 3 = 15.5\) dB of sensitivity.

docs.title: RX Sensitivity
docs.text:
Receiver sensitivity is the weakest signal the receiver can demodulate [9], composed by thermal noise, system noise, and required signal to noise ratio:

\[S = N_{floor} + {SNR}_{req} = {N}_{thermal} + {NF}_{sys} + {SNR}_{req}\]

The HTIT-WB32LAF datasheet gives \(S = -122\) dBm at SF7/125 kHz (Boosted mode). Halving the bandwidth to 62.5 kHz reduces \({N}_{thermal}\) by 3 dB, improving sensitivity to approximately \(-125\) dBm. In what follows we compute board-level sensitivity in detail by first determining \({NF}_{sys}\) for each RX chain configuration.

docs.title: System Noise Figure
docs.text:
The system noise figure \({NF}_{sys}\) quantifies how much noise the entire receive chain — FEM plus SX1262 plus board connectivity — adds to the signal. It is an intrinsic receiver property that is independent of bandwidth but depends on which gain stages are active.

The HTIT-WB32LAF datasheet does not report a system noise figure but it does publish a max RX sensitivity \(S = -122\) dBm with radio in boosted mode (rxgain on) and FEM in bypass mode (fem.rxgain off) at 125 kHz and SF7. Therefore we can extract \({NF}_{sys}\) by rearranging the sensitivity formula. From \(S = N_{thermal} + {NF}_{sys} + {SNR}_{req}\):

\[{NF}_{sys} = S - N_{thermal} - {SNR}_{req} = -122 + 123 + 7.5 = 8.5\ \text{dB}\]

where \(N_{thermal} = -174 + 10\log_{10}(125000) = -174 + 51.0 = -123\) dBm.

Because the noise figure is bandwidth-independent, this value applies at any bandwidth, including our 62.5 kHz preset.

From the SX1262 LoRa radio datasheet, RX sensitivity for the same preset in boosted mode is -124 dBm, and therefore, following the same lines as before, its noise figure is \({NF}_{radio} = {NF}_{boosted} = 6.5\) dB. In power-save mode (rxgain off) the radio noise \({NF}_{radio}\) increases by 2dB to \({NF}_{psave} = 8.5\) dB, since the AGC has no bias anymore.

In contrast, the datasheet of the related KCT8101L FEM specifies a noise figure \({NF}_{fem} = {NF}_{LNA} = 1.9\) dB for when the low noise amplifier is used, and a bypass insertion loss \(L_{bypass} = 2\) dB for when the LNA is bypassed. When the KCT8103L LNA is bypassed, the passive loss before the receiver raises the effective system noise figure by the same amount, and therefore \({NF}_{fem} = {NF}_{bypass} = 2\) dB.

When the KCT8103L LNA is enabled (fem.rxgain on), it becomes the first gain stage and dominates the system noise figure. For a two-stage cascade, the Friis formula [7] gives:

\[{NF}_{sys} = {NF}_{fem} + \frac{{NF}_{radio} - 1}{G_{fem}}\]

where all quantities are linear (not dB). The denominator \(G_{fem}\) is the key: a high first-stage gain suppresses the second stage's noise contribution. Substituting the KCT8103L LNA (\({NF}_{fem} = 1.9\) dB \(= 1.55\), \(G_{fem} = 15\) dB \(= 31.6\)) and the SX1262 Boosted noise figure (\({NF}_{radio} = 6.5\) dB \(= 4.5\)):

\[{NF}_{sys} = 1.55 + \frac{4.5 - 1}{31.6} = 1.55 + 0.11 = 1.66 = 2.2\ \text{dB}\]

The second-stage contribution is just 0.11 — the 15 dB LNA gain divides it by 31.6. This is the central result from Friis: a high-gain, low-noise first stage dominates the cascade, making the SX1262 Boosted/power-save distinction nearly irrelevant when the LNA is on.

With power-save (\({NF}_{radio} = 8.5\) dB \(= 7.08\)):

\[{NF}_{sys} = 1.55 + \frac{7.08 - 1}{31.6} = 1.55 + 0.19 = 1.74 = 2.4\ \text{dB}\]

only 0.2 dB worse.

Putting it all together the, system noise figures for all permutations of RX gain modes are reported below, together with equivalent noise floors as per equation:

\[N_{floor} = N_{thermal} + {NF}_{sys} = -126 + {NF}_{sys}\]

Table 8: Estimated System Noise Figure and Noise Floor

fem.rxgain rxgain \({NF}_{radio}\) \({NF}_{fem}\) \({NF}_{sys}\) \(N_{floor}\) off on 6.5 dB 2 dB 8.5 dB -117.5 dBm off off 8.5 dB 2 dB 10.5 dB -115.5 dBm on on 6.5 dB 1.9 dB 2.2 dB -123.8 dBm on off 8.5 dB 1.9 dB 2.4 dB -123.6 dBm

docs.title: Board-Level RX Sensitivity
docs.text:
We can now compute the board-level sensitivity for each RX configuration by substituting the \({NF}_{sys}\) values from Table 8 into the sensitivity formula from the RX Sensitivity section:

\[S = {N}_{floor} + {SNR}_{req} = {N}_{thermal} + {NF}_{sys} + {SNR}_{req}$$ $$S = -126 + {NF}_{sys} -7.5 = -133.5 + {NF}_{sys}\]

Table 9: Estimated System Sensitivity (SF7, BW 62.5 kHz)

fem.rxgain rxgain \({NF}_{sys}\) Sensitivity \(\Delta\) vs SX1262 Alone off on 8.5 dB -125 dBm +2.0 dB (worse) off off 10.5 dB -123 dBm +4.0 dB (worse) on on 2.2 dB -131 dBm -4.3 dB (better) on off 2.4 dB -131 dBm -4.1 dB (better)

The \(\Delta\) column shows the improvement (negative) or degradation (positive) relative to the SX1262 standalone Boosted sensitivity of \(-127\) dBm at 62.5 kHz. With LNA bypassed, the 2 dB insertion loss makes sensitivity worse than the bare transceiver. With LNA on, the Friis cascade reduces \({NF}_{sys}\) from 6.5 to 2.2 dB — a 4.3 dB improvement. Note that enabling Boosted mode (rxgain on) adds only 0.2 dB when the LNA is already active, confirming that the first-stage gain dominates the cascade.

Note how Table 9 agrees with the \(-122\) dBm sensitivity reported in the Heltec V4.3 datasheet (Table 3.5.2) [10] at SF7/125 kHz. The stock default configuration is LNA bypassed with Boosted gain (fem.rxgain=off, rxgain=on). Since halving the bandwidth improves sensitivity by 3 dB, we expect \(-122 - 3 = -125\) dBm at 62.5 kHz — exactly matching our estimate for the same configuration. This confirms both the \({NF}_{radio}\) derivation and the bypass insertion loss are consistent with published board-level measurements.

docs.title: RX Saturation Limits
docs.text:
The previous sections determined the weakest signal the receiver can detect. Equally important is the strongest signal it can tolerate — beyond this level the receiver saturates and reception fails. This matters both for nearby LoRa transmitters (in-band) and for strong out-of-band sources such as cellular towers.

Let \(P_{ant}\) be the power at the antenna connector and \(G_{path}\) be the gain from the antenna connector through the FEM to the SX1262 input. The SX1262 maximum input level is \(P_{max,SX} = -15\) dBm [1]. There is no attenuator pad in the RX path, so the maximum tolerable power at the antenna connector is:

\[P_{max} = P_{max,SX} - G_{path}\]

Table 10: RX Saturation Limits

Configuration \(G_{path}\) \(P_{max}\) LNA off -2 dB -13 dBm LNA on +15 dB -30 dBm

docs.title: In-Band Saturation
docs.text:
How close can another LoRa transmitter be before it drives \(P_{ant}\) past \(P_{max}\)? Let \(G_{ant}\) be the antenna gain (2.15 dBi for the stock dipole, same on both ends), \({EIRP}\) be the transmitter's effective isotropic radiated power, and \({FSPL}(d)\) be the free-space path loss at distance \(d\). The power at the antenna connector is:

\[P_{ant} = {EIRP} - {FSPL}(d) + G_{ant}\]

The free-space path loss at distance \(d\) (meters) and frequency \(f\) (MHz) is:

\[{FSPL}(d) = 20\log_{10}(d) + 20\log_{10}(f) - 27.55\]

At 910.525 MHz this simplifies to:

\[{FSPL}(d) = 20\log_{10}(d) + 31.7 \text{ dB}\]

The receiver saturates when \(P_{ant} > P_{max}\). Setting \(P_{ant} = P_{max}\) and solving for the minimum safe distance:

\[d_{min} = 10^{\,({EIRP} + G_{ant} - P_{max} - 31.7)\,/\,20}\]

For a nearby Heltec V4 at full power — \(P_{sat} = 28\) dBm and \(G_{ant}\) either 2.15 dBi for normal dipole or 5.6 dBi for a two stage collinear antenna on the receiver:

Table 11: Minimum Safe Distance from a Heltec V4 at Full Power

Configuration \(P_{max}\) \(d_{min}\) (2.15 dBi) \(d_{min}\) (5.6 dBi) LNA off -13 dBm ~5 m ~7 m LNA on -30 dBm ~34 m ~50 m

With a stock 2.15 dBi dipole, the LNA-on configuration requires at least 34 m clearance from another V4 at full power. A higher-gain 5.6 dBi antenna increases \(P_{ant}\) by 3.45 dB, pushing the safe distance to ~50 m. With the LNA bypassed, safe distances are much shorter in both cases.

When bench-testing at close range, an inline attenuator can bring \(P_{ant}\) below \(P_{max}\). The minimum attenuation required is \(A \geq P_{ant} - P_{max}\). At \(d = 2\) m the unattenuated \(P_{ant}\) is \(-5.4\) dBm (2.15 dBi) or \(-2.0\) dBm (5.6 dBi):

Table 12: Minimum Attenuation for Safe Bench Testing at 2 m

Configuration \(A_{min}\) (2.15 dBi) \(A_{min}\) (5.6 dBi) LNA off ~8 dB ~11 dB LNA on ~25 dB ~28 dB

The bench measurements in RF Experiments use a 50 dB attenuator.

Worst-case sizing for a direct cable+attenuator link between two boards. Table 12 assumes normal over-the-air propagation at a known distance and antenna gain. A direct SMA-to-SMA bench connection (TX board → attenuator → RX board, no antennas) removes that path loss entirely, so the attenuator must be sized against the worst case on both ends rather than the configured/expected values: TX board accidentally left at full saturation (\(P_{sat} = 28\) dBm) and RX board with LNA on (the more restrictive \(P_{max} = -30\) dBm limit):

\[A_{min} = P_{sat} - P_{max,\text{LNA on}} = 28 - (-30) = 58 \text{ dB}\]

Pad up to 60 dB for margin (covers the \(\pm 1\) dB TX tolerance and the attenuator's own part tolerance). Prefer cascading multiple smaller pads (e.g. 30+30 dB, or 30+20+10 dB) over sourcing a single 60 dB attenuator — this also splits the ~630 mW worst-case dissipation across stages instead of one pad absorbing it all.

docs.title: Out-of-Band Interference and LNA Saturation
docs.text:
The previous section considers in-band saturation from nearby LoRa transmitters. A more insidious problem is out-of-band (OOB) interference from strong transmitters outside the 902–928 MHz ISM band — LTE/5G cellular towers, two-way radio systems, paging transmitters, or other high-power sub-GHz sources. These signals are outside the LoRa channel bandwidth but fall within the KCT8103L's 860–930 MHz passband, and the board has no SAW bandpass filter to reject them before the LNA.

The KCT8103L LNA amplifies everything within its passband indiscriminately — the desired LoRa signal and any OOB interferers alike. This creates two failure modes:

1. LNA Compression. The KCT8103L's maximum ANT input power is \(P_{max,FEM} = +5\) dBm [3]. If total OOB power at the antenna exceeds this level, the LNA saturates and its gain collapses — the desired LoRa signal is no longer amplified and reception fails. The safe limit at the antenna connector is:

\[P_{ant} < P_{max,FEM} = +5 \text{ dBm (LNA on)}\]

With LNA bypassed, the FEM compression limit does not apply. The constraint reverts to the SX1262 maximum input referred through the bypass path:

\[P_{ant} < P_{max,SX} - G_{path} = -15 - (-2) = -13 \text{ dBm (LNA off)}\]

The bypass path cannot compress, so the failure mode here is SX1262 input overdrive rather than LNA saturation.

2. Receiver Intermodulation. Even below the LNA's compression point, OOB signals can degrade reception through intermodulation. Two interferers at frequencies \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) generate third-order products at \(2f_1 - f_2\) and \(2f_2 - f_1\) that can fall directly on the LoRa channel. The SX1262's IIP3 is \(-5\) dBm. With the LNA providing \(G_{LNA} = 15\) dB of gain before the SX1262, the effective IIP3 referred to the antenna is:

\[{IIP3}_{ant} = {IIP3}_{SX1262} - G_{LNA} = -5 - 15 = -20 \text{ dBm (LNA on)}\]

With LNA bypassed, the bypass insertion loss works in our favor — the SX1262 sees 2 dB less than what arrives at the antenna:

\[{IIP3}_{ant} = {IIP3}_{SX1262} + L_{bypass} = -5 + 2 = -3 \text{ dBm (LNA off)}\]

Intermodulation becomes significant well below IIP3, so these are not hard limits but thresholds above which spurious products begin to degrade reception. Nevertheless, the 17 dB difference between \(-20\) dBm (LNA on) and \(-3\) dBm (LNA off) shows how much more vulnerable the LNA-on configuration is to OOB interference.

Estimating OOB Power Levels. A cellular base station typically transmits 20–40 W (43–46 dBm) per sector in LTE Band 5 (869–894 MHz) or Band 26 (859–894 MHz), which overlaps the KCT8103L's passband. At a distance \(d\) from the tower:

Table 13: Estimated OOB Power from a Cellular Tower (46 dBm EIRP, 880 MHz, 2.15 dBi receive antenna)

Distance Free-Space Path Loss Power at Antenna 50 m 65 dB -17 dBm 100 m 71 dB -23 dBm 200 m 77 dB -29 dBm 500 m 85 dB -37 dBm

At the LNA output (add 15 dB gain), a tower at 100 m delivers approximately \(-23 + 15 = -8\) dBm to the SX1262 — well past the IIP3 of \(-5\) dBm and approaching the absolute maximum input of \(-15\) dBm. Even at 500 m, the LNA output of \(-22\) dBm is within 17 dB of the IIP3, and multiple interferers add.

Note that these are free-space estimates — real-world environments include building attenuation, multipath, and antenna pattern effects that may reduce or increase the actual received power. The 2.15 dBi dipole antenna also has no OOB rejection.

Practical Implication. In urban or suburban environments with cellular towers within a few hundred meters, the LNA may do more harm than good: the roughly 6 dB sensitivity improvement over bypass in Table 9 is negated if the receiver is driven into intermodulation or the LNA compresses. The bypass path sacrifices about 6 dB of sensitivity but provides 17 dB more headroom against OOB interference (\(-3\) dBm vs \(-20\) dBm effective IIP3 at antenna).

The safe default is fem.rxgain=off (LNA bypassed) unless the deployment environment is known to be RF-quiet. The beebo measure noise combined and beebo measure noise in_band procedures described in RF Experiments allow characterizing the local OOB environment: if the noise floor rises significantly with an antenna vs a 50-ohm terminator, and a bandpass filter brings it back down, OOB energy is present and the LNA should remain off — or a SAW filter should be added before the FEM.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
[1] SX1261/2 Data Sheet Rev 1.2, Semtech, June 2019.

[2] KCT Product Portfolio Q1 2025, Kangxi Communication Technologies.

[3] KCT8101L Product Datasheet Rev C, Kangxi Communication Technologies, October 2019.

[4] 47 CFR § 15.247 — Operation within the bands 902–928 MHz, 2400–2483.5 MHz, and 5725–5850 MHz. See also Understanding FCC Power Limits for Meshtastic Devices.

[5] Heltec V4: Measured TX Power Output Table, MeshCore Issue #1708 — conducted power measurements on V4.2 (GC1109) hardware across TX settings 1–24.

[6] MeshCore FAQ — Radio Presets, MeshCore upstream documentation — USA/Canada (Recommended) preset: 910.525 MHz, SF7, BW 62.5 kHz, CR 4/5.

[7] Friis formulas for noise, Wikipedia — cascade noise figure formula showing why the first amplifier stage dominates system noise performance.

[8] Johnson-Nyquist noise, Wikipedia — thermal noise generated by conductors at non-zero temperature; derives the \(kT\) noise power spectral density.

[9] Receiver sensitivity, Wikipedia — derivation of the standard sensitivity formula from thermal noise floor, noise figure, bandwidth, and required SNR.

[10] Heltec LoRa 32 (V4.3) Datasheet, Heltec Automation — Table 3.5.2 lists RX sensitivity at SF7/125 kHz as \(-122\) dBm.

docs.title: Health Check
docs.text:
beebo check is a one-shot check-up: one row per indicator, a verdict, and — when it isn't simply OK — what to do about it. The verdict levels, in the sense a blood-test report uses them:

beebo check on a repeater (the BLE PIN is masked). QoS fails here because only 56.6% of the node's sends were confirmed; the PENDING rows are decisions not yet made Verdict Meaning OK In range. INFO Technically fine, but worth a look — not actually a problem. PENDING Nothing wrong, but a decision hasn't been made yet, or not enough data exists to judge. WARN Outside range but not broken — a choice worth reconsidering. FAIL Actively wrong or hurting the node.

Where each indicator's data comes from matters, because check deliberately does none of beebo analyze's windowed aggregation — it's a point-in-time snapshot, not a historical trend. Every indicator is one of these kinds:

  • Live MonRing counters — QoS, RoS and SoH, computed fresh in firmware (MonRing::computeQos()/computeRos()/computeSoh()) from lifetime running counters on every header request. QoS is a ratio and RoS its raw-volume companion; neither is the same as SoH: a node can be fully healthy (SoH 100%, no internal faults) while QoS is degraded by an honestly weak link, and conversely a struggling node's internal faults show up in SoH even if QoS still looks fine. The tuners score their windows with the weighted objective described in Performance Tuning, not with these lifetime figures.
  • Live device setting — read fresh from the connected node right now (TX Power, RX Boosted Gain, FEM LNA, and the other settings rows).
  • Live tuning setting — the adaptive optimizer's own switches (Dynamic Tuning, Tuning Visibility).
  • Latest resident snapshot — the newest still-in-the-ring batt record (Battery, Battery Present). If the ring has wrapped past it, the check reports PENDING rather than guessing.

beebo analyze is the separate command for the windowed/aggregated indicators (tx_success_rate, wrong_hop_rate, cad_busy_rate, SNR/RSSI/noise-floor means, the tuners' objective score, ...) computed by bucketing a downloaded set of rx/tx/env records over time — see Analysis and In-Field LNA Comparison below. check and analyze are complementary, not overlapping: check answers "is anything wrong right now," analyze answers "how has this been trending."

Indicator Source What it means QoS Live MonRing counters (MonRing::computeQos()) Confirm ratio: (ack_success + echo_success) / (ack_success + ack_timeout + echo_attempts), 0-100%; PENDING until 20 confirmable attempts. OK ≥95%, INFO 80-95%, WARN 60-80%, FAIL <60%. RoS Live MonRing counters (MonRing::computeRos()) Confirmed deliveries per hour of uptime (ack_success + echo_success). OK if above zero, WARN if zero despite enough attempts, PENDING before 20 attempts. No fixed healthy band: traffic varies too much. SoH Live MonRing counters (MonRing::computeSoh()) Internal-health rate: 1 - (internal faults / total rx+tx activity), 0-100%, so a long-uptime node isn't penalized just for having processed more traffic. OK ≥99%, INFO 95-99%, WARN 80-95%, FAIL <80%. TX Power Live role's setting (companion.radio.txpower/repeater.radio.txpower) Bench-verified 16-18 dBm sweet spot for the V4.3 KCT8103L PA — below underdrives it (WARN), above buys no extra delivery benefit (INFO). RX Boosted Gain Live role's setting (companion.radio.rxgain/repeater.radio.rxgain) Recommended on (negligible current cost) — WARN if off. FEM LNA Live role's setting (companion.fem.rxgain/repeater.fem.rxgain) Sensitivity-vs-interference-tolerance tradeoff, site-dependent — always PENDING until verified against real traffic with beebo rxlog --compare or the LNA setting trial, never a pass/fail. BLE PIN Live role's node.ble.pin INFO while unset (falls back to the build's default PIN). Seen Window repeater.routing.seen_window (repeater only) WARN at 0: late echoes are no longer credited (the confirm ratio charges them as failures) and live-eviction counting is off, so rx_dedup_table_full no longer reflects reality. Admin Password Repeater admin password (repeater only) WARN while it is still the firmware's built-in default. Owner Info, Repeater Name repeater.node.owner.info, repeater.node.name (repeater only) INFO while unset. Region Default repeater.node.region.default (repeater only) PENDING when no regions exist yet, INFO when regions exist but no default scope is set. LoRa Preset Live role's radio.lora.* INFO when freq/bw/sf/cr match no known community preset. WiFi/TCP Live role's node.wifi.ssid and node.transport.tcp WARN when TCP is on with no SSID, INFO when an SSID is set but TCP is off. Battery Latest resident batt record PENDING while the trend is still settling after boot/an edge. OK while charging/charged/plugged/stable. While discharging: OK above ~30% estimated charge, WARN 15-30%, FAIL below 15%. Battery Present board.battery.present against the trend state PENDING if never declared; WARN when the flag contradicts the observed state (present yes but always plugged, or no but not plugged). Dynamic Tuning Live settings (repeater.routing.tuning.adaptive.enabled/.applied) PENDING if disabled, or enabled but still observe-only (nothing live-actuated yet). OK once at least one parameter is live-actuating. See The Adaptive Tuner. Tuning Visibility Live setting (monitor.tuning) + Dynamic Tuning's own verdict Only shown when it's actually actionable: the optimizer is live-actuating but adaptive records aren't being captured, so its proposals are invisible — WARN in that specific case, otherwise omitted from the table entirely.

The settings-derived rows (TX Power through WiFi/TCP) are shared with beebo config check, which runs only those against a saved template. Faults, queue drops and the raw diagnostic counters are not part of check; read them with beebo monitor status (see Reading monitor status) and beebo monitor decode -k event.

On the node console, check prints the QoS and SoH lines with the same bands and wording, so a phone can read the two scores that matter most. The other rows need beebo check.

$ gatto check
╭─────────────────┬──────────────────────┬───────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ Indicator       │ Value                │ Status    │ Reference / Action                       │
├─────────────────┼──────────────────────┼───────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ QoS             │ 98.4%                │ ✔ OK      │ Excellent.                               │
│ RoS             │ 41.2/hr              │ ✔ OK      │ Confirmed throughput -- see `beebo       │
│                 │                      │           │ analyze tuning` for trend.               │
│ SoH             │ 100.0%               │ ✔ OK      │ No meaningful fault rate.                │
│ TX Power        │ 18 dBm               │ ✔ OK      │ Within the bench-verified 16-18 dBm      │
│                 │                      │           │ sweet spot.                              │
│ RX Boosted Gain │ on                   │ ✔ OK      │ Recommended on (negligible current       │
│                 │                      │           │ cost).                                   │
│ FEM LNA         │ off                  │ … PENDING │ Site-dependent trade-off -- not verified │
│                 │                      │           │ against real traffic here.               │
│ Battery         │ 3.93 V (discharging) │ ✔ OK      │ ~67% estimated charge, discharging       │
│                 │                      │           │ normally.                                │
│ Battery Present │ yes                  │ ✔ OK      │ Flag matches the observed trend state.   │
│ Dynamic Tuning  │ observe-only         │ … PENDING │ Enabled but not live-actuating any       │
│                 │                      │           │ parameter yet.                           │
╰─────────────────┴──────────────────────┴───────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────╯

Nothing wrong, but some checks need a decision or more data (see PENDING rows).

docs.title: Firmware Internals
docs.text: How the beebo firmware works inside: roles, transports, the clock, diagnostics, the RF bench protocol and board changes. For what each feature does see the features; for updating a node see Update and Service a Node.

docs.title: Multi-Role: Switching Companion/Repeater
docs.text:
examples/multi_role folds companion_radio and simple_repeater into one firmware image. The role is a persisted setting (board.node.role, companion or repeater) and every role-conditional call site — login/ACL handling, self-advert type, self-info replies, packet-forwarding gates — reads the live role. The two roles are mutually exclusive: a node runs exactly one at a time. A role switch needs no reflash but always reboots the node (the user view is on the Roles page). Each role keeps its own identity, prefs, contacts and ACL on flash, loaded once at boot, so the switch itself only changes which role boots (a static-role build, e.g. heltec_v4_3_companion, compiles out the unwanted half entirely).

The role is changed with BEEBO_CMD_SET_NODE_ROLE (binary companion protocol), beebo settings board.node.role, or the node.role <value> text command, all routed through requestNodeRoleSwitch() (examples/multi_role/Beebo.h). On an actual change the firmware:

  • Refuses the switch outright while an OTA or bulk monitor-log transfer (beebo rxlog/monitor) is in flight (ERR_CODE_BAD_STATE) — neither session type has a way to preserve its cursor/handle across a reboot.
  • Flushes any pending dirty contacts/ACL write under the outgoing role.
  • Persists the new role to the board file unconditionally, whatever the autosave state.
  • Acknowledges, then reboots into the new role. Because the reboot always follows, the connection drops and a CLI alias's nodes/<node>/ identity stays valid for the life of the connection.

A switch to the role already running is a no-op. node.role has no equivalent on plain-text simple_repeater/companion_radio firmware (which predate the concept) and no -r/--raw CLI form — see board.node.role in the CLI settings reference. Identities can also be swapped as a unit with beebo config switch NAME, which imports the keypair, sets the name, switches the role if needed and reboots in one server-side call.

docs.title: Static-Role Builds
docs.text:
The switchable multi-role build is the right default, but it means every device carries both roles' static state whether or not it ever switches: the companion contact/channel/message store and the repeater ACL/region-map tables are both always loaded. For a device that will permanently run one role, build.sh --companion or build.sh --repeater produce a smaller image with the other role's state compiled out entirely (BEEBO_ENABLE_COMPANION_ROLE/BEEBO_ENABLE_REPEATER_ROLE, examples/multi_role/Beebo.h) instead of just disabled at runtime:

  • build.sh --companion → heltec_v4_3_companion: compiles out the repeater role's state: the ACL table, key store, region map, the anonymous-login and admin-request handlers.
  • build.sh --repeater → heltec_v4_3_repeater: compiles out the companion role, including the whole BaseChatMesh base class, so the contact table, channel table, connection table and offline message queue are absent from the binary.

Static RAM of the --jtag builds: 167,544 B for multi-role, 153,312 B for the companion build (14 KB less) and 138,096 B for the repeater build (29 KB less). The offline message queue lives in PSRAM in every build, so it no longer counts toward a role's saving.

Both are still examples/multi_role firmware, not a fork: same CMD_BEEBO binary protocol, same beebo CLI compatibility, same OTA mechanism. The only user-visible difference is board.node.role: a static build still reports and accepts its own role, but rejects switching to the role it wasn't built with (ERR_CODE_ILLEGAL_ARG over the binary protocol, a plain error over the text node.role command). A device previously flashed with the multi-role build (or the other static-role build) that has an incompatible persisted role falls back automatically at boot to whichever role the new image actually supports — no crash, no corrupted prefs, and the original persisted role is left untouched on flash (not overwritten) so re-flashing multi-role later restores it.

Pick the multi-role build unless a device's role is permanently fixed and the RAM headroom is worth the loss of runtime flexibility — a repeater-only build is the main case this matters for.

docs.title: Multi-Transport Session Locking
docs.text:
MultiSerialInterface aggregates the enabled transports. They all listen simultaneously when no session is active; the first to deliver a frame locks the session and the others are disabled until it disconnects (checkRecvFrame, src/helpers/MultiSerialInterface.h). A non-exclusive USB session can also be pre-emptied mid-flight if an exclusive transport (BLE/WiFi) wants to lock — USB is never allowed to starve wireless.

When the active client disconnects, disconnectActive() cycles only that one transport — disable() then enable() — and releases the lock so the others re-enable, without restarting the whole aggregator. There's no per-client queueing in this class, just a single active-transport index, so there's nothing to "flush" on takeover.

BLE and TCP are enforced as mutually exclusive at every set site, on both companion_radio and simple_repeater firmware — turning one on live-switches the other off (src/helpers/CommonCLI.cpp). If a toggle would otherwise leave both off, USB is force-enabled instead, since disabling USB saves no meaningful power once both radios are off. USB has no live add/remove path, so if that fallback would strand the caller's active BLE/TCP session with no live transport left, the device force-reboots automatically to bring USB up cleanly. Any transport-set command also accepts an explicit --reboot flag (beebo settings --reboot <path> <value>, or the equivalent admin toggle) to force a clean reboot after the change regardless.

SerialBLEInterface::deinitRadio() stops the NimBLE host and controller with BLEDevice::deinit(false), which also deletes the server; initRadio() rebuilds the server, service and both characteristics on the next BLE enable.

docs.title: Auto Time Sync
docs.text:
On every connection the beebo CLI reads the node's clock and compares it to the host's (an RTT-corrected, ms-precision two-round-trip probe-then-sync). A behind-drift is corrected forward unconditionally, no matter how small, straight through RTCClock::getTime()/setTime() (fw/src/helpers/ESP32Board.h) — no warning is printed first, since the firmware's own backwards-jump guard already protects RTC monotonicity, so there's nothing else to gate on. An ahead-drift can't be corrected live (the RTC only ever moves forward without a reboot): beebo clock --boot reboots the node with the correct time. Only a connected host sets the clock; contacts, adverts and other nodes' timestamps never do. This applies over the companion binary protocol and, via the text-CLI equivalents (clock.epoch/time <secs>), over -r/--raw connections too. Apart from a repeater's own admin-only clock sync, the device clock never syncs itself (no NTP, no sync-on-connect in the firmware) — it free-runs and only advances via a connection's own auto-sync, so nodes reconnected after being off mesh for a while don't silently carry a stale clock.

Run beebo clock any time to see the result of that connection's own auto-sync (Device, the clock's value from before the sync; Source, the host time it was compared/corrected against) without triggering a second, redundant sync. Pass --boot to force an immediate corrective reboot when the device is found ahead, instead of waiting for a future organic reboot to apply the recorded drift — --boot is the only case where beebo clock runs its own live round trip rather than reusing the connection's own auto-sync result, since the automatic sync never reboots the device on its own.

docs.title: RTC Persistence Across Power Cycles
docs.text: A soft reset keeps the RTC alive in RAM, but a true power cycle (ESP_RST_POWERON) would reset it to a fixed epoch. So reboot() saves the current time to NVS before calling esp_restart(), and ESP32RTCClock::begin() restores from that saved value on a power-on boot (src/helpers/ESP32Board.h). Combined with Auto Time Sync, this means a node's clock now survives being fully powered off between visits, rather than only surviving reboots that happen while it stays powered.

docs.title: Diagnostics and Protocol Additions
docs.text:
• Transport debug ring — an in-RAM ring buffer traces connect/disconnect/lock events across BLE/TCP/USB, streamed live by beebo monitor debug (monitor watch skips the backlog) and correlated to wall-clock time.
  • MonRing capture ring — a continuous RX/TX monitor ring in free PSRAM records per-packet RSSI/SNR/noise and disposition, backing beebo monitor/rxlog/analyze. Also carries the tuning optimizer's records (MON_ADAPTIVE decisions, MON_EVAL windows and blocks, MON_TRIAL setting-trial records), setting-change and command-run records, and a general fault event log (MON_EVENT) — see Performance Tuning and the record kinds.
  • RSSI in message frames — RX RSSI is written into the two reserved bytes of the V3 synced-message frame (MSG_INCLUDE_RSSI), so drained messages carry RSSI alongside SNR; wire-compatible, old apps just ignore the bytes.
  • Extended stats — companion stats commands (STATS_TYPE_CORE/RADIO/PACKETS, plus system and profile stats) surface heap/PSRAM/flash usage, loop/dup packet counts and the command-latency ring.
  • Clean session teardown — CMD_APP_DISCONNECT lets a client end its own transport session without tearing down the others.
  • Bulk transfer — BULK_XFER streams large TX frames and paged MonRing drains without buffering the whole payload.
  • Streamed OTA — OTA writes stream straight to flash instead of buffering the image in PSRAM first.

docs.title: RF Bench/Measurement Protocol Additions
docs.text:
These are examples/multi_role additions, dispatched as BEEBO_CMD_* sub-commands under the companion protocol's CMD_BEEBO wrapper (examples/multi_role/BeeboProtocol.h, generated from protocol.yaml), not top-level companion commands:

  • CW carrier mode — BEEBO_CMD_SET_CW (sub-id 6) drives a continuous-wave test carrier with a safety auto-stop deadline, for bench TX power measurement.
  • TX power optimize toggle — BEEBO_CMD_SET_TX_OPTIMIZE (sub-id 7) switches between RadioLib's efficiency-oriented paOptTable and a fixed monotonic PA mapping for SX1262.
  • KCT8103L FEM LNA control — companion.fem.rxgain / repeater.fem.rxgain (a per-role persisted pref, read and written through the prefs TLV opcodes) toggle the V4.3 front-end module's LNA; disabled by default, reports unsupported on GC1109 (V4.2) boards via auto-detection.
  • RX boosted gain — companion.radio.rxgain / repeater.radio.rxgain toggle the SX1262 RX boosted-gain setting the same way.
  • RSSI at the antenna connector — board.fem.rssi_offset.lna / .bypass (default −17/+2 dB) are added to every SX1262 RSSI read for the active FEM path, so packet RSSI and the noise floor read at the antenna connector whatever fem.rxgain is; 0/0 gives raw SX1262 values. See RSSI at the Antenna Connector.
  • Noise floor restart — changing rxgain, fem.rxgain or the active RSSI offset restarts the noise-floor average, so it never mixes samples from two RX paths. The radio itself is not reset; the SX1262 AGC reset stays on the upstream agc_reset_interval timer.

docs.title: Heltec V4 Board FW Changes
docs.text:
The beebo build modifies the upstream Heltec V4 board configuration for headless operation:

  • Optimized settings — default transmission power is set not to exceed the Power Amplifier (PA) compression point.
  • GPS disabled — the bare board has no GPS module (ENV_INCLUDE_GPS=0).
  • Button and display removed — compiled out for headless deployment (no PIN_USER_BTN, no DISPLAY_CLASS).
  • Board name — reports as "Heltec V4.3 Headless" (or "Heltec V4 Headless" for ≤ V4.2) instead of the OLED/TFT variants.
  • LoRa front-end logging — auto-detected PA type (KCT8103L or GC1109) is printed at boot for hardware identification.
  • USB CDC on boot — enabled so the USB port is available for serial debug, and as a companion transport when usb is enabled.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: beebo monitor reads MonRing, a continuous ring buffer in free PSRAM (see Diagnostics and Protocol Additions) that the firmware appends to on its own — nothing needs to be running or connected on the host for capture to happen. beebo monitor just controls it and reads it back: start/stop, clear, capture (per-kind on/off), pull (incremental raw download into a local per-device dataset), list (per-file/per-kind record counts for what's been pulled), decode (view/filter the pulled dataset, or --save it as CSV/JSON for beebo analyze).

docs.title: Using the monitor
docs.text:
$ beebo monitor                          # ring fill, capture state, window and packet totals
$ beebo monitor pull                     # download the new records into the local dataset
$ beebo monitor list                     # what has been pulled, per file and kind
$ beebo monitor decode -k rx --limit 20  # view and filter the pulled records
$ beebo monitor decode --save            # write CSV/JSON for `beebo analyze`
$ beebo monitor capture rx off           # switch one record kind off

docs.title: Live charts
docs.text:
beebo monitor plot draws what the node hears as it happens, in the terminal. monitor plot rssi charts each received packet's RSSI per neighbor, with the noise floor and a level line at the best RSSI since the start, and a table of the last, average and best RSSI, the packet count and the rate of each neighbor. It is meant for placing an antenna: move the antenna and watch the levels follow.

beebo monitor plot rssi: three neighbors (b2, 96 and 7a) and the noise floor over the last 60 s

monitor plot tuning indicators and monitor plot tuning trial chart the tuning indicators and a running setting trial the same way. Every option is in the CLI reference.

docs.title: Reading monitor status
docs.text: beebo monitor status answers "how is the node doing right now?" without downloading the ring. It prints three tables, and monitor status health, service or rates prints one of them. On the node console the same sections come as name=value lines of the counters that are not zero. The counters count from boot; nothing is saved across a reboot.

docs.title: Health: the node's own faults
docs.text:
Health Status counts the node's internal faults and drops, the inputs of the SoH score in Health Check. A healthy node reads zero on every row. A row that grows says what ran out.

beebo monitor status health on a healthy repeater: every counter reads zero Counter What it counts rx_pool_full Incoming frame dropped due to buffer full rx_queue_full Delayed packet dropped with scheduling queue full tx_queue_full ACK reply dropped with send queue full link_tx_queue_full Outbound frame to app dropped: BLE/WiFi/USB queue full link_rx_queue_full Inbound frame from app dropped: BLE queue full tx_pool_full Outgoing/forwarded packet dropped: packet buffer full tx_cad_timeout Channel busy past max CAD duration rx_start_timeout Radio stuck out of RX mode >8s tx_ack_overflow ACK expected-table wrapped onto an unresolved slot tx_echo_overflow Repeat ring wrapped onto an unresolved slot rx_dedup_table_full Hash evicted from the dedup table within the live window. Shown here but not part of SoH

Each name is also an event type of the Event Catalog, where the occurrences carry timestamps.

docs.title: Service: traffic and delivery
docs.text:
Service Status is what the node handled and how its sends fared. The host adds a Rate column, events per minute over a moving 60 s window; see Counter rates.

beebo monitor status service on a repeater: counts, rate per minute and what each counter means Counter What it counts rx_packets Total lifetime packets received rx_flood, rx_direct Flood-routed and direct-routed packets received rx_flood_dup, rx_direct_dup Duplicate receptions of each rx_errors Radio-level receive errors (CRC/malformed) rx_parse_error Frame captured but failed to parse. Counted in QoS, not in SoH tx_packets Total lifetime packets sent tx_flood, tx_direct Flood-routed and direct-routed packets sent tx_direct_success, tx_direct_timeout A direct send's ACK arrived, or its deadline elapsed unconfirmed tx_flood_success, tx_flood_timeout A flood send's repeat was heard, or its window elapsed unconfirmed tx_direct_untracked Direct sends with no ACK expected (replies, adverts, admin frames) tx_flood_pending Flood sends awaiting echo confirmation (recent, not yet resolved) tx_max_hop_no_fwd Repeater: flood packet already past its configured hop limit tx_region_no_fwd Repeater: flood packet's region tag matched no flood-allowed region tx_loop_no_fwd Repeater: flood packet dropped by loop detection

The success and timeout rows are what QoS is computed from. The three *_no_fwd rows are configured policy, not faults, so they are not in SoH.

docs.title: Rates: where the time goes
docs.text:
Service Rates is the node's own time over the latest 10 s window, in percent of the window except where noted. The metrics are explained in Time, Headroom and Routing-Latency Metrics.

beebo monitor status rates: where the node's time went over the latest 10 s window Metric Meaning rx_busy, tx_busy Time spent in RX and in TX lx_busy Time spent on host communication (USB/BLE/TCP) sys_busy Time spent on other main-loop housekeeping lp_idle Time idle loops_per_sec Loop iterations per second (a count) max_loop_latency_ms Worst single loop stall in the window (milliseconds) tx_wait_airtime Time TX waited on the airtime/duty-cycle budget tx_wait_cad Time TX waited on channel-activity detection rx_wait_relay Time an RX relay was delayed past its scheduled time

A firmware built without CPU accounting prints no Rates table.

docs.title: Automating periodic pulls
docs.text:
A cron job or systemd timer that just runs beebo -t <device> monitor pull on an interval is enough to keep an offline dataset in sync — pull is incremental by default (only records newer than the local cursor are fetched), so a routine run only transfers what's new since the last one, not the whole ring. No separate daemon or state file to manage beyond what pull already keeps (monring.cursor.json, next to the pulled .bin files).

The only thing to size is the interval itself, against how fast the ring fills: beebo -t <device> monitor (no subcommand) prints the ring's current fill (e.g. 22,486 / 65,536 records) and its elapsed span, so records ÷ elapsed gives a rough fill rate — pick an interval comfortably shorter than (capacity − typical fill) ÷ rate, so the ring can't wrap (evicting records pull hasn't fetched yet) between two runs. beebo -t <device> monitor list shows the same per-day/per-kind breakdown for what's actually accumulated locally, handy for spot-checking that a scheduled pull is really keeping up.

Example crontab entry, pulling every 15 minutes:

*/15 * * * * /path/to/venv/bin/gatto monitor pull >> ~/.beebo/pull.log 2>&1

Or a systemd user timer (~/.config/systemd/user/beebo-pull@.service/.timer, one instance per device via systemctl --user enable --now beebo-pull@gatto.timer):

# beebo-pull@.service
[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/path/to/venv/bin/beebo -t %i monitor pull

# beebo-pull@.timer
[Timer]
OnBootSec=5min
OnUnitActiveSec=15min

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

docs.title: Record kinds
docs.text:
Each record is a fixed 16 bytes, one of fourteen kinds:

Kind What it captures Cadence sync A time-base relatch (epoch anchor for every record after it, until the next one) Automatic, on ring init/wrap or a clock jump rx One reception: SNR, RSSI, neighbor, packet type/route, and its disposition (see below) Every RX (if monitor.rx is on) tx One of this node's own transmissions: route, type, destination, airtime, result (ok/timeout) Every TX (if monitor.tx is on) radio The live radio config (freq/sf/bw/cr/tx_power/rxgain/fem.rxgain) Only on a real change (dedup'd) env Noise floor, battery, MCU temp, free heap, packet-pool free count, TX queue depth, sticky fault flags, CAD-busy episode count Only on a real change (dedup'd); monitor.env off by default (higher volume) batt One battery voltage sample, with idle/trend state and which transport radios are powered Periodic (board.battery.sample_period) adaptive One adaptive-tuner decision (param, old/proposed value, reward) Once per tuning tick, repeater role only, opt-in (monitor.tuning) — see The Adaptive Tuner eval One closed evaluation window or trial block (indicators, outcome, flags) Once per window/block while a tuner or trial runs, opt-in (monitor.tuning) trial One setting-trial record: a start (setting, sides, schedule), one per block (running mean and bounds) or an end (outcome, statistics) While a trial runs, opt-in (monitor.tuning) — see The setting trial setting One admin-visible setting change: which one, old/new value, and which dispatch path made it Immediately, whenever a change happens command One command run that mutates state or is a deliberate one-shot action (OTA begin/end, reboot, a SET_*/set ...) — routine reads/polling are NOT logged, to keep this from flooding Immediately, whenever an eligible command runs event A discrete, timestamped occurrence with no other fixed shape (faults, overflows, queue drops, ...) — see the full catalog below Immediately, at the moment each occurrence happens route Radio/link utilization and queue-wait snapshots Periodic while capture is enabled debug Firmware diagnostic event: severity, source file/line, event type, detail, and five raw user bytes When firmware emits a persisted high/medium debug event

Enabling a setting trial turns tuning, event and radio capture on and rx and tx capture off for the run. monitor.path is not a record kind: it makes an RX record hold the last three hops of its path (one byte each) instead of the last hop's identity, off by default; analyze paths reads it. setting/command share event's capture toggle (monitor.event) — there's no separate leaf for them, since they're still conceptually part of "admin/event activity capture," just split into their own record kinds because every instance shares one fixed column shape (unlike the genuinely one-off events below).

setting/command were split out of the generic event kind precisely because they always carry the same fixed columns (setting/old_value/new_value/source and command/source respectively) — unlike faults, overflows, and queue drops, which are each their own one-off shape and stay under event.

monitor.event is an all-or-nothing switch for the whole event kind; beebo monitor events is a finer filter underneath it, one on/off bit per individual event TYPE (Event Catalog name, e.g. tx_ack_success) — useful since capture isn't free and a busy node can log a lot of high-volume verdict events. beebo monitor events alone lists every type's current state; beebo monitor events <name> on|off toggles one. Unlike monitor capture's persisted per-kind bits, this mask is RAM-only and resets to capture-everything on every reboot — a live tuning knob, not a standing device policy.

An rx record's disposition is three independent axes packed into one byte, so a single reception can carry several outcomes at once (e.g. accepted and forwarded) instead of one lossy "best" value:

  • endpoint — the local/terminal verdict: accepted, not_for_us, duplicated, wrong_hop, filtered, incomplete, forged_sig, self, unknown_type, parse_err, pool_full, misc_drop.
  • routing — what this node did as a relay: forwarded, no_forward, path_full.
  • invalid — a rider bit meaning the frame's header/path didn't parse (malformed or truncated), so route, neighbor and hash are unknown (doesn't affect actual packet handling).
  • queue_full — a rider bit meaning routing said forwarded but the actual send never happened (send_queue was full when the firmware tried to enqueue it) — see tx_queue_full below for why this is a bit on the record rather than a separate event. beebo analyze tuning indicators excludes forwarded+queue_full records from its routed count.

docs.title: Per-kind capture defaults
docs.text: beebo settings monitor.* (or beebo monitor capture) switches each record kind on or off independently. On a fresh device rx, tx, sync, radio, batt, event, setting and command capture by default. env and tuning are opt-in: env is comparatively high-volume, and tuning covers the adaptive, eval and trial records, so turn it on before running either tuner. This default only applies once, when a device's prefs file is first created. An already-provisioned device that has since been upgraded keeps the capture byte it already had, so a newly added kind (like event, added after some deployed devices' files existed) does not turn on for them. Check beebo settings monitor after upgrading and turn on anything you expect but don't see.

docs.title: Time, Headroom and Routing-Latency Metrics
docs.text: Besides the score, beebo tracks a second family of signals — how the node's own loop/CPU time is spent, and how much of a packet's delay is internal (this node computing) versus external (waiting on channel/budget backpressure). These are diagnostic only and not part of the on-device reward — see Using these signals for tuning below for exactly what's wired in and what isn't.

docs.title: RX/TX/LX/SYS busy and system idle
docs.text:
rx_busy/tx_busy/lx_busy measure wall-clock time spent in checkRecv()/checkSend()/host communication (USB/BLE/TCP), including any blocking wait on hardware inside them (radio SPI, USB/BLE transfer) — not CPU cycles the way an OS "CPU time" figure would be. sys_busy covers everything else in the main loop that isn't rx/tx-dispatched or lx-timed — battery ADC refresh, the slow-stat cache (storage usage, MCU temperature), env sampling, OTA/echo timeout checks — some of it non-trivial (a temperature read averages four ~76ms samples). lp_idle ("loop-idle") is the remainder across every task at once (window - (rx_busy + tx_busy + lx_busy + sys_busy)) — a system-wide figure, not a per-task one; there's no such thing as "TX's own idle time" separate from this. Without sys_busy, that housekeeping time was silently counted as idle, since the main loop never actually sleeps/yields.

Two tiers: a live ~1s window (freshest single sample) and a 10s-averaged reported figure (a genuine average over the full period, not a point-sample) — the reported tier is what reaches the wire and both CLI surfaces. Visible in beebo status resources' "Time" bar and beebo monitor status's "Service Rates" table (busy per task and lp_idle, each its own row).

docs.title: Loop headroom: loops/sec and max loop latency
docs.text: Cause-agnostic, unlike the breakdown above — it doesn't matter why the loop was busy, only that a lower iteration rate or a long single stall both mean less capacity for anything else that runs once per main-loop pass (radio housekeeping, companion polling, tuning ticks included). loops_per_sec and max_loop_latency_ms (worst single-iteration stall in the last 10s) are in the same "Time"/Service Rates surfaces. A stall past 500ms (MAX_LOOP_LATENCY_THRESHOLD_MS) also fires a MON_EVENT record (max_loop_latency, beebo monitor decode -k event) with the exact triggering duration and a running lifetime count — a general watchdog for "something blocked hard," independent of knowing the cause in advance.

docs.title: Routing latency: busy vs. wait (MON_ROUTE/RouteRecord)
docs.text:
A different axis from loop occupancy entirely: where does a packet spend time, not the loop. Split as a clean 2×2 — busy (time actually running the RX/TX code path; same signal as rx_busy/tx_busy above) versus wait (elapsed time a packet sits blocked before busy happens, caused by something external — a resource duty-cycle, not a slice of occupied loop time). A node can show high lp_idle and high TX-wait at the same time without contradiction — loop occupancy and external backpressure are orthogonal, which is exactly why wait is never subtracted from busy or lp_idle.

Field Measures Ties to tx_wait_airtime TX-ready packets blocked on the duty-cycle/airtime budget airtime_factor — the real delay cost of the current budget setting tx_wait_cad TX-ready packets blocked because the radio is receiving a frame, the channel reads busy (RSSI check or hardware CAD), or in the retry backoff after either Reception in progress (not tunable), interference_threshold, radio.cad (and, indirectly, agc_reset_interval) — how often channel sensing is actually the bottleneck rx_wait_relay A delayed flood-relay's actual send time overrunning calcRxDelay()'s own scheduled time rx_delay_base — whether the jitter this parameter introduces is being pushed further out by real backpressure once the scheduled moment arrives

Two ways to read these: live (beebo status resources/beebo monitor status's Service Rates — the same 10s window as the busy/idle figures above, no ring download) or persisted history (beebo monitor decode -k route, a snapshot appended every minute regardless of whether anything changed — a periodic reading of 0% is itself meaningful, not filtered out). The two are separate consumers on separate windows (10s live vs. 1-minute persisted) — don't expect them to match exactly at any given instant.

docs.title: Counter rates
docs.text: beebo monitor status's Service Status table has a Rate column (events per minute) beside Count: a moving 60 s sum of each counter, refreshed every second, so every row shares the same window. Rows that are a current state (tx_direct_untracked, tx_flood_pending) show -. Not symmetrically "successful": the rx_* rows count every structurally-valid received packet before dedup filtering (duplicates included, see the *_dup rows), while tx_packets/tx_flood/ tx_direct count only sends that actually completed on air (forwards included, not echo-confirmed; excludes timeouts/failures) — worth knowing before reconciling either figure against some other packet count. For trended history over a downloaded capture, beebo analyze rate --window <minutes> buckets MON_RX/MON_TX timestamps the same way beebo analyze tuning indicators buckets its indicators.

docs.title: Using these signals for tuning
docs.text: These metrics are diagnostic, not decisional — nothing above feeds AdaptiveController's reward or bandit selection. Reading them alongside a tuning session tells you why a parameter's effect looks the way it does: e.g. if raising airtime_factor doesn't move the score much, check whether tx_wait_airtime was already low — the budget wasn't the actual bottleneck, so tightening it further has nothing to bite on. If rx_wait_relay stays near zero while rx_delay_base changes, the scheduled jitter isn't being pushed further out by real congestion, which argues for spending the tuning budget elsewhere.

docs.title: Event Catalog
docs.text:
event records are MonRing's general-purpose log for occurrences with no fixed shape of their own — one record per notable, discrete thing that happened, each with a real timestamp. Setting changes and command runs have their own setting/command record kinds (see Record kinds above), since every instance shares one fixed column layout, unlike the one-off events below. Every remaining event type names its own cause — there's no generic "something happened" event with a reason code buried in the payload; if two occurrences need telling apart for root-causing, they're different event types. The three fault events (tx_pool_full, tx_cad_timeout, rx_start_timeout) fire on every occurrence, not just the first, so the event trail shows when each started and whether it recurred.

Event Trigger Payload tx_cad_timeout Channel-activity detection got stuck reporting the channel busy past its configured max duration cumulative rx_dedup_table_full The main RX dedup table (160 entries) had no free slot for a new hash and overwrote one that still held a real, previously-inserted hash — not an empty/never-used slot. Every eviction of a live hash is a chance a genuine duplicate goes undetected (its hash is gone by the time the duplicate arrives, so it's wrongly treated as new — re-forwarded, double-counted, and invisible to the ordinary duplicate counters, which only count dups that WERE caught). Expect this to fire on most inserts once the table has filled once after boot — that volume is itself the signal, not a sign something is broken cumulative link_rx_queue_full The node's BLE inbound frame queue was full (WiFi has no equivalent queue — it reads directly off the TCP stream) cumulative link_tx_queue_full The node's transport link (BLE or WiFi, whichever is active) had a full outbound frame queue, or USB's own DebugLog retry queue (DLOG/MLOG/raw-ack telemetry, not the companion session's own USB traffic) dropped a frame — app connectivity/telemetry, NOT mesh routing capacity. Applies regardless of role (companion, repeater) cumulative rx_parse_error A frame WAS captured (briefly allocated) but failed to parse (bad version/path-mode/corrupt/oversize) — different cause from rx_pool_full (radio/allocation capacity vs. a malformed frame), so its own event type cumulative rx_pool_full Dispatcher::checkRecv() had no free packet buffer to receive an incoming frame into — the radio had data, but every slot in the fixed packet pool was already in use. No rx record exists for this occurrence (no Packet was ever allocated) cumulative (lifetime count, after this occurrence) rx_queue_full The scheduling queue for a delayed (score-jittered) flood packet was full — dropped before it was even processed, before any disposition was assigned cumulative rx_start_timeout The radio was stuck out of RX mode for more than 8 seconds cumulative tx_ack_overflow The DM/ACK expected-table wrapped onto a slot that hadn't reached a verdict yet — a real starvation event (too many concurrent in-flight sends for the table's fixed depth), not a silent no-op. A resource fault, not a third verdict alongside success/timeout, hence its own event type pkt_hash, age_ms (how long the evicted slot had been pending, unresolved) tx_ack_success A DM/ACK was matched — delivery confirmed pkt_hash, age_ms (round-trip time) tx_ack_timeout No DM/ACK arrived within the deadline. Never overflow — see tx_ack_overflow above pkt_hash, age_ms (round-trip time) tx_echo_overflow Same starvation case, flood-echo side: the self-tx tracking ring wrapped onto an unresolved slot pkt_hash, age_ms tx_echo_success A neighbor's rebroadcast confirmed this node's own flood transmission was heard pkt_hash, age_ms tx_echo_timeout The echo window elapsed with no rebroadcast heard. Never overflow — see tx_echo_overflow above pkt_hash, age_ms tx_max_hop_no_fwd Repeater role only: a flood packet's path already had as many hops as repeater.routing.flood.max/.max_unscoped/.max_advert allow, so it wasn't relayed further. A configured limit, not a fault — excluded from SoH. The lifetime total is beebo monitor status's Service Status tx_max_hop_no_fwd counter, not duplicated into this payload pkt_hash tx_loop_no_fwd Repeater role only: repeater.routing.loop.detect found this node already appears in the packet's path too many times, so it wasn't relayed further (loop suppression). A configured limit, not a fault — excluded from SoH. Lifetime total lives in beebo monitor status instead, see tx_max_hop_no_fwd above pkt_hash tx_pool_full Dispatcher::obtainNewPacket() had no free packet buffer available when building an outgoing or forwarded packet cumulative tx_queue_full This node's own outbound send_queue was full when trying to queue a self-originated transmission or ACK reply (not a relay of a received packet — a relay's equivalent case is the queue_full disposition bit on that packet's own rx record, not a separate event, since that trace is already richer) cumulative tx_region_no_fwd Repeater role only: a region-tagged flood packet's transport code matched no flood-allowed region this repeater has defined (see beebo region) — either genuinely unrecognized, or it matched a flood-denied region. A configured policy drop, not a fault — excluded from SoH. Lifetime total lives in beebo monitor status instead, see tx_max_hop_no_fwd above pkt_hash tx_suppressed A queued packet was discarded unsent because transmit is off (node.transmit) pkt_hash tx_echo_other A repeat of a send that had already timed out unconfirmed arrived inside the seen window but was not its echo: it did not carry our sent path plus one hash, so a repeater that never heard us relayed it by another route. Not credited; once per send pkt_hash, age_ms, attempt, the echo window in ms trial_pkt_rate The trial sequence started waiting for traffic (the RX rate fell below tuning.trial.min_pkt_rate) or resumed. Logged on each change, checked once a minute while waiting waiting (1) or resumed (0), the RX rate then, the minimum, in packets a minute max_loop_latency The gap between two consecutive loop() calls exceeded the stall threshold. Cause-agnostic: it says something stalled, not which call latency_ms (the triggering gap), cumulative route_stats Measured every 60 s whether or not tuning or a trial runs, and logged only when a value changed (and for the first interval after boot): an interval that is not logged repeated the last values, and analyze tuning indicators fills it in.
