Frames the radio never demodulated, the share of the interval TX was blocked by CAD-busy or backoff, and the mean packet pool occupancy. beebo analyze tuning indicators charts them as RX Errors, CAD Busy and Pool Busy rx_errors (count), cad_busy_pct, pool_busy_pct, interval_s

A setting or command record's source is the dispatch path: binary (a companion-protocol opcode), text_cli (the CommonCLI text command) or tuning (the on-device tuner itself, for example a trial winner being persisted).

monitor decode -k event (and -k setting/-k command) renders one Rich table on the console, with columns for the union of fields across every row in the result — sparse when the set mixes different event types, since each one only fills the columns it actually uses. monitor decode --save NAME.json is often easier to read for a mixed set, since each record is its own compact object instead of one wide table. Mixing kinds (-k event -k setting -k command) interleaves them by position instead of padding to one shared column set:

$ gatto monitor pull
$ gatto monitor decode --save events.json
[
  {"pos": 117, "time": "2026-07-27 14:01:58", "kind": "setting", "setting": "adaptive_enabled",
   "old_value": 0, "new_value": 1, "source": "text_cli"},
  {"pos": 118, "time": "2026-07-27 14:02:11", "kind": "event", "event": "tx_pool_full",
   "cumulative": 1},
  {"pos": 119, "time": "2026-07-27 14:02:11", "kind": "event", "event": "rx_pool_full",
   "cumulative": 1},
  {"pos": 120, "time": "2026-07-27 14:03:02", "kind": "event", "event": "tx_echo_success",
   "pkt_hash": "2dac9975", "age_ms": 3144},
  {"pos": 121, "time": "2026-07-27 14:05:40", "kind": "event", "event": "tx_ack_overflow",
   "pkt_hash": "99887766", "age_ms": 8120},
  {"pos": 122, "time": "2026-07-27 14:11:05", "kind": "event", "event": "rx_dedup_table_full",
   "cumulative": 4},
  {"pos": 123, "time": "2026-07-27 14:12:30", "kind": "command", "command": "reboot",
   "source": "text_cli"}
]

_save_records()/_json_row() derive columns from the union of row keys across every record in the set, so a new event type never needs a schema change on the CLI side to show up in monitor decode, printed or --saved.

docs.title: The Phone Feed
docs.text:
Beebo creates two private channels in the app's channel list:

Channel What it is beebo-status Lines the node posts about itself. Anything you type here is ignored. beebo-cli Type a command and the node's reply appears in the channel.

They are ordinary channels with a random secret, listed like any other. Nothing in them is ever sent over the air, and a message received over the air on these channels is dropped. You can rename them. A feed that you delete is recreated at the next boot with a new secret.

Both roles have them. A repeater has no contacts and refuses messages to normal channels, but the feed works as in a companion.

docs.title: Status lines
docs.text:
Every line starts with the node's name.

Line When boot <version> <role> <reset reason> The node has started. mon <on or off> rx=<n> tx=<n> qos=<pct or -> soh=<pct> A minute after boot, then hourly: packets received and sent, the share of sends confirmed by an ACK or a heard repeat (- until there is data) and the node's health score. warn: txpower=<n> dBm underdrives the PA, run: settings radio.txpower 18 At boot and when a trial is enabled, if the transmit power is under 16 dBm. trial waiting for traffic A trial is on but the node hears too little traffic to start. trial <setting> start profile=<name> a=<a> b=<b> blocks=<n> block=<s>s A trial begins. trial <setting> blk <i>/<n> pairs=<p> gain=<%> [<low>,<high>] A block closed. The interval appears once the trial has one. trial <setting> <result> a=<a> b=<b> pairs=<p> gain=<%> se=<%> A trial ended. See Setting Trials. trial <setting> <outcome> A switch declined to run: skipped_same, skipped_no_control or skipped_underpowered. See Setting Trials. The beebo-status channel with hourly monitor lines

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
The beebo-cli channel runs the command on the live role. A reply over 160 characters is split into up to four numbered parts. A command with no output answers (no output). The same commands work in the app's own CLI screen, which shows the first 160 characters of a reply. They use the words of the beebo command line:

Command What it does settings <path> Reads a setting, with the path beebo settings uses settings <path> <value> Sets it settings and settings <branch> List the names below the top level or a branch (settings routing.tuning.trial) status, status node, status radio, status resources Name, role, version, uptime, supply, faults; noise floor, RSSI, SNR and airtime; memory, contacts, messages and ring fill check The QoS and SoH verdicts of beebo check monitor Capture state and ring fill monitor status, monitor status health, ... service, ... rates The counters that are not zero (health faults, traffic and delivery) and the time shares of the node monitor start, monitor stop, monitor clear Resume or pause the capture, or empty the ring monitor capture and monitor capture <leaf> on\|off Show or set what is captured: enabled, rx, tx, radio, env, batt, tuning, event, path monitor tuning trial, ... start [switch...\|all], ... stop The trial state, start it with the named switches, stop it (repeater role) battery state Whether a battery is present, the voltage and the charge state; battery state <state> forces the state for testing battery calibrate <volts> Sets board.adc.multiplier from a voltmeter reading at the battery; 4.2 V is a fully charged battery. The host takes the same argument advert flood, advert direct Send a flood or a direct advert neighbors peek, neighbors forget <hex>, neighbors discover [-t type] The live neighbor table, prune an entry, ask nearby nodes who they are (repeater role) region tree, region allow <name>, region deny <name>, region put, region remove, region save, region def The flood regions (repeater role) clock, reboot, ver The node's time, restart it, firmware version and build date

settings reaches the trial, routing, radio, FEM, battery, node and board settings that have a plain value. Commands lists what runs on the node and what stays on the computer. A repeater-only path answers ERR: needs role 'repeater', node is 'companion' on a companion. The rest of the tree, the downloads, the plots and the analysis are in beebo, on a computer. The older text commands (get, set) keep working: see the key list.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The feed queue lives in RAM, so a reboot loses lines that the app had not synced. The boot line is posted again.
  • When the queue is full, feed lines take priority over other messages.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
beebo.api exposes the same device logic as a library, without the Typer CLI: no argv[0] node identity, and errors raised as BeeboError (with BeeboTimeoutError and BeeboDeviceError) instead of a printed message and an exit code. SyncNode is the blocking facade; Node is the async primitive with the same methods.

from beebo.api import SyncNode

with SyncNode(node="gatto").connect() as node:
    print(node.name, node.role, node.transport)
    print(node.status()["node"]["uptime_secs"])
    node.settings.repeater.routing.tuning.trial.block_size_s = 300
    files = node.monitor_pull()
  • Target: at most one of node=, ble=, tcp=, usb=, on the constructor or on connect(). node= reads ~/.beebo/nodes/<node>/profile.toml; a connect() target persists on the object.
  • Methods: status(), battery(), reboot(), advert(), region_*(), channels_*() and channel_*() (list, get, set, remove, send, push, pull), traffic_inject(), sustain_start()/sustain_stop()/sustain_status(), download_messages(), send_message(), refresh_contacts(), lookup_contact(), monitor_stats()/monitor_status()/monitor_clear()/monitor_pull(), and get(path)/set(path, value) for one setting by dotted path. Properties: name, role, transport, mc. Every signature is in the Python API Reference.
  • Settings tree: node.settings.<path> reads or writes a leaf as an attribute, and with group.restored(): puts every setting under that group back on exit.
  • Trials: beebo.trials.Trial.latest(node.monitor_pull()) (or Trial.from_files(files) for all of them) reads pulled trials offline (outcome, change, se, confidence, pairs, report()).
  • Context managers disconnect on exit but do not connect on entry, so a connect failure is an ordinary exception you can catch around the with.

SyncNode runs one background event loop for the whole process, so drive each SyncNode from one thread and use Node for concurrent event streams. Runnable examples: beebo/examples/two_nodes_{sync,async,with}.py, and beebo run api-demo / api-sync-demo.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: From a stock MeshCore board to a beebo node you run from your phone, in about ten minutes. You do not need the beebo command line for any of it.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
• A Heltec WiFi LoRa 32 V4 (headless use; the V4.3 is the reference board) and a USB cable.
  • A computer to flash from, and the MeshCore app on your phone.
  • A board that has run MeshCore before. A brand-new board needs one stock image first: see Troubleshooting.

If the board already runs MeshCore v1.18.0, beebo keeps its settings and starts in the role it had.

docs.title: 1. Flash
docs.text:
Open the MeshCore Web Flasher, choose Custom Firmware, and select heltec-v4-1.18.0.beebo.1.0.bin from the releases page.

Check: the flasher reports success and the board restarts.

docs.title: 2. Connect
docs.text:
Connect the MeshCore app over BLE as you always do. The default pairing PIN is 123456. If the app cannot connect to a board you paired before, remove the board from your phone's Bluetooth list and pair again.

Check: the app shows your node.

docs.title: 3. Find the feed
docs.text:
Two new channels appear in the channel list: beebo-status and beebo-cli. Within a few seconds of a restart, beebo-status shows the boot line:

beebo-mr: boot 1.18.0.beebo.1.0 repeater SW (esp_restart)

Each line starts with the node's name, then the firmware version, the role and why it restarted.

The app's channel list with the beebo-cli and beebo-status channels The beebo-status channel after a restart: the boot line, then the first monitor line a minute later

If the transmit power is below 16 dBm you also see a warning:

beebo-mr: warn: txpower=10 dBm underdrives the PA, run: settings radio.txpower 18

A board that came from stock keeps the stock setting of 10, which is why this is common. Raise it to 18 in the app's radio settings, or send settings radio.txpower 18 from the CLI screen. 18 dBm drives the V4.3's power amplifier to its full output, 27.3 dBm at the antenna connector in bench measurements. Check your region's transmit limits before you raise the power, and use a lower value if they require it.

Check: you see the boot line, and the warning disappears at the next boot once the power is 18.

docs.title: 4. Use the CLI screen
docs.text:
Open the app's CLI screen. Commands run on the node you are connected to, and they use the same words as the beebo command line: settings <path> reads a setting and settings <path> <value> sets it. In the examples, the lines you type are plain and the node's replies follow them (a read answers with > <value>):

ver
1.18.0.beebo.1.0 (Build: <date>)
settings fem.rxgain
> off
settings fem.rxgain on
OK - LoRa FEM RX gain on

fem.rxgain switches the board's receive amplifier (LNA). It is off by default, and turning it on is only an example here: put it back with settings fem.rxgain off.

The CLI screen answering settings fem.rxgain and settings fem.rxgain on

Check: settings fem.rxgain reads > on.

docs.title: 5. Choose a role
docs.text:
settings board.node.role
> companion
settings board.node.role repeater

The node reboots into the new role and does not reply, so the app drops the connection. Reconnect. board.node.role now answers > repeater. Each role keeps its own name, keys and settings, so switching back restores them.

Check: the role reads back as you set it.

docs.title: 6. Run a trial (repeater)
docs.text:
A trial tests a setting on the live node. For each setting it runs the current value (A) against one alternative (B) in alternating blocks, and keeps the better one. The default profile, main, tests four settings: the front-end LNA, channel-activity detection (CAD), the retransmit delay and the route retry.

settings routing.tuning.trial.enabled on
> on

The feed now follows the trial. These are the line formats; the numbers change with every run:

beebo-mr: trial cad start profile=main a=0 b=1 blocks=260 block=493s
beebo-mr: trial cad blk <n>/260 pairs=<p> gain=<+/-x.x>%
beebo-mr: trial cad <result> a=0 b=1 pairs=<p> gain=<+/-x.x>% se=<s>%
beebo-mr: trial <next setting> start profile=main a=<a> b=<b> blocks=<n> block=<s>s

The first line is a real start line. a and b are the two values compared (here CAD off against on).

Result Meaning keep_a The current value stays. B was no better. adopt_b The node switched to B, and keeps it across reboots. inconclusive, undecided Not enough evidence. The current value stays.

The planner sizes each trial to the traffic the node hears. That start line plans 260 blocks of about 8 minutes, up to 36 hours for that one setting, so a whole sequence takes days on a quiet node and less on a busy one. You can close the app: the node keeps working and queues the feed lines until the app next syncs. If the node hears too little traffic to start, the feed says trial waiting for traffic.

Turning a trial on also sets what its records need on the monitor, with packet capture off so that a long run does not fill the ring. monitor tuning trial shows where the trial stands, and monitor tuning trial stop ends it at any time.

Check: the feed shows a trial … start line, or trial waiting for traffic; monitor tuning trial answers trial running … or trial waiting for traffic.

docs.title: What next
docs.text: I want to … Go to Understand what each role is for Roles Read the feed lines and commands The phone feed Get more from trials Setting trials Know why a connection behaves as it does Connections Fix a problem Troubleshooting Update firmware, script, or analyze data Commands See everything beebo adds Feature reference

docs.title: RF Experiments
docs.text:
The preceding analysis relies on datasheet parameters and free-space models. The measurements below verify these predictions on real hardware in the actual deployment environment. Specifically, we want to:

  1. Confirm the TX chain — measure conducted power across TX settings to find the actual P1dB compression point and verify what radio.txpower reaches \(P_{sat}\).
  2. Characterize the RX noise floor — measure the system noise floor with a 50-ohm terminator (system noise only), with an antenna (system + environmental), and with a bandpass filter (in-band only). Comparing the three reveals how much OOB energy the local environment contributes and whether the LNA raises or lowers the effective noise floor in practice.
  3. Decide the LNA configuration — if the antenna noise floor with LNA on is significantly higher than with LNA off, OOB interference dominates and the LNA should remain bypassed. If the two are comparable, the environment is quiet enough to benefit from the LNA's sensitivity improvement of about 6 dB over bypass.

docs.title: Equipment
docs.text:
The bench measurements use the equipment listed in the table below, a 50-ohm SMA terminator (any standard terminator — RX-only measurement, no significant power dissipation) and SMA cables and adapters as needed.

Asset Property Value Notes NanoVNA-F v2 Max Output Power -5 dBm Max Input Power 0 dBm Bandwidth 50kHz-3GHz TinySA Ultra+ ZS-406 Max Input Power 6 dBm Bandwidth 100kHz-5.4GHz Wide Band Attenuator Attenuation 50 dB +/-2.5 dB Max Power CW dB 50 W CW Impedance 50 ohm Bandwidth DC - 3 GHz VWSR 1.2 ISM Band Filter Attenuation 22 dB / 1.6 dB Max Power CW 1 W Bandwidth 902MHz-928MHz

Safety rule — never connect PA output directly to any instrument port. PA output may reach 30 dBm (1 W) damaging equipment. After the 50 dB attenuator: 30 - 50 = -20 dBm at the instrument input. The attenuator is mandatory in every measurement path downstream of the PA.

docs.title: TX Radiated Power
docs.text:
In this experiment we measure the actual power radiated at the antenna port across SX1262 TX power settings, with two main objectives:

  1. Find the optimal radio.txpower value that achieves the board maximum power at the inception of the PA saturation.
  2. Quantify the transmission chain board and connection loss \(L_{tx}\)

In this experiment we first connect the antenna SMA port to the input port of the spectrum analyzer through an attenuator, to reduce the power so as not to damage the instrument. Then we use the CLI to set different values of radio.txpower and measure the power at the SMA port across the TX chain, including gains and losses.

For this, beebo provides an automated procedure with the measure txpower command:

$ beebo measure txpower -h

 Usage: beebo measure txpower [OPTIONS]

 Sweep TX power and read peaks on a spectrum analyzer (advert or CW).

╭─ Options ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ --carrier   -c                   [advert|cw]  Carrier type: advert bursts (max-hold) or a steady CW tone.            │
│ --optimize      --no-optimize                 CW only: paOptTable (optimize) vs fixed PA / monotone low end.         │
│                                               [default: optimize]                                                      │
│ --help      -h                                Show this message and exit.                                            │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

The command sweeps SX1262 TX power from -9 to 22 dBm, sends an advert at each step, and prompts for the TinySA reading. It computes gain and compression at each point, identifies the P1dB compression point, and outputs results as a markdown table and CSV file. The 1dB compression point P1dB here is the output power level where the PA actual gain drops by 1 dB compared to its ideal, linear gain.

Measuring the power of an advert is possible but tricky, and requires setting the analyzer to carefully persist the generated short burst signals for reading. To simplify the reading, option --carrier cw can be used to have the radio generate a steady continuous wave tone that is straightforward to read from the analyzer.

The --optimize option controls an underlying PA optimization process that makes the PA's behavior non-monotonic, where one would expect the output to rise steadily. We can optionally disable the optimization to have a more monotonic behavior using --no-optimize.

The command reminds the user of the experiment requirements and sequence of steps.

$ beebo measure txpower
TX Power Measurement Procedure:
  1. Power off board and tinySA Ultra+
  2. Connect antenna output to tinySA RF input through 50 dB attenuator
  3. Turn on and configure tinySA Ultra+ (see README)
  4. Turn on board
  5. Run this test (beebo measure txpower)
  6. At each power level, read the peak on tinySA and enter the value

  Press Enter to start the test...

Once the procedure is complete a CSV file with the measurements is produced (expand the table to see the details).

Table TX Power Measurements: | txpower (dBm) | measured (dBm) | gain (dB) | compression (dB) | | ------------: | -------------: | --------: | ---------------: | | -9 | 3.3 | 12.3 | -0.3 | | -8 | 3.8 | 11.8 | 0.2 | | -7 | 4.8 | 11.8 | 0.2 | | -6 | 6.3 | 12.3 | -0.3 | | -5 | 7.3 | 12.3 | -0.5 | | -4 | 8.3 | 12.3 | -0.3 | | -3 | 9.3 | 12.3 | -0.3 | | -2 | 9.8 | 11.8 | 0.2 | | -1 | 10.8 | 11.8 | -0.2 | | 0 | 11.8 | 11.8 | 0.2 | | 1 | 12.3 | 11.3 | 0.7 | | 2 | 13.3 | 11.3 | 0.7 | | 3 | 14.3 | 11.3 | 0.7 | | 4 | 16.8 | 12.8 | -0.8 | | 5 | 17.8 | 12.8 | -0.8 | | 6 | 18.3 | 12.3 | -0.3 | | 7 | 18.3 | 11.3 | 0.7 | | 8 | 19.3 | 11.3 | 0.7 | | 9 | 19.8 | 11.8 | 0.2 | | 10 | 22.3 | 12.3 | -0.3 | | 11 | 22.8 | 11.8 | 0.2 | | 12 | 23.3 | 11.3 | 0.7 | | 13 | 24.3 | 11.3 | 0.7 | | 14 | 25.3 | 11.3 | 0.7 | | 15 | 25.8 | 10.3 | 1.7 | | 16 | 26.3 | 10.3 | 1.7 | | 17 | 27.3 | 10.3 | 1.7 | | 18 | 27.3 | 9.3 | 2.7 | | 19 | 27.3 | 8.3 | 3.7 | | 20 | 27.3 | 7.3 | 4.7 | | 21 | 27.3 | 6.3 | 5.7 | | 22 | 27.3 | 5.3 | 6.7 |

In the table, txpower_dBm is the SX1262 radio.txpower setting, measured_dBm is the measured TX output at the SMA, gain is the difference between the two, and compression is the difference between the computed gain and the expected ideal gain.

The data is further analyzed by a plotting script that generates the chart below. Here ideal gain is the gain of the TX chain previously computed without losses. The actual linear gain after losses is computed regressing the first half of the gain column to exclude the saturation region, and nicely superimpose itself on the curve.

We can now estimate the transmission chain loss with the difference between ideal and real linear gains:

\[L_{tx} = ideal - linear = 16 - 12.02 ≈ 4 \ \text{dB}\]

The P1dB compression point is roughly at txpower = 16 dBm with the SMA TX power plateauing at 27.3 dBm from txpower 17 dBm, which corresponds to our optimal settings. The resolution of the measurement is ±0.5 dB and the estimated accuracy ±1 dB. Beebo therefore ships radio.txpower 18.

docs.title: System Noise Floor
docs.text:
We would like to evaluate the system noise floor across different gain and antenna configurations, verify our analytically computed estimations and determine whether the use of a bandpass filter would help.

For noise floor measurements we rely on the noise_floor function computed by the MeshCore FW, reported with resolution of ±1dB and estimated accuracy of ±2dB. However, this is not a direct measurement of \(N_{floor}\), rather it is an estimate derived from 64 averaged SX1262 RSSI readings, sampled every 2 seconds, where spikes and regular packets are filtered out and result clamped to a minimum of -120 dBm. The RSSI readings from the SX1262 are made through the GetRssiInst command which returns the instantaneous RSSI value seen after filter and gain before demodulation. Internally, the SX1262 refers the RSSI values back to its input, factoring out gain stages and AGC. Therefore noise_floor is an estimate of the noise floor seen at the input of the SX1262, not after demodulation.

To measure system noise floor we isolate the receiver chain from environmental RF by using a 50-ohm terminator stub instead of an antenna. This measures thermal + receiver noise only. Measurements are performed through the measure noise internal command. The command reminds us of the procedure requirements and steps:

$ beebo measure noise internal
Internal Noise Floor Measurement Procedure:
  1. With the antenna still connected, set TX power to -9 to protect the termination stub: beebo settings companion.radio.txpower -9
  2. Power off board
  3. Replace antenna with 50 ohm termination stub
  4. Power on board
  5. Run the test: beebo measure noise internal
  6. Power off board
  7. Replace stub with antenna
  8. Set companion.radio.txpower to original value

  The test itself runs at -9 dBm on the preset you choose and restores
  every setting after; step 1 covers the adverts sent before it starts.
  combined and in_band use this run as the reference for the LNA gain.

  LoRa preset [USA/Canada]:

  Press Enter to start the test...

The test asks for a LoRa preset (Enter keeps the one the node is on), so the RX chain is measured at the bandwidth and spreading factor it normally runs at. For the run it holds settings in RAM, applies the preset, txpower -9 and FEM RSSI offsets 0/0 (raw SX1262-input readings), then restores everything from flash. --antenna-ref keeps the node's offsets instead (see RSSI at the Antenna Connector).

The test cycles 3 times through all permutations of radio.rxgain and fem.rxgain, waiting 5 s for the floor to settle and taking 10 noise_floor samples on each visit. Each config reports the median of its 30 samples after dropping those more than 3 MADs (at least 1 dB) from it, with the min and max for the spread. The medians are also saved as JSON next to the report, for combined and in_band to use. The tables below were taken with an earlier version that reported min/max of 5 samples:

Table 14: Measured Noise Floor by Configuration

fem.rxgain rxgain min (dBm) max (dBm) off on -113 -113 off off -113 -113 on on -94 -94 on off -94 -94

Because we are using a stub as antenna we expect to see little or no variation in the readings. If readings show min and max value far apart, position the board away from interferers like laptops, WiFi routers or other transmitting devices.

From the table we should be able to verify that changes in rxgain do not produce different values, since the gain in the SX1262 is factored out.

Since we have no visibility in the SX1262 RX chain we can just consider the noise floor value where rxgain = on, its boosted default mode.

Comparing the \(N_{stub}\) values in the table with the \(N_{floor}\) values we have calculated in Table 8.

But before we can do that, to compare apples to apples, we first need to translate \(N_{floor}\) to the SX1262 input plane \(N_{sx}\), since \(N_{floor}\) is input-referred to the antenna port and not the SX1262 input.

The noise at SX1262 input is:

\[N_{sx} = N_{thermal} + {NF}_{fem} + G_{fem}\]

When the LNA is used (fem.rxgain = on):

  • \(G_{fem} = G_{LNA} = 15\) dB
  • \({NF}_{fem} = {NF}_{LNA} = 1.9\) dB
  • \(N_{LNA} = N_{thermal} + {NF}_{LNA} + G_{LNA}\)

when the LNA is bypassed (fem.rxgain = off):

  • \(G_{fem} = - L_{bypass} = -2\) dB
  • \({NF}_{fem} = L_{bypass} = 2\) dB.
  • \(N_{bypass} = N_{thermal} + L_{bypass} - L_{bypass} = N_{thermal}\)

Note how for the bypass gain and noise cancel each other out since a passive matched attenuator only contributes spectral noise (at \(T_0\)).

Looking closely, though, there is an opportunity for us to compute the LNA gain \(G_{LNA}\) straight from the noise floor measurement. In fact, the difference between \(N_{LNA}\) and \(N_{bypass}\) is:

\[N_{LNA} - N_{bypass} = ΔN = N_{thermal} + {NF}_{LNA} + G_{LNA} - N_{thermal}$$ $$ΔN = {NF}_{LNA} + G_{LNA}\]

Solving for \(G_{LNA}\):

\[G_{LNA} = ΔN - {NF}_{LNA}\]

From the measurement table \(ΔN = -94 + 113 = 19\) dB, therefore:

\[G_{LNA} = 19 - 1.9 ≈ 17\ \text{dB}\]

That is 2 dB more than the approximate published 15 dB number.

We can now compute \(N_{sx}\) for the two cases:

  • \(N_{bypass} = N_{thermal} = -126\) dBm
  • \(N_{LNA} = N_{thermal} + {NF}_{LNA} + G_{LNA} = -126 + 1.9 + 17 ≈ -107\) dBm

And compare with measured \(N_{stub}\) values:

fem.rxgain \(N_{sx}\) \(N_{stub}\) \(N_δ\) off -126 dBm -113 dBm +13 dB on -107 dBm -94 dBm +13 dB

Note how the offset between predicted and measured is +13 dB in both configurations. It is a fixed offset inside the SX1262 that does not change in gain, not a modeling error that varies with gain. If the reference planes were wrong, the two offsets would differ.

The delta offset could be attributed to SX1262 sampling the instantaneous RSSI before the channel filter therefore raising thermal noise by several dBs. To test this theory we sweep noise floor with different values of BW:

bw (kHz) min (dBm) max (dBm) Δ meas (dB) Δ thermal (dB) 62.5 -94 -94 +0 +0.0 125.0 -91 -91 +3 +3.0 250.0 -89 -88 +5 +6.0

The measured noise floor nicely tracks the thermal noise, therefore the SX1262 samples RSSI after the band filter.

One consideration is that although GetRssiInst refers the RSSI back to the input plane removing gain, it does not remove the noise power injected up to the sampling point across filter, LNA, AGC, etc. Therefore a component of 13dB offset could be attributed to the SX1262 \({NF}_{radio}\) noise figure adding 6.5 dB. In that case the offset shrinks to 6.5 dB.

fem.rxgain \(N_{sx}\) \(N_{stub}\) \(N_δ\) off -119.5 dBm -113 dBm +6.5 dB on -100.5 dBm -94 dBm +6.5 dB

The remaining 6.5 dB difference could be attributed to electromagnetic interference (EMI) on the board by SPI, MCU, WiFi, or Digital Filtering & Equivalent Noise Bandwidth (ENBW) from the channel digital filter or who knows what else.

docs.title: RSSI at the Antenna Connector
docs.text:
The SX1262 reports RSSI at its own input, after the FEM, so every reading includes the FEM path gain: about +17 dB through the LNA and about −2 dB through the bypass. The same signal therefore reads about 19 dB apart depending on fem.rxgain. The firmware adds a per-path offset to every RSSI read, so packet RSSI and the noise floor refer to the antenna connector instead:

Setting Default Applies when board.fem.rssi_offset.lna −17 dB LNA on (fem.rxgain on), and always on the GC1109 (V4.2), which has no bypass board.fem.rssi_offset.bypass +2 dB LNA bypassed (fem.rxgain off)

The offsets are board-level settings, persisted and shared by both roles, from −30 to 30 dB; 0/0 gives raw SX1262 values. Switching the LNA, or changing the offset of the path in use, restarts the noise floor. The offsets are compiled in with BEEBO_RSSI_ANT_REF, which every multi-role build sets.

On bench, measure noise internal (raw, USA/Canada) reads −113 dBm in bypass and −94 dBm with the LNA (Table 14), a 19 dB step, the same as the 19 dB the nominal offsets correct. We keep −17/+2. The stub step is a ratio of noise powers, which also depends on each path's noise figure, so it confirms the offsets only to about a dB; a CW measurement at a known level would pin each path separately.

With the offsets applied, the two paths read the same floor: −113 + 2 = −111 dBm in bypass, −94 − 17 = −111 dBm with the LNA. measure noise internal --antenna-ref measures this directly.

docs.title: Environmental Noise (with antenna)
docs.text:
Same procedure as above but with the antenna connected (measure noise combined). Compare results with the terminated measurements to see how much of the noise floor comes from the RF environment vs the receiver chain. A large difference suggests a bandpass filter before the LNA would help.

$ beebo measure noise combined
Combined Noise Floor Measurement Procedure:
  1. Connect the real antenna (not 50 ohm stub)
  2. Power on board
  3. Run this test
  4. Repeat test if needed

  Noise floor is sampled during idle gaps between packets
  (firmware filters out active reception automatically).
  Compare with noise internal to see environmental noise contribution.

  LoRa preset [USA/Canada]:

  Press Enter to start the test...
fem.rxgain \(N_{env}\) \(N_{stub}\) off -110 dBm -113 dBm on -90 dBm -94 dBm

The environment, in our case an urban area not in proximity of cellular towers, adds around 3-4 dB of noise with respect to the 50Ω stub antenna, seemingly for both LNA on/off cases.

combined and in_band also print the LNA path gain over bypass, from the latest internal run on the same node and preset. Per path, the stub reading is subtracted from the antenna reading in mW, which cancels the noise added after the SMA (SX1262 noise figure, board EMI). The gain is the LNA path's result minus the bypass path's, in dB, shown for each rxgain. A path less than 3 dB above the stub gives no gain: the subtraction would be dominated by drift between the two runs.

docs.title: In-Band Noise (with bandpass filter)
docs.text:
Same as environmental noise but with a bandpass filter inline (measure noise in_band). The CLI prompts for the filter's insertion loss and shows both raw measured values and corrected values (measured minus insertion loss) so you can directly compare with the unfiltered antenna measurements.

The specs of the bandpass filter we use are the following:

  • Model: SAW Bandpass Filter for 915MHz
  • Bandwidth: 902-928MHz
  • Maximum withstand power: 1W (30dBm)
  • Insertion loss: 1.6dB
  • Return loss: -22dB
  • SWR: 1.1
  • Verified with NanoVNA-F v2, loss and BW edges 1.7dB - 2dB

As usual, beebo reminds us of requirements and procedure steps:

$ beebo measure noise in_band
In-Band Noise Floor Measurement Procedure:
  1. Power off board
  2. Connect bandpass filter between antenna and board RF port
  3. Power on board
  4. Run this test
  5. Repeat test if needed
  6. Power off board
  7. Remove bandpass filter, reconnect antenna directly

  Noise excess over noise internal is due to in-band signals only.
  Compare with noise combined to compute out-of-band noise:
    out_of_band = noise_combined - noise_in_band

  Enter bandpass filter insertion loss (dB, e.g. 1.5): 1.6

  LoRa preset [USA/Canada]:

  Press Enter to start the test...

The table reports the previous \(N_{env}\) combined internal/in-band, the new \(N_{band}\) noise corrected from bandpass insertion loss, and the internal only noise \(N_{stub}\).

fem.rxgain \(N_{env}\) \(N_{band}\) \(N_{stub}\) off -110 dBm -110 dBm -113 dBm on -90 dBm -90 dBm -94 dBm

\(N_{env}\) and \(N_{band}\) are equal, so the band-pass filter has no influence. Since GetRssiInst readings are after the SX1262 digital bandpass filter, a difference here would reveal noise injected through ENBW.

We can conclude that all of the injected noise is in-band noise.

docs.title: Spectrum Survey (tinySA)
docs.text:
To do. In practice the LNA setting trial tells whether the LNA can be used at a site, so this survey is optional.

To determine whether out-of-band interference is significant enough to saturate the LNA we could:

  1. Connect the antenna to the tinySA input.
  2. Wide scan (800-1000 MHz) to identify interference sources.
  3. Narrow scan around the LoRa frequency (e.g. 906-916 MHz) to see in-band noise.
  4. Compare with and without the ESP32 WiFi radio active.

If significant out-of-band energy is present, a SAW bandpass filter placed before the KCT8103L would reject it before LNA amplification.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
One board, one site, one run of each measurement. The transmit power readings have a resolution of ±0.5 dB and an estimated accuracy of ±1 dB. The noise floor comes from the firmware's noise_floor estimate, which has a resolution of ±1 dB and an accuracy of about ±2 dB. Treat differences smaller than that as noise.

Question Measurement Result Where does the transmit chain compress? TX power sweep, radio.txpower −9 to 22, at the SMA through a 50 dB attenuator The chain gain is about 12 dB (about 4 dB of loss against the ideal 16 dB) and the output compresses around radio.txpower 16. It plateaus at 27.3 dBm from 17 up. What does the stock setting give? Same sweep radio.txpower 10 gives 22.3 dBm, about 5 dB below the plateau. Above 17 the extra drive adds nothing: the gain falls from 10.3 dB at 17 to 5.3 dB at 22. What is the receiver's own noise floor? measure noise internal, 50 Ω terminator, 62.5 kHz −113 dBm with the LNA off and −94 dBm with it on, the same with radio.rxgain on or off. How much gain does the LNA path add? Difference of the two floors The floors differ by 19 dB. With the LNA's 1.9 dB noise figure that is a gain of about 17 dB, 2 dB above the published 15 dB. Does the floor follow the model? Same measurement against the predicted floor at the SX1262 input Measured is a fixed +13 dB above the prediction on both paths. Attributing 6.5 dB of it to the SX1262 noise figure leaves 6.5 dB unexplained (board interference or the digital filter's noise bandwidth are candidates). Where in the chain is RSSI sampled? Floor at 62.5, 125 and 250 kHz It rises by 0, 3 and 5 dB, against 0, 3 and 6 dB for thermal noise, so the SX1262 samples RSSI after the channel filter. What does the environment add? measure noise combined, antenna connected, urban site away from cell towers The floor is −110 dBm with the LNA off and −90 dBm with it on: 3 to 4 dB above the terminator in both cases. Is the added noise in band? measure noise in_band with a 902 to 928 MHz SAW filter (1.6 dB loss) The floor does not change (−110 and −90 dBm after correcting for the loss), so all of the added noise is in band. A bandpass filter before the LNA would not help at this site. Do the RSSI offsets work? The same floors with the offsets of −17 dB (LNA) and +2 dB (bypass) applied The raw floors are 19 dB apart, which the nominal offsets correct exactly: both paths read −111 dBm at the antenna connector.

What follows from it:

  • Transmit power. radio.txpower 18 is at the top of the plateau, which is why beebo ships it. Local radiated-power limits still apply: see EIRP and regulatory limits.
  • The LNA stays off by default, as in stock. It buys about 6 dB of sensitivity over the stock bypass setting (4.3 dB better than the bare SX1262) and costs tolerance to out-of-band interference. At this site the antenna adds the same 3 to 4 dB with the LNA on and off, so out-of-band energy does not dominate here, but one site does not decide it for yours. beebo rxlog --compare measures it on your own mesh traffic with the chassis closed.
  • Noise figures. The measured floors sit 6.5 to 13 dB above the datasheet-based prediction. The relative results (the LNA step and the bandwidth scaling) track the model, so they are the ones to rely on.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text: One beebo firmware runs as a companion or a repeater. The role is a setting (board.node.role) and a node runs exactly one at a time.

docs.title: Switching
docs.text:
From the app's CLI screen:

settings board.node.role
> companion
settings board.node.role repeater

The node saves the new role, reboots and does not reply, so the app drops the connection and reconnects. Each role keeps its own name, keys, contacts and settings on the node, so switching back restores them. A switch is refused while an over-the-air update or a bulk monitor download is running.

docs.title: What each role is for
docs.text:
• Companion. The gateway between your phone and the mesh: messages, contacts and channels, over BLE, WiFi or USB. Beebo adds the status feed and the CLI screen.
  • Repeater. Relays packets for other nodes and is configured from the CLI screen. It is the role that runs setting trials.

docs.title: Static builds
docs.text: A static build, heltec-v4-<version>.companion or .repeater, compiles the other role out. It cannot switch, and board.node.role rejects the role it does not have. Use the multi-role image unless you need a fixed role.

docs.title: Transports
docs.text: BLE, WiFi (TCP) and USB are each switched on or off by a setting; see Connections for the defaults and how one conversation at a time is kept, and Install and Connect to provision WiFi.

docs.title: How a Repeater Routes
docs.text: The MeshCore routing and timing mechanics behind the settings that trials and the tuner change. Without knowing what each parameter controls, tuning them is guesswork.

docs.title: How MeshCore Routes a Packet
docs.text:
Every packet carries a route type in its header (docs/packet_format.md): flood (ROUTE_TYPE_FLOOD/ _TRANSPORT_FLOOD) or direct (ROUTE_TYPE_DIRECT/_TRANSPORT_DIRECT). The two build and consume their path very differently, and the tunable timing parameters below apply almost entirely to the flood case:

  • Flood: no path is set by the sender — each repeater that forwards it appends its own identity hash to the packet's path buffer before re-queuing it (Mesh::routeRecvPacket()). The path buffer has a fixed capacity (MAX_PATH_SIZE), so a flood packet that has already changed hands too many times gets dropped rather than appended to (RX_DISP_PATH_FULL) — this is flood's de facto hop limit, not an explicit TTL counter.
  • Direct: the sender supplies the full path up front. Each hop checks whether it is the next hash in that path; if so, it strips itself off the front and forwards to whatever's left (removeSelfFromPath()). A node that isn't the expected next hop logs RX_DISP_WRONG_HOP and drops.

Because a flood packet has no path to begin with, the exact same packet reaches a repeater from multiple neighbors, multiple times, as it spreads outward. Deduplication is what keeps this from cascading forever: every received packet's hash (Packet::calculatePacketHash(), essentially a digest of its payload) is checked against a rolling table of recently-seen hashes. First sight: process it (and, for a repeater, schedule a forward). Every repeat sight after that: RX_DISP_DUP, dropped without forwarding. This table's size (MAX_PACKET_HASHES) is a boundary condition, not a tuning knob — the parameters below govern when a genuinely new flood packet gets forwarded, not whether a duplicate does.

A repeater's own forward-or-drop decision for a freshly-received packet is one of (RxDisposition, src/Dispatcher.h):

Disposition What it means RX_DISP_FORWARDED Repeater accepted and scheduled a retransmission (flood or direct). RX_DISP_NO_FORWARD This node is the correct next hop, but packet forwarding is administratively disabled here (client_repeat/repeat_mode off). RX_DISP_WRONG_HOP Direct-routed packet; this node isn't the path's next hop. RX_DISP_PATH_FULL Would forward, but the path buffer has no room left to append/consume. RX_DISP_DUP Already seen this packet's hash — dropped, not forwarded. RX_DISP_FILTERED Rejected pre-dispatch (e.g. region/scope filtering).

beebo monitor's "RX conditions" histogram and the offline delivery_proxy of beebo analyze tuning indicators are built from this disposition breakdown. The tuners themselves do not score it: they reward confirmed delivery instead (see The Objective Function).

docs.title: Where This Sits in Routing Taxonomy
docs.text:
It's worth being precise about what kind of routing this actually is, since the term "dynamic routing" usually means something more specific: protocols like RIP (distance-vector), OSPF (link-state), or BGP (path-vector), where routers periodically exchange routing information and maintain forwarding tables computed from a metric (hop count, cost, path attributes) — the "dynamic" part being that the tables update automatically as topology changes, ahead of any actual data needing to move (see Dynamic routing).

MeshCore doesn't do any of that:

  • No routing tables, no route advertisements, no periodic exchange at all. Nodes don't know the topology and don't compute paths in advance.
  • Flood + path accumulation is the discovery mechanism. A flood packet has no path; each repeater that forwards it appends its own hash to the packet's path buffer. By the time it reaches the destination, the packet itself carries a complete accumulated path.
  • Direct packets are then source-routed using exactly that accumulated path, hop by hop stripping itself off the front — no lookup, no table.

That combination — on-demand path discovery via flooding, with the discovered path embedded directly in subsequent packets rather than stored in per-node tables — sits much closer to the reactive/source-routing family of MANET protocols (DSR is the closest analogue) than to any of the table-maintaining dynamic routing protocols the term usually refers to. If forced onto that taxonomy at all, MeshCore sits outside "dynamic routing" as classically defined — arguably closer to the absence of a routing table, with the path riding along in the data itself instead.

This is also why the tuning beebo adds is not "route optimization" in the RIP/OSPF/BGP sense: the parameters it adjusts shape when a node retransmits and how it avoids collisions (forwarding-timing/collision- avoidance discipline), never which path a packet takes or any routing metric — there is no metric to optimize, since there's no routing table to begin with.

docs.title: The Tunable Parameters
docs.text: Six parameters govern a repeater's forwarding timing, collision avoidance, and airtime discipline, and a seventh, route retry, covers a forward nobody echoed. All are persisted NodePrefs/ComPrefs fields, reachable via beebo settings repeater.routing.*. rx_delay_base/ airtime_factor also have a separate, independent companion-role copy at companion.routing.* (the stock upstream CMD_GET/SET_TUNING_PARAMS opcode) — tuning the repeater's forwarding timing never affects a simultaneous companion session's behavior, or vice versa. See the Settings reference for the exact leaf paths.

docs.title: rx_delay_base — flood forward jitter
docs.text:
Only applies to flood packets a repeater is about to forward for the first time. calcRxDelay(score, air_time) computes:

delay = (rx_delay_base ^ (0.85 - score) - 1) * air_time

score (Radio::packetScore(), roughly 0-1) reflects how good the received link was (SNR-driven) — a stronger link gives a higher score, which shrinks the exponent and pulls the delay toward zero. In effect: the node that heard the flood packet best jitters least and is likely to retransmit first, giving the mesh a natural, no-coordination-needed ordering that thins out redundant near-simultaneous retransmissions from several repeaters that all heard the same flood packet. Raising rx_delay_base widens the spread between a well-scored and poorly-scored node's delay — more separation, generally fewer collisions, at the cost of slower propagation. rx_delay_base <= 0 disables this jitter entirely (fires immediately).

docs.title: tx_delay_factor / direct_tx_delay_factor — retransmit jitter window
docs.text: Once a repeater has decided to forward (flood or direct respectively), it still doesn't transmit instantly — getRetransmitDelay()/ getDirectRetransmitDelay() pick a random delay in [0, 5 * estimated_airtime * factor]. Raising the factor widens this random window, spreading out when different repeaters (or the same repeater's queued packets) actually key up, at the direct cost of added latency per hop. This is the primary knob for reducing collisions between repeaters that all decided to forward around the same time — rx_delay_base orders who goes first, this decides how spread out the actual transmissions are.

docs.title: interference_threshold — RSSI-over-noise-floor busy check
docs.text: One of the channel busy/clear checks checkSend() makes before every transmit. isReceiving() runs three, ORed: a frame in progress (the radio's preamble or valid-header flag, always on and not tunable, see tx_wait_cad), then this RSSI check and the hardware scan (radio.cad) inside isChannelActive(). This check is busy when getCurrentRSSI() > noise_floor + interference_threshold, where noise_floor is tracked separately via periodic RSSI sampling (triggerNoiseFloorCalibrate() only resets that sampling, it does not use the threshold itself). A threshold of 0 turns this RSSI check off; the hardware scan, if radio.cad is on, still runs. Raising the threshold makes the radio tolerate a noisier floor before treating it as channel activity — useful in a persistently noisy RF environment, at the cost of being slower to detect genuine channel activity (more collision risk) if raised too far. The check reads wideband RSSI, so any energy above the threshold counts, LoRa or not. Not used by packetScore(), which scores purely from SNR/SF/packet length.

docs.title: tx_wait_cad includes reception in progress
docs.text:
Before the two checks above, isReceiving() returns busy while the radio is receiving a frame: the SX1262 preamble-detected or header-valid flag (CustomSX1262::isReceiving()). It is always on, so tx_wait_cad is non-zero with interference_threshold 0 and radio.cad off: a packet ready to send waits out the frame and then a 120-480 ms backoff. A preamble with no header is dropped as noise after _preambleMillis, a header that never completes after _maxPayloadMillis. Time in the indicator therefore tracks on-air traffic heard by the node, plus those flag timeouts.

beebo monitor splits tx_wait_cad by the check behind each busy verdict: tx_wait_cad_frame (a frame in progress), tx_wait_cad_rssi (interference_threshold) and tx_wait_cad_hw (radio.cad, plus any backoff not set by a verdict). tx_cad_verdicts counts the verdicts per minute, saturating at 255. The backoff after a verdict is charged to the check that caused it.

docs.title: radio.cad — hardware channel activity detection
docs.text:
A switch (0/1, default off; PREFS_TLV_CAD, upstream's set cad on/off) that adds the radio's own channel scan to isChannelActive(): when on and the RSSI check above did not already say busy, the radio runs scanChannel(), which looks for a LoRa preamble at the node's SF and BW, and anything but "channel free" counts as busy. The two checks are ORed, RSSI first, so turning both on can only produce more busy verdicts than either alone. CAD is more selective than the RSSI check (LoRa only) and catches a weak transmission under the RSSI threshold, but it can also fire on a distant transmission that could not have collided, and each scan interrupts RX (the radio is put back in receive afterwards, the scan's interrupt flag cleared so it is not counted as a receive error).

A busy verdict defers the send by a random 120, 240, 360 or 480 ms (Mesh::getCADFailRetryDelay()). After 4 s of continuous busy (getCADFailMaxDuration()) the node sends anyway and raises the ERR_EVENT_CAD_TIMEOUT fault, so a channel that stays busy delays every send by up to that long but never blocks forever. All of that waiting is the tx_wait_cad time (the CAD Busy indicator); it does not depend on radio.cad being on, and stays non-zero with the threshold at 0 and CAD off (see above). With a tight interference_threshold CAD adds little and costs scan time; with a loose or zero one it is the main collision avoidance. radio.cad is a trial switch, so a trial can decide it from measured goodput.

docs.title: agc_reset_interval — AGC re-convergence cadence
docs.text: Purely a radio-frontend concern: on a timer, the radio does a brief sleep/wake cycle (doResetAGC()) to force its automatic gain control to re-converge, preventing a "stuck" gain state from skewing RSSI/noise-floor readings (which, again, feed packetScore()). Not really a collision/delivery lever on its own — its effect is indirect, through keeping the inputs to the other parameters accurate.

docs.title: airtime_factor — duty-cycle budget
docs.text: Independent of the above: a token-bucket budget (tx_budget_ms) refills over time at a rate set by duty_cycle = 1 / (1 + airtime_factor) and drains by each transmission's measured airtime. When the budget runs low, checkSend() blocks new transmissions until it recovers — this is airtime discipline (regulatory/fairness budget enforcement), separate from CAD's collision avoidance (reacting to a channel that's busy right now). Raising airtime_factor tightens the budget (lower effective duty cycle, less total airtime spent, but transmissions queue up and wait longer once the budget is exhausted).

docs.title: Route retry
docs.text:
A repeater that forwards a flood and never hears a neighbor rebroadcast it can send it again, at a more robust LoRa coding rate. One setting controls it, also trialed (see Setting Trials):

Setting Range Meaning repeater.routing.retry 0, or 1 to 3 coding rates from 5 to 8 separated by \|, default 0 The coding rate 4/x of each retry of a forward whose echo timed out, in order: 8 is one retry at 4/8, 5\|6 a first retry at 4/5 and a second at 4/6. 5 is the rate of the first send; 0 turns retry off

A retry has the same packet hash as its first send. beebo analyze retries reports how many retries were heard, went unanswered or are pending, the rescue rate and the extra airtime; beebo analyze packets marks each retry in its Try column. Only floods the repeater forwards are retried, never direct packets or packets the node originates.

A flood's echo window starts when the packet is sent, so it measures the neighbor's turnaround only: 4500 ms plus 6 x the packet's airtime, rounded up from a fit to measured captures. A packet that is never sent gets no window, and a forward heard from another repeater before ours went out does not count as an echo. The window is fixed in the firmware, not a setting: echoes of a repeater's forward can arrive later than the window allows for, and beebo analyze timing shows the share past the window, the window that would cover 95% and 99% of the echoes, and a fit of base + factor x airtime to compare with the one in use.

docs.title: How They Interweave
docs.text:
None of these parameters acts alone:

interference_threshold ──▶ noise floor ──▶ packetScore() ──▶ rx_delay_base's exponent
                                               │
agc_reset_interval ──▶ (keeps the above accurate over time)
                                               │
                                               ▼
                              flood forward jitter (who retransmits first)
                                               │
                                               ▼
                    tx_delay_factor / direct_tx_delay_factor (when they actually key up)
                                               │
                                               ▼
                              airtime_factor's budget (whether they're allowed to yet)

A change to one can shift the effective behavior of another: e.g. raising interference_threshold changes packetScore()'s inputs, which changes how much spread rx_delay_base actually produces between two given nodes, even though rx_delay_base itself didn't change. This is exactly why the tuning work changes one parameter at a time and waits to observe the result before touching another (see Setting Trials) — changing several simultaneously would make it impossible to attribute an outcome to any single knob.

docs.title: Scoring
docs.text: How the node turns a block of traffic into the score that setting trials and the adaptive tuner judge.

docs.title: The objective function
docs.text:
Both tuners, the adaptive bandit and the setting trial, score a closed measurement window with the same objective. It is computed on the node (Objective.h) and mirrored offline by beebo analyze tuning trial, so the two are always comparable.

What is measured: confirmed delivery. When this node transmits (its own packet, a forward or an ACK reply), a neighbor either rebroadcasts it (flood) or ACKs it (direct): a reception that arrives later and was caused by the earlier transmission succeeding. From that, per window:

  • routed: packets routed per hour, the confirmable attempts (ack_success + ack_timeout + echo_attempt).
  • delivered: the share of them confirmed (ack_success + echo_success over the routed count). Routed times delivered is the confirmed deliveries per hour (ACKs plus flood echoes), which the trial's confirm-ratio guard reads.

Absence of an echo or ACK does not prove a failure (no repeater may have been in range), so this is much less confounded than the forwarding decision, but it is not perfect ground truth. The earlier proxy, forwarded / (forwarded + no_forward + path_full), is not used for scoring: no_forward is admin policy, path_full a hop-count limit and forwarded only means "scheduled", so none of the tunable parameters changes those counts. It remains available offline as delivery_proxy in beebo analyze tuning indicators, as a diagnostic.

The score. repeater.routing.tuning.score.* holds one signed weight per indicator, in tenths (10 = 1.0):

  • routed and delivered, as above. A retry is not a new routed packet, so a retry setting cannot raise routed.
  • received: valid packets received per hour.

Every indicator is put on a 0 to 100 scale (per-hour volumes as a percent of the channel's usable capacity, about 2800 events per hour at SF7 / 62.5 kHz) and the score is the weighted sum of ln(1 + x/0.1) of the indicators, so a weight says how much a 10% change in that indicator is worth: weight 0 ignores it and a negative weight treats it as a cost. The defaults (routed 10, delivered 10, received 0) give the confirmed deliveries per hour, routed times the delivered share, with no indicator counted twice. Give received a weight to judge receive-side switches (LNA, RX boost), which barely move the TX confirmations. Both tuners use the same weights; a weight cannot be changed while a trial runs (stop it first). Between trials a change restarts the trial sequence and the bandit's statistics. The trial's confirm-ratio guard and the bandit's rollback check are separate safety checks and stay fixed.

beebo analyze tuning indicators and analyze tuning trial report wider diagnostics that are not part of the score (TX Dispatched, RX Invalid and Errors, neighbors, Pool Busy, CAD Busy, TX success rate, wrong-hop rate, SNR/RSSI/noise-floor trends).

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Everything configurable on a beebo node — radio parameters, board tuning, transport enables, WiFi credentials, monitor capture flags, node identity, the tuning optimizer and trial, even the CLI's own defaults — lives in one place: a single settings tree, addressed by dotted path. There's no separate wifi command, no separate transport command, no scattered one-off flags to remember; it's all just beebo settings <path> [value].

Run it with no arguments and you get the whole tree. Point it at a category and you get that subtree. Point it at a leaf and you get (or set) just that value:

$ beebo settings
settings
├── board
│   ├── adc
│   │   ├── multiplier: 5.464
│   │   └── resolution: 12 bits  [10, 12]
│   ├── battery
│   │   ├── present: yes  {yes|no}
│   │   ├── sample_period: 300 s  [30 to 3600]
│   │   └── sample_window: 30 s  [1 to 300]
│   ├── node
│   │   ├── id: 5552594e5230
│   │   ├── name: Beebo
│   │   ├── password: (set)
│   │   └── role: companion  ['companion', 'repeater']
│   └── state.quiet: off
├── companion
│   ├── fem
│   │   ├── rxgain: off
│   │   └── txgain: on
│   ├── monitor
│   │   ├── batt: on
│   │   ├── command: on
│   │   ├── debug: on
│   │   ├── enabled: on
│   │   ├── env: off
│   │   ├── event: on
│   │   ├── radio: on
│   │   ├── route: on
│   │   ├── rx: on
│   │   ├── setting: on
│   │   ├── tuning: off
│   │   └── tx: on
│   ├── node
│   │   ├── adv_loc_policy: 1  (share)  [0=none, 1=share, 2=prefs]
│   │   ├── autoadd_config: 0x01
│   │   ├── ble.pin: 123456
│   │   ├── coords: 0.0, 0.0 deg
│   │   ├── manual_add_contacts: off
│   │   ├── multi_acks: 1
│   │   ├── name: Beebo
│   │   ├── path_hash_mode: 1  [0=1 byte, 1=2 bytes, 2=3 bytes]
│   │   ├── public_key: 5552594e…
│   │   ├── region.scope: (none)
│   │   ├── repeat: off
│   │   ├── telemetry
│   │   │   ├── base: 0  [0 to 3]
│   │   │   ├── env: 0  [0 to 3]
│   │   │   └── loc: 0  [0 to 3]
│   │   ├── transport
│   │   │   ├── ble: off
│   │   │   ├── tcp: on
│   │   │   └── usb: on
│   │   └── wifi
│   │       ├── password: (set)
│   │       └── ssid: myssid
│   ├── radio
│   │   ├── allowed_repeat_freq: 433.0-433.0 MHz, 869.495-869.495 MHz, 918.0-918.0
│   │   │   MHz
│   │   ├── lora
│   │   │   ├── bw: 62.5 kHz  [7.8, 10.4, 15.6, 20.8, 31.25, 41.7, 62.5, 125, 250,
│   │   │   │   500]
│   │   │   ├── cr: 5  [5 to 8]
│   │   │   ├── freq: 910.525 MHz  [137 to 1020]
│   │   │   └── sf: 7  [7 to 12]
│   │   ├── rxgain: on
│   │   └── txpower: 18 dBm  [-9 to 22]
│   ├── profile.enabled: off
│   └── routing
│       ├── airtime: 0  [0 to 9]
│       ├── seen_window: 0 s
│       ├── dutycycle: 100 %  [1 to 100]
│       └── rxdelay: 0 s  [0 to 20]
└── console
    ├── autosave: on
    ├── ble.address: scan
    ├── dbg_level: L  {H|M|L}
    ├── log_level: WARNING  {DEBUG|INFO|WARNING|ERROR|CRITICAL}
    ├── tcp.host: beebo
    ├── transport: tcp  {ble|tcp|usb}
    └── usb.port: /dev/ttyACM0
repeater.* hidden (board.node.role) — 'beebo settings repeater' shows it anyway.

A few things worth knowing about how the tree is organized:

  • Only leaves hold a value — categories like board, companion.radio, companion.node.transport are just groupings, and asking for one prints the subtree rather than a value.
  • The top-level namespace is the firmware struct that actually backs the value — board.* is genuinely single-instance, board-wide state (one physical board, not one per role); companion.*/repeater.* are each role's own fully independent, resident copy of everything in BeeboBasePrefs (radio params, transport enables, WiFi credentials, monitor flags, identity/behavior), addressed explicitly per role rather than "whichever role happens to be live" — asking for repeater.radio.lora.freq while companion is live still reads repeater's own stored value, not companion's. companion.*/repeater.* each nest further into radio.*, fem.*, monitor.*, routing.*, and node.* (identity/behavior leaves that aren't their own subsystem). console.* is the odd one out: it covers the CLI's own local config (the node alias's ~/.beebo/nodes/<alias>/profile.toml) plus the connected node's autosave flag, so reading/writing console.transport, console.tcp.host, etc. never opens a connection at all.
  • The whole-tree view hides the branch the live role can't use — a companion node hides repeater.* and vice versa; naming it explicitly (beebo settings repeater) still shows it.
  • board.node.role is multi_role firmware's companion/repeater role (companion or repeater). A change is persisted and the node reboots into the new role, so the connection drops; it has no -r/--raw equivalent — plain-text simple_repeater/companion_radio firmware predates the concept entirely, so this leaf is only reachable without -r; see Multi-Role: Switching Companion/Repeater for the details.
  • board.battery.*/board.state.quiet cover the battery-trend sample cadence (sample_period/sample_window, see Battery State of Charge) and a bench-only IR-drop test toggle (quiet) — shared identically between companion and repeater roles, since there's one physical VBAT ADC/battery per board, not one per role.
  • companion.node.transport.ble/tcp/usb/repeater.node.transport.ble/tcp/usb are each role's own persisted enables that decide which radios come up at boot when that role is live — the tree is where transports are switched.
  • companion.node.wifi.ssid/.wifi.password hold the WiFi credentials. They're independent leaves, and the password one is write-only — it never reads back, for obvious reasons.
  • repeater.* mirrors CommonCLI's own dotted keys for repeater-only preferences that have no companion-radio equivalent (repeater.node.repeat, repeater.node.name, repeater.admin.password, ...), plus repeater.routing.* for everything that shapes forwarding/routing behavior: the timing/collision-avoidance/duty-cycle knobs (rxdelay, airtime, dutycycle, txdelay, direct.txdelay, agc.reset.interval, interference.threshold) and the tuning settings listed below), plus flood-routing behavior (loop.detect, flood.max/.max_advert/.max_unscoped — see How a Repeater Routes). repeater.node.advert.interval/.advert.flood_interval (local vs flood advert timing) are presence/broadcast policy, not routing, so they stay outside repeater.routing.*. -r/--raw is only needed to reach a legacy simple_repeater node over CommonLink; a multi_role node exposes every repeater.* leaf over its normal binary connection regardless of which role it's currently running as, since the dedicated CMD_BEEBO sub-ids work independently of board.node.role.
  • companion.node.transmit / repeater.node.transmit {on|off}, default on: off makes the radio receive-only, with no forwards, adverts, ACKs or replies, and beebo cw is refused. Stricter than node.repeat, which only stops relaying. Per role and persisted; the repeater text CLI has get/set transmit. Setting it off over the mesh also silences the node's replies to that admin session, so use USB to turn it back on.

Setting a leaf is the same pattern everywhere — path, then new value:

$ beebo settings companion.radio.txpower 18
companion.radio.txpower = 18 dBm

$ beebo settings companion.node.transport.tcp off
companion.node.transport.tcp = off

The console.autosave option is special and is used to quickly change radio settings during experiment commands without continuously writing to flash avoiding unnecessary stress. Since console.autosave can hold changes in RAM before they hit flash, commit and restore are settings subcommands too — flush what's pending, or throw it away and reload from flash:

$ beebo settings commit
committed

$ beebo settings restore
restored

docs.title: On the node console
docs.text: The same command runs on the node itself, from the app's CLI screen or the beebo-cli channel: settings <path> reads, settings <path> <value> writes, and settings or settings <branch> lists the names below it. The console reaches the settings with a plain value (trial, routing, radio, FEM, battery, node and board settings); the role prefix is optional. Secrets, the composite settings and console.* need the beebo command line. Commands has the full list of what runs where.

docs.title: Tuning settings
docs.text:
Everything under repeater.routing.tuning.* belongs to the repeater role. On the CLI screen the repeater. prefix is optional. Trial settings are RAM-only and return to their defaults after a reboot.

Leaf What it sets Details trial.enabled Runs the trial sequence (on/off) Setting Trials trial.profile main (default, four switches) or exhaustive (twelve) Trial Reference trial.switches.<name>.enable and .values Whether a switch runs, and the values it tries (A first) Trial Reference trial.start stored (default) or list: where the sequence starts Trial Reference trial.combined One combined trial instead of one per switch Trial Reference trial.block_size_s, trial.block_count Block length and count (0 = planned by the node) Trial Reference trial.block_spread_pct Advanced: the block spread the first plan starts from Trial Reference trial.confidence_pct, trial.min_gain_pct How sure the node must be (90, 95 or 99), and the smallest gain worth taking Trial Reference trial.min_pkt_rate Events a minute a fixed schedule needs to start Trial Reference score.routed, score.delivered, score.received The weights of the score both tuners judge Scoring adaptive.enabled, adaptive.applied The adaptive tuner on/off, and which parameters it may change The Adaptive Tuner adaptive.window.min_s, adaptive.window.max_s Shortest and longest evaluation window, in seconds The Adaptive Tuner

beebo settings repeater.routing.tuning prints the live values with their ranges.

docs.title: Console Configuration
docs.text:
The console.* settings leaves cover the CLI's own local config, the node alias's ~/.beebo/nodes/<alias>/profile.toml (override the directory with $BEEBO_NODES_DIR; a bare beebo uses the alias beebo), separate from anything stored on the node. It's created with a commented template on first use:

default_transport = "tcp"   # ble | tcp | usb — used when none is given
log_level = "WARNING"       # DEBUG | INFO | WARNING | ERROR | CRITICAL
dbg_level = "L"             # minimum firmware debug severity `monitor debug` streams: H | M | L

[ble]
address = "scan"            # BLE MAC/name; "scan" discovers and picks a device

[tcp]
host = "beebo"               # host[:port]; default port is 5000

[usb]
port = "/dev/ttyACM0"       # COM6 on Windows

Every command shares one set of --ble/--tcp/--usb options, each pre-filled from this file as its default value. default_transport decides which one actually gets used when none of the three flags is typed on the command line — typing exactly one flag overrides it for that invocation, and typing more than one is an error. The chosen transport's own address/host/port then comes from its matching [ble]/[tcp]/[usb] entry unless overridden inline (e.g. --tcp other-node).

Because these values never touch the device, console.transport, console.ble.address, console.tcp.host, console.usb.port, console.log_level and console.dbg_level all read and write the toml file directly — get/set never open a connection:

$ beebo settings console.transport
console.transport = tcp  {ble|tcp|usb}

$ beebo settings console.transport tcp
console.transport = tcp

$ beebo settings console.tcp.host other-node
console.tcp.host = other-node

Note that console.autosave is the one console.* leaf that isn't local — it's the connected node's own autosave flag, round-tripped like any node.* setting (see commit/restore above).

docs.title: Settings Reference
docs.text: Every leaf of the beebo settings tree with its help text, range or choices, generated from the settings tree itself. For how the tree works see Settings. On the node's CLI screen the role prefix (companion. or repeater.) is optional and the live role is implied. companion.* and repeater.* hold each role's own copy of the settings they share.

docs.title: companion.routing
docs.text:
• companion.routing.airtime: Transmit budget [#] [0 to 9]. Scales the enforced wait between this node's transmissions; 0 is unthrottled, higher values ease congestion.
  • companion.routing.rxdelay: Base delay before relaying [s] [0 to 20]. Staggers repeats so neighbors that all heard a packet don't collide.
  • companion.routing.dutycycle: Airtime budget expressed as a channel-occupancy percent [%] [1 to 100]. A friendlier view of airtime; writes airtime_factor = 100/percent - 1.
  • companion.routing.seen_window: How long [seconds, fractional] [0 to 60] a repeat of a packet still counts as the same packet: a duplicate, or the echo of our own send that arrived after its echo window (credited as heard, so the confirm ratio and the trial scores do not charge a late echo as a failure; beebo analyze dup-latency sizes it). It also decides whether a dedup-table eviction counts as a live risk (beebo monitor status's rx_dedup_table_full row). Companion value; see repeater.routing.seen_window for the independent repeater copy. Stored as milliseconds. 0 turns the late credit and the live-eviction counting off (a real, literal setting, not a 'reset to default' sentinel); firmware default is 30.

docs.title: companion.fem
docs.text:
• companion.fem.rxgain: Front-end module RX gain / LNA — {on|off}. Switches the FEM's low-noise amplifier into the receive path for better weak-signal sensitivity, at a little extra receive current. Distinct from the SX1262's own boosted gain (radio.rxgain); only present on boards whose FEM supports it. This role's own independent copy -- see companion.fem.rxgain/repeater.fem.rxgain.
  • companion.fem.txgain: Front-end module TX gain / PA — {on|off}. Software-selectable external FEM transmit gain; not a PA power switch. Only present on boards whose FEM supports it. This role's own independent copy -- see companion.fem.txgain/repeater.fem.txgain.

docs.title: companion.radio
docs.text:
• companion.radio.lora.freq: Carrier frequency [MHz] [137 to 1020]. Must sit in a band legal for your region and match the nodes you talk to directly.
  • companion.radio.lora.bw: Channel bandwidth [kHz] [7.8, 10.4, 15.6, 20.8, 31.25, 41.7, 62.5, 125, 250, 500]. Wider is faster but less sensitive; must match the nodes you talk to directly.
  • companion.radio.lora.sf: Spreading factor [#] [5 to 12]. Higher reaches further but is slower; must match the nodes you talk to directly.
  • companion.radio.lora.cr: Coding rate denominator [#] [5 to 8] (4/N). More redundancy survives noise but costs throughput.
  • companion.radio.lora.preset: Named community-suggested freq/bw/sf/cr quadruplet for a region (from presets.json, mirroring meshcore.nz's own app config) — reading reports the matching preset title or '(custom)' if the live quadruplet doesn't match any of them; writing applies all four fields from the named preset at once, e.g. 'beebo settings companion.radio.lora.preset "USA/Canada"'.
  • companion.radio.txpower: Output power at the PA [dBm] [-9 to board max].
  • companion.radio.rxgain: SX1262 RX boosted-gain mode for weak-signal reception — {on|off}. Independent of the FEM/LNA (fem.rxgain). This role's own independent copy -- see companion.radio.rxgain/repeater.radio.rxgain.
  • companion.radio.cad: Hardware channel activity detection before each transmit — {on|off}. This role's own independent copy -- see companion.radio.cad/repeater.radio.cad.
  • companion.radio.allowed_repeat_freq: Frequency ranges [MHz] this node is allowed to repeat on (read-only). Companion-only: it doesn't apply under repeater role, which has its own (currently unexposed) frequency config.

docs.title: companion.monitor
docs.text:
• companion.monitor.enabled: Global capture switch — {on|off}. Pause/resume the ring by toggling this.
  • companion.monitor.rx: Capture RX records — {on|off}.
  • companion.monitor.tx: Capture TX records — {on|off}.
  • companion.monitor.radio: Capture RADIO reference records (config changes) — {on|off}.
  • companion.monitor.env: Capture ENV reference records (noise/battery/heap) — {on|off}.
  • companion.monitor.batt: Capture BATT records (every Vbat sample, idle/forced + trend state) — {on|off}.
  • companion.monitor.tuning: Capture tuning records — {on|off}: the adaptive tuner's proposals (tuner), the evaluation windows (eval) and the A/B trials (trial).
  • companion.monitor.path: RX path mode — {on|off}: an RX record's nbr holds the last three hops of its path, one byte each (the first byte of each hash), instead of the last hop's identity. Off by default. With 2- and 3-byte hashes two neighbors can share a byte.
  • companion.monitor.event: Capture EVENT records (fault transitions and other notable state changes, timestamped instead of a bare sticky flag) — {on|off}. On by default. Same bit as setting/command/route/debug below (see their own help) -- toggling any of the five toggles all five.
  • companion.monitor.setting: Capture SETTING records (admin-visible setting changes) — {on|off}. Alias of event -- same bit, no independent toggle (see its help).
  • companion.monitor.command: Capture COMMAND records (admin commands run) — {on|off}. Alias of event -- same bit, no independent toggle (see its help).
  • companion.monitor.route: Capture ROUTE records (periodic routing-latency snapshot) — {on|off}. Alias of event -- same bit, no independent toggle (see its help).
  • companion.monitor.debug: Capture DEBUG records (folded-in RLOG transport/boot/session trace) — {on|off}. Alias of event -- same bit, no independent toggle (see its help).

docs.title: companion.profile
docs.text: • companion.profile.enabled: Enable/disable ProfileLog (command/span latency profiling ring, see beebo profile) — {on|off}. Off by default; inactive until turned on explicitly. Distinct from monitor.* (MonRing's own capture config) -- ProfileLog measures span duration, a separate concern. This role's own independent copy -- see companion.profile.enabled/repeater.profile.enabled.

docs.title: companion.node
docs.text:
• companion.node.coords: Companion's own PREFS-mode advertised coordinates [deg] (used when adv_loc_policy=2/prefs), as 'LAT,LON' -- distinct from repeater.coords (repeater_settings.py, a separate /beebo_repeater field) and from the shared, role-agnostic live-GPS SHARE register (no CLI leaf -- no GPS hardware on beebo, so SHARE always advertises 0,0).
  • companion.node.multi_acks: Whether companion sends multiple ACKs for multi-path replies [#] -- distinct from repeater.multi_acks (repeater_settings.py, a separate /beebo_repeater field).
  • companion.node.path_hash_mode: Path hash length used for companion's new contacts [0=1 byte, 1=2 bytes, 2=3 bytes] -- distinct from repeater.path_hash_mode (repeater_settings.py, a separate /beebo_repeater field).
  • companion.node.name: This node's advertised name (companion persona).
  • companion.node.region.scope: Default flood-advert scope name (channel messages fall back to this scope when none is given); 'none' clears it. Companion's own field (NodePrefs.default_scope_key, stock companion_radio's only scoping mechanism -- it has no RegionMap at all) -- unrelated to repeater.node.region.default, which is repeater's own independent RegionMap default_id.
  • companion.node.adv_loc_policy: Location advertising policy [0=none, 1=share, 2=prefs].
  • companion.node.manual_add_contacts: Whether new contacts must be manually approved — {on|off}.
  • companion.node.autoadd_config: Bitmask of contact types auto-added when manual_add_contacts is off [hex] (1=overwrite, 2=chat/client, 4=repeater, 8=room, 16=sensor). Set with a raw bitmask (e.g. 0x07) or a comma-separated flag name list (e.g. "chat,repeater"); read with no value for a table of which flags are set.
  • companion.node.telemetry.base: Telemetry advertising mode for base [#] [0 to 3].
  • companion.node.telemetry.loc: Telemetry advertising mode for loc [#] [0 to 3].
  • companion.node.telemetry.env: Telemetry advertising mode for env [#] [0 to 3].
  • companion.node.repeat: Whether this node relays other nodes' flood traffic while in companion role — {on|off} (_prefs.client_repeat, CMD_SET_RADIO_PARAMS's trailing byte). Distinct from repeater.repeat, which maps to a different field entirely (the repeater role's own forwarding toggle, disable_fwd) -- this one only matters while board.node.role is companion. Read via CMD_DEVICE_QUERY (stock meshcore's repeat field, fw_ver >= 9); written by re-sending freq/bw/sf/cr from self_info alongside the new value, since CMD_SET_RADIO_PARAMS rewrites all five at once.
  • companion.node.public_key: Companion's own Ed25519 public key (read-only) -- distinct from repeater.node.public_key (repeater_settings.py).
  • companion.node.tz_offset: Hours from UTC [-12 to +14], stored for the app's CLI (get/set tz.offset); nothing on the node uses it. This role's own independent copy -- see companion.node.tz_offset/repeater.node.tz_offset.
  • companion.node.transmit: Whether the radio sends anything — {on|off}. Off is receive-only: no forwards, adverts, ACKs or replies, and beebo cw is refused; stricter than node.repeat, which only stops relaying. This role's own independent copy -- see companion.node.transmit/repeater.node.transmit.
  • companion.node.transport.ble: Whether this role brings up BLE at boot — {on|off}. This role's own independent copy -- see node.transport.* for the general semantics (live-apply behavior, ble/tcp mutual exclusion, usb fallback).
  • companion.node.transport.tcp: Whether this role brings up TCP at boot — {on|off}. This role's own independent copy -- see node.transport.* for the general semantics (live-apply behavior, ble/tcp mutual exclusion, usb fallback).
  • companion.node.transport.usb: Whether this role brings up USB at boot — {on|off}. This role's own independent copy -- see node.transport.* for the general semantics (live-apply behavior, ble/tcp mutual exclusion, usb fallback).
  • companion.node.wifi.ssid: WiFi network name (SSID) the node joins to offer the TCP companion transport. This role's own independent copy -- see companion.node.wifi.ssid/repeater.node.wifi.ssid.
  • companion.node.wifi.password: WiFi password, write-only (see node.wifi.password's help for why). This role's own independent copy. (write-only, prompts for the value)
  • companion.node.wifi.ip: Current WiFi station IP address, assigned at run time by DHCP once the node joins its configured network -- read-only. Not really a per-role value (there's one physical WiFi radio, whichever role is live) -- companion.node.wifi.ip/repeater.node.wifi.ip both read the same run-time cache regardless of role. Empty means WiFi is off or the node hasn't associated yet.
  • companion.node.wifi.rssi: Current WiFi STA RSSI in dBm -- read-only, same run-time/role-agnostic shape as node.wifi.ip. No BLE equivalent: BLE RSSI can't be read synchronously on this hardware without racing a live BLE teardown (see fw's SerialBLEInterface::requestHealthSample() comment), so it isn't exposed at all. WIFI_RSSI_UNAVAILABLE (127) means WiFi is off or the node hasn't associated yet.
